Collective Licensing for Gen AI Training: Feasible or Flawed? – Part 1

# Collective Licensing for Gen AI Training: Feasible or Flawed? – Part 1

![Image created by AI](https://legalblogs.wolterskluwer.com/copyright-blog/uploads/sites/49/styles/large_16_9/public/2026/05/Image%20Part%201.png.webp?itok=O_5s6SQv)

On 10 March 2026, the European Parliament adopted a [resolution on copyright and generative AI](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/TA-10-2026-0066_EN.html) urging the EU Commission to clarify and potentially update the existing copyright framework for generative AI (GenAI), facilitate voluntary collective licensing agreements, propose full transparency obligations for AI providers and establish a rebuttable presumption of infringement where those obligations are not met, while also calling on the EUIPO to become the trusted intermediary to manage rightsholder opt-outs. As the Commission prepares to [review the CDSM Directive](https://digital-strategy.ec.europa.eu/en/funding/copyright-dsm-directive-commission-launches-call-tenders-study-support-review-directive) no sooner than June 2026, statutory licensing and collective rights management could now be on the agenda as a potential fix. But can it deliver?

This blog post series examines potential collective licensing models and finds that each carries significant structural limitations. Part 1 of this blog post will explain why the existing text and data mining (TDM) exceptions framework falls short and will explore voluntary and statutory collective licensing. Part 2 of this blog post will turn to extended collective licensing before concluding with reflections on the most effective and least disruptive paths forward.

**Why the TDM framework falls short**

Article 4 of the [CDSM Directive](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/legal-content/EN/TXT/?uri=CELEX%3A32019L0790) permits commercial text and data mining subject to a rightsholder opt-out. In practice, the opt-out mechanism is widely considered to fall short (see for example [Senftleben](https://legalblogs.wolterskluwer.com/copyright-blog/the-tdm-opt-out-in-the-eu-five-problems-one-solution/), [Mezei](https://ssrn.com/abstract=4695119), or the [EU Parliament`s March 2026 resolution](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/TA-10-2026-0066_EN.html)). Namely, there is no standardised format for machine-readable opt-outs, rightsholders have multiple imperfect means of expressing reservations, while developers face serious difficulty reliably detecting them across numerous individual signals across jurisdictions. Technical measures such as robots.txt or metadata flags depend on voluntary crawler compliance (while empirical [studies](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.21733) suggest many crawlers ignore them entirely), lack granularity and may block legitimate uses such as search indexing (for more details, see [Hamman](https://www.jipitec.eu/jipitec/article/view/407), [Havlikova](https://www.jipitec.eu/jipitec/article/view/422) or [Löbling](https://www.jipitec.eu/jipitec/article/view/16)). National implementation has fragmented the picture further, with courts in [Germany](https://legalblogs.wolterskluwer.com/copyright-blog/copyright-in-formaldehyde-how-gema-v-openai-freezes-doctrine-and-chills-ai-part-1/), the [Netherlands](https://ipkitten.blogspot.com/2025/02/dutch-court-holds-that-tdm-opt-out-must.html), and [Hungary](https://legalblogs.wolterskluwer.com/copyright-blog/do-ai-models-dream-of-dolphins-in-lake-balaton/) reaching divergent conclusions on what constitutes a valid opt-out. Fundamentally, the opt-out model offers only a binary choice: exclusion or uncompensated use. Individual licensing contracts are possible in theory but unworkable for individual authors at the scale AI training requires - leaving a gap that serves neither creators nor the goal of a functioning licensing market for AI training data.

Compounding this, the TDM exception does not address what happens after training of a model. Some empirical studies show that GenAI models can "[memorise](https://www.muni.cz/en/research/publications/2491502)" and "[regurgitate](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.07646)" verbatim snippets of training data -  a risk the [Munich Court](https://www.justiz.bayern.de/gerichte-und-behoerden/landgericht/muenchen-1/presse/2025/11.php) found capable of constituting copyright infringement in its [GEMA v. OpenAI ruling](https://legalblogs.wolterskluwer.com/copyright-blog/copyright-in-formaldehyde-how-gema-v-openai-freezes-doctrine-and-chills-ai-part-1/). Even state-of-the-art mitigation techniques such as [deduplication](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.06499) and [filtering](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.17546) cannot fully eliminate this risk. These gaps have pushed major AI developers toward individual licensing deals – for example, [study issued by the British Film Institute](https://www.bfi.org.uk/industry-data-insights/reports/ai-screen-sector-perspectives-paths-forward) reports that over 79 such agreements were signed globally between March 2023 and February 2025 - but this route is only viable for well-capitalised players, creating a two-tier market at odds with the CDSM Directive's goal of a level playing field.

**Voluntary collective licensing: a useful but insufficient complement**

Voluntary collective licensing - where rightsholders authorise a CMO to negotiate and enforce licences on their behalf - requires no legislative reform and can coexist with the Article 4 exception. Early efforts exist: Swedish CMO [STIM announced launch](https://www.stim.se/en/news/stim-launches-the-worlds-first-ai-license-for-music) of what it described as the world's first collective AI license for music in September 2025; the [Copyright Clearance Center](https://www.copyright.com/media-press-releases/ccc-pioneers-collective-licensing-solution-for-content-usage-in-internal-ai-systems/) introduced a Collective AI License in the US; and the [CLA announced](https://cla.co.uk/development-of-cla-generative-ai-licence/) a Generative AI Training Licence in the UK.

Yet the 2025 [EU Council questionnaire](https://data.consilium.europa.eu/doc/document/ST-10355-2025-REV-1/en/pdf) reveals that "*licensing of protected works by CMOs for the purpose of AI-training remains rare in the EU*." The fundamental problem is scalability: the scheme can only cover those rightsholders who are aware of it and choose to participate. Smaller and independent creators - precisely those most at risk from AI market disruption - often lack the knowledge, time, or administrative capacity to join. As a result, the licensed catalogue remains incomplete and cannot provide the legal certainty developers need. In the context, of voluntary licensing, CMOs also lack sufficient bargaining power when facing major AI companies that can negotiate directly with large content suppliers.

The [EU Parliament`s March 2026 resolution](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/TA-10-2026-0066_EN.html) highlighted voluntary licensing as a potential solution, calling for sector-based collective licensing agreements and assigning the EUIPO responsibility for supporting that process - steps that would certainly help mitigate some of these shortcomings.

**Statutory licensing and mandatory collective management: proportionality problems**

With the increasing number of copyright disputes, policymakers and scholars have floated statutory or mandatory collective licensing as a potential solution (for example [Geiger and Iaia](https://ssrn.com/abstract=4594873) and [Lucchi](https://www.europarl.europa.eu/RegData/etudes/STUD/2025/774095/IUST_STU(2025)774095_EN.pdf)). Such regimes risk reducing authors’ freedom to a mere claim for remuneration while stripping the authors of the freedom to decide whether to license or not. Although [mandatory collective management](https://www.elgaronline.com/edcollchap/edcoll/9781785361425/9781785361425.00022.xml) enables the CMO (as the licensor) to refuse granting a license, this element of discretion is absent in statutory licensing and limitation-based remuneration schemes.

When measured against the Berne three-step test, these schemes face significant legal headwinds.

A statutory license covering virtually any work capable of being ingested into a training dataset - although having a narrow purpose and group of beneficiaries - risks failing the condition of being limited to “*certain special cases*”. In interpreting the TRIPs Agreement version of the text, a [WTO Panel](https://www.wto.org/english/tratop_e/dispu_e/1234da.pdf) required exceptions to be clearly defined and narrow in scope - and the broad quantitative reach of AI training is problematic on that reading. That said, existing exceptions like private copying also affect large volumes of works yet survive this scrutiny; the decisive factor is whether eligible uses are framed with sufficient conceptual precision as to purpose, nature, and scope. Whether a statutory license for a GenAI training scheme would pass that test depends heavily on how narrowly those parameters would be drawn.

On the second step (*conflict with normal exploitation of the work*), much depends on the scope of rights covered. A regime limited to reproduction rights - permitting ingestion (i.e. reproduction) without authorising onward dissemination (i.e. communication to the public) - is more likely to satisfy the condition, since the revenue attributable to any single work within a vast training dataset is unlikely to constitute exploitation of "[*considerable economic or practical importance*](https://www.wto.org/english/tratop_e/dispu_e/1234da.pdf)" As [Senftleben](https://ssrn.com/abstract=5373903) noted, the benchmark should be the commercialisation of the individual work. Given the enormous number of works in a typical training dataset, the revenue attributable to any single work is likely too small to constitute "considerable economic importance" to its rightsholder. The calculus shifts if the regime extends to dissemination and communication to the public, where AI-generated outputs could directly compete with rightsholders' own markets. However, while limiting the regime to reproduction rights may satisfy the second step, it reintroduces the data memorisation and regurgitation problem (as explained by [Mezei](https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/papers.cfm?abstract_id=5404367) or [Havlikova](https://www.muni.cz/vyzkum/publikace/2491502)) - leaving AI developers without sufficient certainty to rely on such a regime without seeking additional licenses.

On the third step (*unreasonable prejudice to rightsholders' legitimate interests*), [Senftleben](https://ssrn.com/abstract=5373903) has aptly concluded that equitable remuneration can prevent unreasonable prejudice, and that even a broad exception may satisfy this condition if compensation is adequate and opt-out rights are preserved. But statutory licensing goes further than the TDM exception: it removes authors' ability to refuse use altogether, converting exclusive rights into bare remuneration claims. A scheme that strips authors of any ability to exclude objectionable uses risks crossing the proportionality threshold regardless of the compensation offered.

Taken together, these considerations reveal a structural tension: a statutory licensing regime which would be narrow enough to satisfy the three-step test would likely be too restrictive to offer AI developers meaningful legal certainty, while one broad enough to serve that purpose would struggle to meet the test's cumulative conditions, not to mention that such framework would likely require either an expansion of the existing TDM exception or the introduction of a new exception covering subsequent communicative uses.

Not to mention that - as [Senftleben](https://ssrn.com/abstract=4964460) cautioned - upfront remuneration imposes costs at the wrong stage of the value chain, potentially impeding the AI innovation these regimes are meant to enable.

**To be continued ... see Part 2.**

# How ‘learnrights’ would compensate creators for AI model training

By

**What you’ll learn:** U.S. law hasn’t determined whether using copyrighted content to train AI models is fair use or infringement. Three researchers make the case for “learnright” laws that would give copyright holders the right to license their content for AI training and claim some share in the revenues coming from generative AI systems.

Human content creators are protected by copyright law, in part to ensure that they’re fairly compensated for their work.

But whether these laws allow artificial intelligence models to learn from human-created content is up for debate — both in court and on Capitol Hill. Encyclopedia Britannica’s [lawsuit against OpenAI](https://www.reuters.com/legal/litigation/encyclopedia-britannica-sues-openai-over-ai-training-2026-03-16/), for example, is one of the latest allegations of misuse of reference materials. Meanwhile, the U.S. Copyright Office has not made a binding determination about whether using copyrighted works to train AI models is fair use.

To deal with these issues, in 2023 MIT Sloan School of Management professor [Thomas Malone](https://cci.mit.edu/malone/) proposed [“learnright” laws](https://news.bloomberglaw.com/us-law-week/ai-will-profit-from-artists-but-new-learnright-laws-could-help) that would give copyright holders the exclusive right to license their content to AI companies for model training.

“Copyright law wasn’t designed for a world with generative AI, and without something like learnright laws, the incentives for people to create new content are likely to be greatly reduced,” said Malone, who is also the director of the [MIT Center for Collective Intelligence](https://cci.mit.edu/).

In a more recent article, Malone and co-authors [Frank Pasquale](https://www.lawschool.cornell.edu/faculty-research/faculty-directory/frank-pasquale/) of Cornell Law School and [Andrew Ting](https://www.law.gwu.edu/andrew-s-h-ting) of George Washington University Law School [outlined the argument for learnrights](https://scholarlycommons.law.northwestern.edu/njtip/vol23/iss1/3/) and described how they could work legally, economically, and practically.

## **AI and copyright pose thorny legal questions**

U.S. copyright law lets content creators charge others a fee to copy their work, and this potential for profit motivates creators to produce valuable content. But copyright law does not prevent humans from learning from copyrighted material and then producing content of their own that’s different from the original. This is generally referred to as a kind of “fair use,” and it’s permissible under the law.

The problem is that copyright law did not anticipate technologies like generative AI models that can learn from massive amounts of content at a scale no human could ever hope to match. That ability allows AI systems to generate new content that isn’t a direct copy of the original material but couldn’t be generated at all without it. Generative AI providers claim that this is fair use. But [dozens of copyright owners have sued generative AI providers](https://copyrightalliance.org/ai-copyright-lawsuit-developments-2025/), alleging that the resulting output is a derivative work that infringes on their original copyright.

[Past copyright cases](https://www.congress.gov/crs-product/LSB10922) (including ones involving [Anthropic](https://www.npr.org/2025/06/25/nx-s1-5445242/federal-rules-in-ai-companys-favor-in-landmark-copyright-infringement-lawsuit-authors-bartz-graeber-wallace-johnson-anthropic) and [Meta](https://www.wired.com/story/meta-scores-victory-ai-copyright-case/)) suggest that fair use is flexible and contextual, depending on factors like whether the new content affects the potential market value for the copyrighted work.

But none of these cases has completely resolved the legal issues, and no generative AI cases have reached the Supreme Court. The question of the livelihood of creators in a world of AI-driven content remains unanswered.

## **Licensing content for AI training**

Enter learnright. Rather than expanding fair use to include AI learning, learnright is an exclusive right to license copyrighted content for AI training. As Malone and his co-authors write, “there are substantial grounds for predicting that a robust market for learnrights, with reasonable and fair licensing fees, would emerge.”

Then, they argue, generative AI providers could explicitly obtain legal licenses to train their AI models using content created by others, and the creators of that content would be fairly compensated.

Malone, Pasquale, and Ting outline an opt-in program through which creators would register their copyrighted content and AI companies could obtain a license from the creator to use it. AI companies would negotiate compensation either with the creators themselves or with the creators’ literary or artistic agents.

The authors assert that working with agents would benefit both sides: AI companies would negotiate with far fewer entities, and agents would likely have a better sense of market value than individual creators would. Additionally, an opt-in model is more favorable than automatically providing learnright coverage to any copyrighted material, which is impractical and could lead to learnright protections for content of little value.

## **Benefits of learnright**

Malone and his co-authors presented three arguments that support compensating copyright holders whose work is used to train generative AI.

Some argue that giving AI models free, broad access to content will lead to better-performing and more diverse AI systems. The authors contend that this isn’t likely to work in the long term because it would erode the incentives for people to create new content in the future.

“In short, learnright law is a promising way for both content creators and AI providers to benefit in a flourishing information marketplace,” Malone said.

"In short, learnright law is a promising way for both content creators and AI providers to benefit in a flourishing information marketplace," Malone said. "there are substantial grounds for predicting that a robust market for learnrights, with reasonable and fair licensing fees, would emerge," write Malone and co-authors.
args.summary: This MIT Sloan article explores 'learnright' laws proposed by Professor Thomas Malone and co-authors Frank Pasquale and Andrew Ting to address the unresolved legal question of whether using copyrighted content to train AI models constitutes fair use or infringement. The U.S. Copyright Office has not made a binding determination, and no generative AI cases have reached the Supreme Court. Learnright would give copyright holders the exclusive right to license their content to AI companies for model training, rather than expanding fair use to include AI learning. The authors outline an opt-in program where creators register copyrighted content and AI companies negotiate compensation either directly or through literary/artistic agents, arguing this would create a robust licensing market. They contend that without such laws, incentives for human content creation will be greatly reduced, and that learnright benefits both creators and AI providers in a flourishing information marketplace.

Stability AI, Ltd.** (Case No. 3:25-cv-06891), filed in the **U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California** on **August 14, 2025**. The case is assigned to **Judge Trina L. Thompson**, with discovery referred to **Magistrate Judge Sallie Kim**. The cause of action is **17 U.S.C. § 501 Copyright Infringement**, and the plaintiff has demanded a jury trial.

**Key Events Chronology:**

- **Aug 14, 2025**: Getty Images filed a Complaint against Stability AI, Ltd., Stability AI, Inc., and Stability AI US Services Corporation, along with exhibits and motions for pro hac vice admission for attorneys Benjamin Marks, Jared Friedmann, and Brian Liegel.
- **Aug 20, 2025**: Waivers of service were executed by all three defendants (answer due Oct 14, 2025). The case was reassigned from Magistrate Judge Lisa J. Cisneros to Judge Trina L. Thompson after plaintiff declined magistrate judge jurisdiction.
- **Oct 14, 2025**: Defendants (Stability AI entities) filed a **Motion to Dismiss** the complaint.
- **Oct 28, 2025**: Getty filed its opposition to the motion to dismiss.
- **Nov 4, 2025**: Defendants filed their reply in support of dismissal.
- **Nov 13, 2025**: The court issued a **Case Management and Scheduling Order**, setting: Fact Discovery close by 9/18/2026; Expert Discovery by 2/12/2027; Dispositive Motions due by 3/12/2027; Final Pretrial Conference on 12/2/2027; and **Jury Trial set for 1/18/2028 – 2/9/2028** (14-day estimated length).
- **Jan 21, 2026**: The court granted a joint stipulation continuing the motion to dismiss hearing from Feb 10 to **Apr 7, 2026**.
- **Apr 7, 2026**: Motion hearing held; taken under submission.
- **Apr 23, 2026**: **Order GRANTING IN PART AND DENYING IN PART** the motion to dismiss (Doc. 53).
- **May 5, 2026**: Case referred to Magistrate Judge Sallie Kim for discovery purposes.
- **May 21, 2026**: Defendants filed their **Answer to the Complaint**.
- **Jul 2, 2026**: Defendants filed an **Amended Answer**.
- **Aug 6-12, 2026**: The most recent filings involve administrative motions related to the case (Docs. 68-71).

The parties were referred to private ADR, with mediation to be completed by 10/19/2026. The case is actively proceeding through discovery, with a further case management conference scheduled for Nov 5, 2026.

<webpage_content>
Decided in part — UK Active in U.S.

# Getty Images v. Stability AI

A dual-front fight: a six-week UK High Court trial decided in November 2025 and a parallel U.S. federal action — dismissed in Delaware and refiled in the Northern District of California in August 2025 — over the training and outputs of Stable Diffusion.

🏛️ UK High Court (Chancery)· N.D. Cal. (3:25-cv-06891) — refiled from D. Del.· Filed Jan-Feb 2023; U.S. refiled Aug 2025

## Case summary

Plaintiff
:   Getty Images (US), Inc. and Getty Images International

Defendant
:   Stability AI Ltd. (UK), Stability AI, Inc., and Stability AI US Services Corporation

Courts
:   UK High Court of Justice (Chancery Division) · U.S. District Court, Northern District of California (refiled from D. Del.)

Filed
:   January 17, 2023 (UK); February 3, 2023 (D. Del., later dismissed); refiled August 14, 2025 (N.D. Cal., 3:25-cv-06891)

Judges
:   Mrs Justice Joanna Smith DBE (UK) · Hon. Trina L. Thompson (N.D. Cal.)

Trial
:   June–July 2025 (UK), six weeks before Mrs Justice Joanna Smith

UK ruling
:   November 4, 2025 — [2025] EWHC 2863 (Ch). Secondary copyright claim rejected; limited trademark infringement found on watermark reproduction. Getty granted leave to appeal December 16, 2025.

U.S. status
:   Active in N.D. Cal. following August 2025 refile

Claim types
:   Copyright infringement · database right · trademark · passing off · §1202 (U.S.) · Lanham Act

## TL;DR

Mixed — UK decided 2025 (Getty granted appeal); U.S. refiled in N.D. Cal.

Getty alleged Stability scraped roughly 12 million Getty-licensed images to train Stable Diffusion. The UK case narrowed sharply at trial; the U.S. action was voluntarily dismissed in Delaware in August 2025 and refiled the same day in the Northern District of California.

* FiledJan/Feb 2023UK · D. Del.
* UK trialJun-Jul 2025Smith, J.
* UK rulingNov 4 2025[2025] EWHC 2863 (Ch); appeal granted Dec 16
* U.S. statusActiveN.D. Cal. 3:25-cv-06891 (Thompson, J.)

The UK High Court rejected the theory that Stable Diffusion's model weights are themselves "infringing copies" stored in the UK, but found limited trademark infringement and passing off because outputs reproduced recognizable Getty and iStock watermarks. Getty was granted leave to appeal in December 2025. In the U.S., Getty voluntarily dismissed the Delaware action (1:23-cv-00135) on August 14, 2025 after Stability argued the court lacked jurisdiction over its UK parent, and refiled the same day in the Northern District of California (3:25-cv-06891) before Judge Trina L. Thompson, advancing direct copyright, DMCA §1202, and Lanham Act trademark claims.

## Why it matters

* **The "model weights are infringing copies" theory failed in the UK.** The court held weights are not themselves copies of the training images. That ruling will be cited by every defendant facing a similar theory.
* **Trademark survives where copyright did not.** Stable Diffusion's reproduction of Getty's watermarks gave the court a clean trademark/passing-off basis to find liability — a roadmap for rights holders whose marks are visible on training data.
* **Territorial scope matters.** The UK court's reluctance to find UK-located infringement based on extraterritorial training shifts strategic value to forums where training itself occurred.
* **The N.D. Cal. refile is the next U.S. test.** After voluntary dismissal in Delaware and refile as 3:25-cv-06891 before Judge Trina L. Thompson, a U.S. ruling on §1202 and direct infringement will bear on every image-generation case.

## Related cases

[**Bartz v. Anthropic**NDCA · $1.5B settlement](../bartz-v-anthropic/) [**Andersen v. Stability AI**NDCA · Active (public docket)](https://www.courtlistener.com/?q=Andersen+Stability&type=r) [**GEMA v. OpenAI**Munich · Output reproduction](../gema-v-openai/)

## More to come

Full N.D. Cal. docket tracker, the UK appellate posture, and a side-by-side of the U.S. and UK holdings coming soon. [Sign up for ruling alerts](../../pro/alerts/) to be notified when the next major U.S. or UK opinion drops.

## Getty v. Stability — frequently asked questions

What is Getty v. Stability about?

Getty Images sued Stability AI in both the UK and the United States over Stable Diffusion training on Getty's copyrighted images. The UK High Court decided the case on November 4, 2025 ([2025] EWHC 2863 (Ch)) — rejecting the central "model weights as infringing copies" theory but finding limited trademark infringement on Getty watermarks reproduced in generated images. Getty was granted leave to appeal in December 2025. The original Delaware action was voluntarily dismissed on August 14, 2025 and refiled the same day in the Northern District of California as 3:25-cv-06891.

  What court is Getty v. Stability in?

Getty v. Stability is now in the UK High Court of Justice (Chancery Division), docket IL-2023-000007 / [2025] EWHC 2863 (Ch), before Mrs Justice Joanna Smith DBE; and in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California, docket 3:25-cv-06891, before Hon. Trina L. Thompson — refiled August 14, 2025 after voluntary dismissal of the original Delaware action (1:23-cv-00135).

  What is the current status?

Status: UK — decided November 4, 2025 ([2025] EWHC 2863 (Ch)); Getty granted leave to appeal December 16, 2025. U.S. — active in the Northern District of California (3:25-cv-06891) following the August 2025 refile from Delaware. The UK court rejected the secondary-infringement theory but found limited trademark infringement based on watermark reproduction in Stable Diffusion outputs.

  Where can I find the docket?

The current U.S. docket (3:25-cv-06891, N.D. Cal.) is on [Justia](https://dockets.justia.com/docket/california/candce/3:2025cv06891/454636). The original Delaware docket is on [CourtListener](https://www.courtlistener.com/docket/66801014/getty-images-us-inc-v-stability-ai-ltd/). The UK judgment is published by the [judiciary](https://www.judiciary.uk/wp-content/uploads/2025/11/Getty-Images-v-Stability-AI.pdf). args.summary: Getty Images v. Stability AI is a dual-front legal battle (UK and U.S.) over the training of Stable Diffusion on approximately 12 million Getty-licensed images. The UK High Court decided the case on November 4, 2025 ([2025] EWHC 2863 (Ch)), rejecting the theory that model weights constitute "infringing copies" but finding limited trademark infringement and passing off where Stable Diffusion outputs reproduced recognizable Getty and iStock watermarks. Getty was granted leave to appeal on December 16, 2025. In the U.S., Getty voluntarily dismissed the original Delaware action on August 14, 2025 after Stability challenged jurisdiction, and refiled the same day in the Northern District of California (3:25-cv-06891) before Judge Trina L. Thompson, advancing direct copyright, DMCA §1202, and Lanham Act trademark claims. The UK case was tried over six weeks before Mrs Justice Joanna Smith DBE (June–July 2025). The case is significant because the "model weights are infringing copies" theory failed in the UK (a precedent likely cited by other defendants), trademark liability survived where copyright did not, territorial scope was a key issue, and the N.D. Cal. refile represents the next major U.S. test for image-generation AI litigation.

# Trademark Law Meets Generative AI: Key Takeaways from the Getty v. Stability AI Ruling

#### Get in touch

A federal court ruling recently confirmed that AI generated content may not be immune from trademark liability. In August 2025, Getty Images filed its complaint against Stability AI in the Northern District of California, alleging that Stability AI unlawfully copied and used millions of Getty images and associated metadata to train and commercialize its AI models. In addition to bringing copyright claims, Getty also brought Lanham Act claims of trademark infringement, false designation of origin, and dilution, alleging that the outputs produced by Stability AI—which may bear distorted versions of the Getty watermark—are likely to cause consumer confusion as to the source of the image. Stability AI moved to dismiss all Lanham Act claims, but on April 23, 2026, the court denied the motion. The court found that Getty’s allegations that Stability AI is a direct competitor, along with reports of users encountering AI generated images bearing distorted Getty watermarks were sufficient to support a reasonable inference of likely consumer confusion. As to false designation of origin, the court concluded that Stability AI's commercially distributed AI generated images constituted “goods” under the Lanham Act, and that the presence of distorted Getty watermarks without attribution to Getty could mislead consumers as to the image’s source or affiliation. The court also allowed Getty's dilution claims to proceed, finding that Getty had sufficiently alleged its marks were “famous” based on decades of nationwide use, extensive advertising and media exposure, and a large global customer base.  Going forward, the case may help define how traditional trademark principles apply to the commercial outputs of generative AI systems, particularly where altered marks appear in the AI generated content.

![](https://image-processor-storage.s3.us-west-2.amazonaws.com/images/e384d9b7f477dff91ddf84277f43bd8a/abstract-gradient-background-with-delicate-waves.jpg)

**NEW YORK, November 4, 2025** – [Getty Images](http://www.gettyimages.com) (NYSE: GETY), a preeminent global visual content creator and marketplace, today issued the following statement on the ruling of its litigation against Stability AI in the UK:  
  
*Today’s ruling confirms that Stable Diffusion’s inclusion of Getty Images’ trademarks in AI‑generated outputs infringed those trademarks. Crucially, the Court rejected Stability AI’s attempt to hold the user responsible for that infringement, confirming that responsibility for the presence of such trademarks lies with the model provider, who has control over the images used to train the model. This is a significant win for intellectual property owners.*  
  
*The ruling delivered another key finding; that, wherever the training and development did take place, Getty Images' copyright‑protected works were used to train Stable Diffusion. The ruling also established a powerful precedent that intangible articles, such as AI models, are subject to copyright infringement claims in the same way as tangible articles. We will be taking forward findings of fact from the UK ruling in our US case.*  
  
*Beyond the specifics of the decision, we remain deeply concerned that even well‑resourced companies such as Getty Images face significant challenges in protecting their creative works given the lack of transparency requirements. We invested millions of pounds to reach this point with only one provider that we need to continue to pursue in another venue. We urge governments, including the UK, to establish stronger transparency rules which are essential to prevent costly legal battles and to allow creators to protect their rights.*

# *Getty Images v. Stability AI*: Intellectual Property Rights in the Age of Generative AI

November 14, 2025

[Download PDF](/epc/print?AdvisoryID=192680&Web=True)

The English High Court has delivered its long-awaited judgment in *Getty Images v. Stability AI*. The case relates to the alleged infringement of intellectual property (IP) rights, in photos owned by Getty Images, Inc (Getty), by Stability AI (Stability) in the training and use of its deep learning AI model, "Stable Diffusion" (the Model). It has been very closely followed across the legal, creative and AI sectors alike, with the decision widely expected to shed light on how UK IP law applies to the rapidly evolving field of generative AI. However, whilst on the surface, the judgment may appear to have provided some clarity on the interplay between AI and IP infringement, there remains significant uncertainty in reality.

### Key Takeaways

* Getty succeeded only in part, and narrowly, on its trade mark infringement claims. Findings were confined to specific examples of outputs from early versions of the Model involving "iStock" and "Getty Images" watermarks.
* Getty's secondary copyright infringement claim failed. The court held that the Model’s weights were not an "infringing copy" of Getty's works because the Model did not at any time contain or store a copy of the underlying Getty images.
* The judgment leaves critical questions unanswered relating to the relationship between IP rights and generative AI, particularly whether the use of copyright protected works to train AI models constitutes copyright infringement. It was hoped that these issues would be addressed by the court, but this element of the claim was withdrawn during trial.
* Looking ahead, the UK government's ongoing work with expert groups from both the creative and technology sectors will be closely watched, as it seeks to balance the protection of human creativity with technological innovation.

### Background

Getty, a leading global provider of stock photography representing more than 600,000 photographers and artists, brought proceedings in the English courts against Stability, an open-source generative AI company. Getty alleged that Stability had unlawfully scraped over 12 million Getty-owned images, which it described as "*the lifeblood"* of its business, to train the Model without Getty’s consent.

Stability accepted that "*many*" copyrighted works had been used to train the Model and admitted, in its statements of case, that "*at least some*" of those images were from Getty's websites and were used in training earlier versions of the Model. Yet, Stability denied any wrongdoing and maintained that it neither copied nor stored any of Getty's copyrighted works. Instead, the Model learned from them in an abstracted form, extracting patterns rather than reproducing original content.

Getty's original 2023 claim alleged primary copyright infringement, asserting that Stability had copied millions of Getty-owned images both to train and develop its Model (the Training Claim), as well as in the outputs generated by the Model (the Output Claim). However, the Training Claim was abandoned during the trial due to jurisdictional difficulties; specifically, there was insufficient evidence to show that the training or development of the Model had occurred within the United Kingdom. The Output Claim was also withdrawn, as it was demonstrated that Stability had blocked the prompts said to have produced the disputed outputs.

### The Court's Key Findings

**1. Trade Mark Infringement**

Getty argued that the Model generated images which included watermarks bearing the Getty registered trade marks "Getty Images" and "iStock" (the Getty Signs) and that such use constituted trade mark infringement. The court found that, on balance, at least one user of certain earlier versions of the Model would have produced AI-generated outputs containing a Getty Signs watermark. The court emphasised, however, that the evidence of infringement related to a limited number of examples and that the true scale of such outputs could not be determined. The court confirmed partial trade mark infringement, which it described as "*both historic and extremely limited."*

In making that determination, the court made a number of interesting findings when applying the law to the facts, namely:

* **Whether Stability used the Getty Signs in the course of trade**: Stability argued that it did not use either of the Getty Signs in the course of trade (a necessary test to satisfy for a finding of trade mark infringement), but instead simply provided the Model and maintained that it was the user who was then in control of the Model's output. Getty asserted to the contrary, claiming that Stability's Model offered the service of generating images and putting those images on to the market, and that, as such, Stability was using the Getty Signs for its own commercial communication. Getty argued that the case involved active behaviour and control on the part of Stability because: (i) Stability is the entity that trained the Model; (ii) Stability is the entity that could have filtered out watermarked images; (iii) Stability makes the Model available to consumers; and (iv) Stability is the entity making the communication that bears the Getty Signs. The court agreed with Getty on this question.
* **Whether Stability used the Getty Signs in relation to goods and services**: Stability argued that it did not use the Getty Signs in the context of a commercial activity or "*in relation to any goods and services*" (another necessary test to satisfy for a finding of trade mark infringement). In its finding against Stability, the court stated that, "*Essentially [Stability] contends that the appearance of the watermarks on synthetic images is not 'trade mark use' in that it is not liable to affect the functions of the trade mark, in particular its essential function of guaranteeing to consumers the origin of the goods"*. The court held that the use of the Getty Signs in the Model outputs will be perceived by the average consumer as a commercial communication by Stability, "*[t]he [Getty] Signs are affixed to synthetic images generated by customers owing to the functionality of the Model, itself dependant upon its training data (over which Stability has absolute control and/or responsibility). It is in this way that Stability 'offers and puts synthetic images bearing the Signs on the market' and this is Stability's commercial communication to the customer."*
* **Comparison of goods and services**: For the purposes of comparing Stability's acts to the specification of the Getty registered trade marks, the court held that: (i) Stability used the signs in relation to "*synthetic image outputs*" and "*the provision of synthetic image outputs*," and (ii) that "*synthetic image outputs*" are identical to "*downloadable digital illustrations and graphics*" and "*digital media, digital materials, digital content (namely images)*" in Class 9, while "*the provision of synthetic image outputs*" is identical to "*digital imaging services*" in Class 41.

**2. Secondary Copyright Infringement and "Article" Claims**

Getty argued that the Model is an "*infringing copy*" of Getty works on the basis that it had been imported (primarily through downloading) into the United Kingdom. An important point to note is that Getty did not allege that the Model includes or comprises a reproduction of any of the Getty images. Instead, Getty asserted that the Model was an infringing copy because the making of the model weights would have constituted copyright infringement if it had been carried out within the United Kingdom. The court therefore had to answer two important questions: (i) whether the model weights were an "*article*" under the legislation, and (ii) if so, whether they were an infringing copy. On (i) the Court held that an "*article*" is capable of being an electronic copy stored in an intangible form. However, on (ii), the Court held that since the model weights never contained or stored a copy of any of the Getty images, they could not constitute an infringing copy. Accordingly, the court rejected Getty's secondary copyright infringement claim.

### The Road Ahead

Getty has not indicated whether it intends to appeal the judgment but has stated it would take forward findings of fact in the UK ruling in their ongoing US case. Getty also expressed deep concern that "*even well-resourced companies*" such as itself "*face significant challenges in protecting their creative works*," and urged the UK government introduce stronger transparency measures to reduce costly disputes and better safeguard creators' rights[1](#1).

Looking ahead, the UK government's ongoing work with industry groups from both the creative and technology sectors will be closely watched, as it seeks to balance the protection of human creativity with technological innovation[2](#2). Yet, the debate over IP rights and AI is far from settled, and further developments, whether through appeal, further case law or legislative reform, are inevitable. As ever, it's a matter of watching this space.

\**Lavinia Puder, a trainee in our London office, contributed to this advisory.*

# Andersen v. Stability AI: The Landmark Case Unpacking the Copyright Risks of AI Image Generators

[![Zach Schor, JD '26](https://jipel.law.nyu.edu/wp-content/uploads/2024/12/D8F8B3C6FFAA4A3292BB4A55FDFC5AD6.jpg)](https://jipel.law.nyu.edu/author/zach-schor/) 

#### By[Zach Schor, JD '26](https://jipel.law.nyu.edu/author/zach-schor/)

 Dec 2, 2024

With the rise of AI image generators, even an artistically untalented law student like myself can depict nearly anything imaginable within minutes. By typing “Mario eating a slice of pizza in Washington Square Park, watercolor” into [Dall-E](https://openai.com/index/dall-e-3/), I can quickly conjure an image of Nintendo’s iconic character reenacting my post-class lunch from last Tuesday.

[![](https://jipel.law.nyu.edu//wp-content/uploads/2024/12/OIG3.TAiSa_TpbfSkRPK40vg8.jpeg)](https://jipel.law.nyu.edu//wp-content/uploads/2024/12/OIG3.TAiSa_TpbfSkRPK40vg8.jpeg)

[A Dall-E Creation](https://perma.cc/ND8S-LVKN)

This seemingly new image exists at the convergence of my imagination, a vast database of billions of existing images, and a complex algorithm that, after being trained on these images, assembles new art by recognizing patterns and blending elements of the database. But as you look at Mario enjoying his slice, several copyright law questions should naturally come to mind. Is this truly a new image? Or is it a copy, pieced together from other images? And does this image violate the copyright rights of the artists whose works contributed to the dataset? These very issues are at the heart of [*Andersen v. Stability AI*](https://perma.cc/U9VG-XRPV), a landmark lawsuit from the Northern District of California concerning the copyright implications of AI-generated art.

## **Background**

In late 2022, popular internet cartoonist Sarah Andersen penned a New York Times guest essay titled “[The Alt-Right Manipulated My Comic. Then A.I. Claimed It](https://perma.cc/8AEZ-7B3W),” where she shared her experience of having her art misappropriated, first by far-right online groups and later by AI tools trained on her art. In the essay, she recounted that simply using her name as a prompt on AI image generator “[Stable Diffusion](https://perma.cc/855Y-J8KK)” generated new images in her distinct artistic style. While the recreations of her comics weren’t perfect, they had the signature elements of her comics, leading her to write, “I see a monster forming,” regarding the potential threat of image generators to the livelihoods of artists like herself.

[*An example of Andersen’s comics and Stability AI’s recreation from late 2022*](https://perma.cc/8AEZ-7B3W)

On January 12, 2023, Andersen, along with several other artists, acted on these concerns and filed a class-action copyright infringement lawsuit against several AI companies (Stability AI, [Midjourney](https://www.midjourney.com/home), [DeviantArt](https://perma.cc/QGQ9-7SUP)) in federal court. While there had been prior lawsuits by copyright owners against AI developers, this case was among the first where creatives united to challenge the use of their works for AI training, with many [similar cases](https://perma.cc/SKV6-M5HG) following shortly after. The lawsuit focuses on the [LAION data set](https://perma.cc/5CVW-HN48), which consists of 5 billion images that were scraped from the internet and used by Stability AI and other companies to develop their AI image generators. Among other legal claims, the complaint accuses said companies of copyright infringement for including the plaintiffs’ work in the dataset to train AI systems, allowing the case to serve as a precedent-setting moment in the ongoing legal battle between artists and AI companies.

## ****Artists Recently Scored a Major Win****

While several of the plaintiffs’ many claims, such as unjust enrichment and breach of contract, have been dismissed by the Northern District of California Court, the artists recently secured a significant win with an [August 12th ruling](https://perma.cc/HCT3-NHVV). Here, U.S. District Judge William Orrick denied Stability AI and MidJourney’s motion to dismiss the artists’ copyright infringement claims, allowing the case to move towards discovery.   
  
In reaching this decision, the judge found both direct and induced copyright infringement claims to be plausible. The induced infringement claim against Stability AI argued that by distributing their model “Stable Diffusion” to other AI providers, the company facilitated the copying of copyrighted material. In allowing this claim to proceed, the judge noted a statement by Stability’s CEO, who claimed that Stability compressed 100,000 gigabytes of images into a two gigabyte file that could “recreate” any of those images. The judge also pointed to the plaintiffs’ presentation of [academic papers](https://perma.cc/U7KU-BTQA) demonstrating that training images could be reproduced as outputs from AI products by using precise prompts.

As for direct infringement claims against Stability AI and others, Judge Orrick found the plaintiffs’ model theory, which argues that the AI product itself constitutes an infringing copy because it embodies the transformations of the plaintiffs’ works, and distribution theory, which asserted that distributing the AI product is equivalent to distributing their copyrighted works, to both be plausible. When moving these claims forward, Judge Orrick noted that these theories depended on whether the plaintiffs’ protected works were found within the AI systems in some form and would be addressed again at the summary judgment stage.

## **Going Forward**

With Judge Orrick’s August 12th decision, *Andersen v. Stability AI* will move into the discovery stage with the trial set to begin on September 8, 2026. This ruling opens the door to a deeper examination of how AI companies use copyrighted works to train their systems and whether these practices violate existing copyright laws. If the plaintiffs ultimately succeed in proving their claims, this case could set a transformative legal precedent that will reshape the way AI-art is regulated in the United States. As the legal battle unfolds, this case will undoubtedly set a guiding tone for how courts interpret the relationship between AI innovation and intellectual property rights.

args.summary: This article from the NYU Journal of Intellectual Property & Entertainment Law discusses Andersen v. Stability AI, a landmark copyright infringement lawsuit concerning AI image generators. The case was filed on January 13, 2023, by artist Sarah Andersen and other creators against Stability AI, Midjourney, and DeviantArt. The lawsuit centers on the LAION dataset (5 billion images scraped from the internet) used to train AI systems like Stable Diffusion. In a key ruling on August 12, 2024, U.S. District Judge William Orrick denied motions to dismiss the copyright infringement claims, allowing both direct and induced infringement theories to proceed toward discovery. The induced infringement claim relied on Stability AI's CEO statement that the company compressed 100,000 gigabytes of images into a two-gigabyte file that could "recreate" any of those images, along with academic papers showing training images could be reproduced through precise prompts. The trial is scheduled to begin on September 8, 2026. The case could set a transformative legal precedent for how AI-generated art is regulated in the United States.

The trial in Andersen v. Stability AI has been set for September 8, 2026. The case was filed in January 2023 by visual artists Sarah Andersen, Kelly McKernan, and Karla Ortiz, along with a certified class, against Stability AI Ltd., Stability AI, Inc., DeviantArt, Inc., and Midjourney, Inc. The plaintiffs allege copyright infringement, DMCA violations, right of publicity violations, breach of DeviantArt's Terms of Service, unfair competition, and unjust enrichment.

In 2025, Judge William Orrick, presiding in the Northern District of California, advanced all copyright infringement and trademark claims. His order found that Stable Diffusion may have been "built to a significant extent on copyrighted works" and that the defendants may have created the system with the intent to "facilitate" infringement. That finding is significant because it allowed the core copyright claims to survive to trial rather than being dismissed at the motion-to-dismiss stage.

DeviantArt's inclusion in the case is worth noting specifically. The plaintiffs' theory includes the argument that DeviantArt, as a platform that hosted artists' work under terms of service that promised protection for that work, had an obligation it didn't honor when it allowed its catalog to be used in AI training. That's a different legal exposure than the companies that built the models: it's a platform accountability argument.

The Thaler ruling that the Supreme Court declined to revisit last March addressed a distinct question: who can hold copyright in AI-generated output. Andersen addresses the input side: whether training a model on copyrighted images, without obtaining a license or providing compensation, constitutes copyright infringement under existing law.

These are legally separate questions, and they can resolve differently. A court could find that AI cannot hold a copyright (Thaler: yes) and simultaneously find that training on copyrighted images without a license was infringement (Andersen: pending). Both findings would be consistent.

September will be the first time any of these cases reaches a jury. A verdict, regardless of direction, will be the first data point the industry has from a trial rather than a motion. Appeals will follow, and the legal picture will take years to fully resolve. But September will still change the shape of the conversation.

args.summary:
The trial in Andersen v. Stability AI has been set for September 8, 2026. The case was filed in January 2023 by visual artists Sarah Andersen, Kelly McKernan, and Karla Ortiz against Stability AI, DeviantArt, and Midjourney, alleging copyright infringement, DMCA violations, right of publicity violations, breach of contract, unfair competition, and unjust enrichment.

In 2025, Judge William Orrick of the Northern District of California advanced all copyright infringement and trademark claims, finding that Stable Diffusion may have been "built to a significant extent on copyrighted works" with intent to "facilitate" infringement. This ruling allowed core claims to survive to trial.

Key legal distinction: The Thaler ruling (declined by SCOTUS in March 2025) addressed whether AI can hold copyright in AI-generated output. Andersen addresses the input side — whether training on copyrighted images without license constitutes infringement. These are separate legal questions that can resolve differently.

This will be the first time any of these cases reaches a jury. A verdict will be the first trial data point for the industry, though appeals will follow and legal resolution will take years.

<webpage_content>
Trial Apr 5, 2027 Last updated: 2026-05-16

# Andersen v. Stability AI

Direct copyright; inducement; DMCA 1202(a)/(b)(1); Lanham Act; state law

🏛️ NDCA·Case No. **3:23-cv-00201**·Judge Orrick·Filed January 13, 2023

## Case summary

Plaintiff
:   Andersen

Defendants
:   Stability AI · DeviantArt · Midjourney · Runway

Court
:   U.S. District Court, Northern District of California

Case number
:   3:23-cv-00201

Filed
:   January 13, 2023

Judge
:   Orrick

Category
:   Copyright

Status
:   Trial Apr 5, 2027

## Claim types asserted

A group of visual artists led by cartoonist Sarah Andersen, joined by Kelly McKernan, Karla Ortiz, and additional artists added through later amendments, alleges that Stability AI, Midjourney, DeviantArt, and Runway AI copied billions of internet images — including the plaintiffs’ registered works — to train Stable Diffusion and downstream products. The operative surviving claims after Judge Orrick’s August 12, 2024 order are: (1) direct copyright infringement against Stability and (under the amended complaint) against Midjourney and DeviantArt for use of the artists’ works as training data; (2) induced copyright infringement against Stability and Runway for distributing infringing Stable Diffusion models to third parties; and (3) Lanham Act trade dress and unfair competition claims tied to outputs generated “in the style of” named artists. The DMCA § 1202(a) and 1202(b) claims (false copyright management information and CMI removal) were dismissed with prejudice in the August 2024 order, and the unjust enrichment and breach of contract theories were also dismissed. Plaintiffs filed a Second Amended Complaint on October 31, 2024 and a Third Amended Complaint on February 27, 2026 adding allegations based on training-dataset discovery, including details about DeviantArt’s DreamUp product and Midjourney’s use of the Datacomp xLarge dataset.

## Background

This is the marquee artist-versus-image-AI lawsuit and the case most courts and commentators look to for the framework on whether training a generative model on copyrighted images is itself an act of infringement. It was filed January 13, 2023 in the Northern District of California and assigned to Judge William H. Orrick.

The case has moved through three motion-to-dismiss rounds. In an October 30, 2023 order, Judge Orrick called the original complaint “defective in numerous respects” and dismissed most claims with leave to amend, but left intact Andersen’s direct copyright infringement claim against Stability AI based on the alleged copying of her registered works into the LAION dataset used to train Stable Diffusion. As [TheFashionLaw](https://www.thefashionlaw.com/court-refuses-to-dismiss-artists-copyright-claim-against-stability-ai/) noted in its analysis of the order, Judge Orrick framed the central dispute as a question of timing — whether an infringing reproduction took place while the model was being trained on the scraped images, or only later when a user prompts Stable Diffusion to generate an output.

After the first amended complaint added Runway as a defendant and added several artists as plaintiffs, the court issued a second order on August 12, 2024 ([ECF 223](https://law.justia.com/cases/federal/district-courts/california/candce/3:2023cv00201/407208/223/)). That order denied the motions to dismiss the direct copyright, induced infringement, and Lanham Act claims, but dismissed the DMCA § 1202 claims with prejudice on the “double scienter” rationale and the absence of identical-output allegations — the [Copyright Alliance walks through](https://copyrightalliance.org/andersen-v-stability-ai-copyright-case/) each holding. Judge Orrick notably accepted at the pleading stage the plaintiffs’ theory that copyrighted works “may be contained in Stable Diffusion as algorithmic or mathematical representations,” rejecting the argument that storage in a different medium defeats a direct infringement claim — a doctrinal move analyzed by the [Columbia Undergraduate Law Review](https://www.culawreview.org/current-events-2/copyright-in-the-age-of-generative-ai-part-ii-reinterpreting-dmca-1202-and-encoded-representations).

The plaintiffs filed a Second Amended Complaint on October 31, 2024 and defendants answered on December 6, 2024 (no further motion to dismiss). A Third Amended Complaint followed on February 27, 2026 with defendant answers on March 13, 2026, per the [Mesh IP litigation tracker](https://www.meshiplaw.com/litigation-tracker/andersen-v-stability-ai). The case is in fact discovery; a February 10, 2026 discovery order from Magistrate Judge Cisneros ([govinfo PDF](https://www.govinfo.gov/content/pkg/USCOURTS-cand-3_23-cv-00201/pdf/USCOURTS-cand-3_23-cv-00201-18.pdf)) resolved disputes over Midjourney’s interrogatories about the plaintiffs’ “distinctive” artistic styles and accused outputs, deferring substantive style-protection questions to summary judgment.

## What to watch next

* **Trial date.** The current schedule sets trial to begin April 5, 2027 in San Francisco. Earlier scheduling orders had targeted September 8, 2026 (per [NYU JIPEL](https://jipel.law.nyu.edu/andersen-v-stability-ai-the-landmark-case-unpacking-the-copyright-risks-of-ai-image-generators/)), so the docket has slipped roughly seven months as discovery has expanded.
* **Training-data production.** Plaintiffs have been seeking deeper discovery into the LAION-5B dataset and into Midjourney’s use of Datacomp xLarge. Per the Joseph Saveri firm’s [public case-updates page](https://imagegeneratorlitigation.com/case-updates.html), demands for Runway’s training-data disclosure were delayed by production-time issues, and the court has denied requests to compel production of training data sources beyond LAION as overly burdensome.
* **Style-mimicry theory.** The Lanham Act trade-dress claim — that AI outputs “in the style of” a named artist create false association — is the live theory most likely to reach merits-stage briefing. The magistrate’s February 2026 order signaled that style-protection arguments are reserved for summary judgment rather than being resolved at discovery.
* **Summary judgment briefing.** The fair-use defense has not yet been adjudicated. Defendants are expected to move on fair use after expert discovery closes, and the resulting opinion will become the most cited fair-use ruling in the image-AI context regardless of outcome.

args.summary:
Andersen v. Stability AI (Case No. 3:23-cv-00201) is a landmark copyright lawsuit filed January 13, 2023 in the Northern District of California, assigned to Judge William H. Orrick. Lead plaintiff Sarah Andersen, along with Kelly McKernan, Karla Ortiz, and other artists, alleges that Stability AI, DeviantArt, Midjourney, and Runway AI copied billions of internet images—including plaintiffs' registered works—to train Stable Diffusion and downstream AI products.

**Surviving Claims (after August 12, 2024 order):** (1) Direct copyright infringement against Stability, Midjourney, and DeviantArt for use of works as training data; (2) Induced copyright infringement against Stability and Runway for distributing infringing models; (3) Lanham Act trade dress/unfair competition claims for outputs generated "in the style of" named artists. DMCA §1202(a)/(b) claims, unjust enrichment, and breach of contract claims were dismissed with prejudice.

**Key Developments:**
- Oct 30, 2023: Initial order dismissed most claims but preserved direct copyright claim against Stability AI based on alleged copying of registered works into LAION dataset.
- Aug 12, 2024: Second order denied motions to dismiss direct copyright, induced infringement, and Lanham Act claims. Judge Orrick accepted plaintiffs' theory that copyrighted works "may be contained in Stable Diffusion as algorithmic or mathematical representations."
- Oct 31, 2024: Second Amended Complaint filed; Feb 27, 2026: Third Amended Complaint filed.
- Feb 10, 2026: Magistrate discovery order on Midjourney interrogatories, deferring style-protection questions to summary judgment.

**Trial:** Scheduled for April 5, 2027 in San Francisco (slipped from September 8, 2026).

**What to Watch:** Fair-use defense not yet adjudicated; summary judgment briefing expected after expert discovery closes. The case is in fact discovery. Outcomes will shape related cases including Disney v. Midjourney, Warner Bros. v. Midjourney, and Getty image-AI litigation.

# AI in Fashion Design: A Complete Review of Tools Transforming Creative Workflows in 2025

You've spent months perfecting a collection concept, only to discover your target audience has already moved on to the next trend. Your design team burns through countless hours creating sketches that don't resonate, while competitors seem to predict market demand with uncanny accuracy. This frustration is driving fashion brands toward **AI in fashion design**—a technological revolution that's transforming how designers create, predict, and produce from initial concept to final textile pattern.

After extensively testing the leading AI fashion design platforms throughout 2024 and early 2025, I've evaluated how these tools genuinely impact creative workflows, cost efficiency, and market responsiveness. This comprehensive review examines the most significant AI fashion technology solutions currently reshaping the industry.

## First Impressions: The Current State of AI Fashion Design Tools

The **AI fashion technology** landscape has matured dramatically since 2023. What began as experimental concept generators has evolved into sophisticated platforms that handle everything from trend forecasting to 3D garment simulation. The standout observation: these tools don't replace creativity—they amplify it exponentially.

Leading platforms like Heuritech, Style3D, and Onbrand AI Design now deliver production-ready outputs that would have taken design teams weeks to develop manually. The integration between **machine learning in fashion** and traditional design workflows has reached a tipping point where adoption isn't just beneficial—it's becoming essential for competitive survival.

**📌 Key Takeaway:** AI fashion design tools have shifted from experimental novelties to mission-critical platforms that can reduce design cycles from months to days while improving market accuracy.

## Key Features Overview: What Modern AI Fashion Design Platforms Deliver

Current **AI fashion design software** encompasses five core capabilities that address the entire design pipeline:

| Feature Category | Primary Function | Industry Impact |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Trend Forecasting | Predictive analysis of colors, patterns, styles | +20% accuracy in seasonal predictions |
| Generative Design | Concept creation from text prompts/sketches | 70% faster ideation cycles |
| 3D Simulation | Virtual garment prototyping and fitting | 80% reduction in physical samples |
| Pattern Generation | Automated textile and trim design | 50% cost reduction in pattern development |
| Fit Optimization | Size prediction and adjustment algorithms | 30% decrease in return rates |

## In-Depth Feature Analysis: How AI Tools Transform Each Design Stage

### Trend Forecasting and Market Intelligence

Heuritech represents the gold standard in AI-powered trend forecasting. Their algorithms analyze over 3 million social media images daily, cross-referencing with sales data and runway archives. For Spring/Summer 2025, their predictions showed +8% growth in turquoise and +20% in sequins—predictions that proved 87% accurate when tested against actual sales data.

**💡 Pro Tip:** Use AI trend forecasting 6-8 months ahead of traditional fashion calendars. The algorithms often identify micro-trends before they appear in mainstream fashion weeks.

### AI Sketching Tools and Concept Generation

**AI sketching tools** like Onbrand AI Design have revolutionized ideation. Input a simple text prompt like "sustainable streetwear with Japanese minimalist influence," and the system generates 20-30 concept sketches in minutes. The quality has improved substantially—these aren't rough thumbnails but detailed illustrations with proper proportions, fabric suggestions, and construction details.

### 3D Digital Fashion Design and Prototyping

Style3D and CLO3D lead the **3D fashion design AI** category. Their platforms simulate over 1,000 fabric types with physics-accurate draping, allowing designers to test fit, movement, and aesthetic before creating physical samples. Brands using these tools report 70-80% reduction in pre-production sample costs.

**🎯 Expert Insight:** The most successful implementations combine AI-generated concepts with human creative direction. AI handles the computational heavy lifting while designers focus on brand vision and emotional connection.

### AI Textile Design and Pattern Creation

**AI textile design** tools excel at creating complex, repeating patterns that would take human designers days to perfect. Platforms like PatternAI and Adobe Firefly's textile module generate seamless patterns, color variations, and scale modifications instantly. The real breakthrough is their ability to maintain design coherence across different applications—from apparel to home goods.

## User Experience and Interface: The Learning Curve Reality

The user experience varies significantly across platforms. Enterprise solutions like Heuritech require substantial onboarding but deliver sophisticated analytics dashboards. Mid-market tools like Style3D balance accessibility with professional features, while consumer-focused platforms prioritize ease of use over advanced functionality.

Most platforms now offer intuitive drag-and-drop interfaces, but mastering their full potential requires 2-3 months of dedicated use. The steepest learning curve involves understanding how to write effective prompts for **AI pattern generation** and interpreting trend forecasting data.

**⚠️ Warning:** Don't expect immediate productivity gains. Plan for a 60-90 day learning period where output may initially be slower as teams adapt to new workflows.

## Pricing and Value Assessment: ROI Analysis

AI fashion design platform pricing ranges from $49/month for basic pattern generators to $50,000+ annually for enterprise trend forecasting. Here's the realistic ROI breakdown:

* **Small studios (1-5 designers):** $200-800/month investment typically pays for itself through reduced sampling costs within 3-4 months
* **Mid-size brands (20-100 employees):** $2,000-10,000/month platforms show ROI through faster time-to-market and improved trend accuracy
* **Enterprise brands (500+ employees):** $15,000-50,000/month systems justify costs through waste reduction and supply chain optimization

## Comprehensive Pros and Cons

### Advantages

* **Speed:** 10-20x faster concept development and iteration cycles
* **Cost reduction:** 70% decrease in physical sampling and prototyping expenses
* **Market accuracy:** Data-driven trend prediction significantly outperforms human intuition alone
* **Sustainability:** Reduced waste through virtual prototyping and accurate demand forecasting
* **Personalization:** AI enables mass customization previously impossible at scale

### Limitations

* **Learning curve:** 2-3 month adaptation period for maximum productivity
* **Creativity concerns:** Risk of homogenized design if over-reliant on AI suggestions
* **Technology dependence:** Platform outages can halt entire design workflows
* **Cost barrier:** High-quality solutions require significant upfront investment
* **Data requirements:** Most effective tools need substantial historical data to perform optimally

## Who Is AI Fashion Design Best For?

**Ideal candidates for AI fashion design tools:**

* Fast-fashion brands needing rapid trend response
* Sustainable fashion companies focused on waste reduction
* Independent designers seeking to compete with larger studios
* Brands with data-rich customer bases enabling personalization
* Companies struggling with accurate demand forecasting

**Less suitable for:**

* Ultra-luxury brands where handcraft tradition is core to brand identity
* Very small operations without budget for learning curve investment
* Brands in niche markets with limited historical data

## Final Verdict: The State of AI in Fashion Design

### Overall Rating: 8.5/10

**AI in fashion design** has reached genuine maturity in 2025. While not perfect, these tools deliver measurable improvements in speed, cost efficiency, and market responsiveness that justify adoption for most fashion businesses.

**Best Overall Platform:** Style3D for comprehensive design workflows  
 **Best Value:** Onbrand AI Design for small to mid-size studios  
 **Best Enterprise Solution:** Heuritech for trend forecasting and analytics

The **future of AI in fashion** isn't about replacing human creativity—it's about augmenting it with computational power that handles repetitive tasks, predicts market trends, and optimizes production workflows. Brands that master this balance will dominate the next decade of fashion innovation.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How accurate are AI trend predictions compared to traditional forecasting?

AI trend forecasting achieves 75-85% accuracy compared to 45-60% for traditional methods. The key advantage is processing vast data sets—social media, sales history, and cultural signals—that humans cannot analyze at scale.

### Can AI fashion design tools work with sustainable and eco-friendly practices?

Absolutely. AI tools significantly support sustainability through reduced physical sampling (70-80% decrease), accurate demand forecasting that minimizes overproduction, and optimization algorithms that reduce material waste in pattern cutting.

### What's the realistic timeline for seeing ROI from AI fashion design investments?

Most brands see initial ROI within 3-6 months through reduced sampling costs and faster design cycles. Full ROI, including improved market accuracy and reduced waste, typically materializes within 12-18 months.

### How do AI-generated designs handle intellectual property and originality concerns?

Leading platforms train on publicly available images and generate novel combinations rather than copying existing designs. However, always review outputs for potential similarities and maintain creative oversight to ensure brand-appropriate originality.

### Is AI in garment manufacturing ready for full production integration?

AI excels in design and pre-production phases but physical manufacturing integration varies. Pattern optimization and cutting algorithms are production-ready, while robotic sewing and finishing remain in early development stages for most applications.

### What skills do fashion design teams need to develop for effective AI tool usage?

Key skills include prompt engineering for AI generation, data interpretation for trend analysis, 3D modeling basics, and strategic thinking about when to use AI versus human creativity. Most platforms offer training programs ranging from 2-8 weeks.
