The process-related constructs were organized into three cognitive load categories following CLT. Intrinsic load was assessed through two indicators: task difficulty, the primary measure of inherent task complexity, and personal style articulation, an auxiliary indicator capturing the qualitative dimension of intrinsic processing. The latter reflects the challenge of expressing stylistic identity while integrating multiple design elements, an essential cognitive demand in creative design tasks.

Extraneous load was operationalized through task efficiency and editability as primary measures reflecting procedural demands during design execution. Three additional process indicators—ease of idea generation, idea quantity, and design engagement—were also positioned within the extraneous load category to capture the multifaceted influence of procedural characteristics on creative execution. Ease of idea generation and idea quantity captured learners’ exploratory activity, corresponding to the CSI dimension of exploration. Design engagement represented affective and attentional immersion during the design process, aligning with CSI’s immersion and enjoyment dimensions. Total cognitive load was measured through workload, representing the overall mental effort invested during task execution, encompassing both intrinsic and extraneous load as proposed in CLT.

Outcome-related constructs were conceptually distinct from process measures. Perceived creativity, aesthetic value, satisfaction, and design goal fulfillment captured post-task evaluative judgments of design performance. These outcomes align with CSI’s Results Worth Effort dimension, reflecting holistic assessments of creative output quality rather than process-level experience.

The conceptual clarity and relevance of surgery questionaries were reviewed and verified by six experts with doctoral degrees in clothing and textiles through individual expert reviews and consensus meetings, confirming content validity. Quantitative data were analyzed using paired-sample t-tests and descriptive statistics in IBM SPSS Statistics 29.0. Beyond the 12 core comparative items (24 questions across both conditions), the survey also included four open-ended questions about the perceived strengths and weaknesses of each workflow, along with demographic items and questions on prior GenAI experience, usage frequency, and confidence in digital tools—bringing the total to 50 questions.

In addition, Semi-structured interviews were conducted with 18 participants who voluntarily indicated their willingness to participate at the end of the post-task survey. All interviewees had completed both design conditions (GenAI-assisted and conventional workflows), enabling direct comparative reflection on their experiences. This ensured data linkage between the quantitative survey responses and qualitative interview accounts, strengthening the interpretive validity of the mixed-methods analysis.

While the survey quantified how participants perceived task difficulty, efficiency, engagement, and creative outcomes, the interviews pursued to uncover the underlying reasoning and contextual factors behind those perceptions. In alignment with CLT and CSI, questions encouraged participants to reflect on how they interpreted cognitive effort, managed procedural challenges, and experienced shifts in creative workflow. A complete outline of the interview questions is presented in Table[3](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40691-026-00459-w#Tab3).

**Table 3 Semi-structured interview questions**

[Full size table](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40691-026-00459-w/tables/3)

Each interview lasted between 45 and 60 min and explored participants’ experiences in depth. All interviews were video recorded and transcribed. The thematic analysis followed the six-phase approach of Braun and Clarke ([2012](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40691-026-00459-w#ref-CR52 "Braun, V., & Clarke, V. (2012). Thematic analysis. In H. Cooper, P. M. Camic, D. L. Long, A. T. Panter, D. Rindskopf, & K. J. Sher (Eds.), APA handbook of research methods in psychology, Vol. 2: Research designs (pp. 57–71). American Psychological Association. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1037/13620-004
                  
                ")), which included initial coding, theme development, and refinement. NVivo 14 (Mac) was used to support coding reliability. Both deductive and inductive strategies were applied. High-level codes were guided by the research questions, while subthemes emerged from the participants’ narratives. The author iteratively reviewed the coding structures and refined themes through multiple rounds of analysis, with intercoder reliability checked by an independent expert. The qualitative findings contextualized the quantitative results and offered insights into the evolving role of AI in textile design education.

## Results and Discussion

### Analysis of cognitive load and design outcomes

To investigate how GenAI reshaped participants’ cognitive effort and creative performance, paired-sample t-tests were conducted on twelve constructs across two conditions, conventional illustrator-based and GenAI-assisted workflows (Table[4](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40691-026-00459-w#Tab4); Fig.[1](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40691-026-00459-w#Fig1)).

**Table 4 Paired t-test results of the survey**

[Full size table](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40691-026-00459-w/tables/4)

**Fig.1**

![Image 7: Fig. 1](https://media.springernature.com/lw685/springer-static/image/art%3A10.1186%2Fs40691-026-00459-w/MediaObjects/40691_2026_459_Fig1_HTML.png)

[Full size image](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40691-026-00459-w/figures/1)

Comparison of participant ratings across design process and outcome metrics

Regarding intrinsic aspects of cognitive load, participants reported significantly lower task difficulty under the AI-assisted condition (_M_ = 2.09, _SD_ = .933) than under the conventional workflow condition (_M_ = 3.68, _SD_ = .878), _t_ = –6.855, _p_< .001. This indicates that GenAI simplified the inherent complexity of the design task by automating lower-level operations, thereby reducing the intrinsic cognitive demands required to integrate multiple visual and conceptual elements. In contrast, users found it significantly more difficult to articulate their personal design style using AI tools (_M_ = 1.53, _SD_ = .788) than with traditional tools (_M_ = 4.24, _SD_ = .699), _t_ = –13.212, _p_< .001. Although GenAI lowered task difficulty, it simultaneously restricted the qualitative aspect of intrinsic processing, the ability to internalize and express one’s stylistic identity. This suggests that while automation decreases structural complexity, the intrinsic processing linked to creative reasoning and aesthetic judgment remains demanding without sufficient expressive control.

For extraneous load factors, GenAI tools were perceived as significantly more efficient (_M_ = 4.06, _SD_ = 1.013) than traditional tools (_M_ = 2.29, _SD_ = .836), _t_ = 7.891, _p_< .001. This improvement reflects a reduction in extraneous cognitive load, as automation minimized repetitive procedural steps and allowed designers to focus on higher-level creative decisions. However, editability was rated lower for AI-assisted designs (_M_ = 2.47, _SD_ = .861) than for conventional designs (_M_ = 3.91, _SD_ = .900), _t_ = –5.838, _p_< .001, suggesting reduced procedural control.

These results indicate a trade-off between procedural efficiency and expressive flexibility: while GenAI enhanced operational speed, it limited the designer’s ability to adjust or rework generated outputs. Participants also mentioned that although Firefly generates vector-based outputs, the practical editability of these AI-generated vectors within Adobe Illustrator was limited by the system’s functional characteristics. While the vectors were technically modifiable, refining them often required reverting to manual, traditional editing techniques rather than leveraging AI assistance. Some participants described situations in which correcting unintended shapes, restructuring motifs, or adjusting proportions demanded such extensive manual rework that starting from scratch felt more efficient than modifying the generated output. This perception that AI-generated assets were ‘editable in theory but not in practice’ further constrained their sense of expressive flexibility and reduced the functional utility of the outputs in subsequent design stages. Such practical constraints on post-generation editing also contributed to a diminished sense of control, which helps explain why the efficiency–control trade-off became so pronounced. The efficiency–control trade-off suggests that removing extraneous burden may narrow the designer’s active involvement window. Participants described executing tasks with greater speed but reduced deliberation, implying that the cognitive effort typically invested in exploratory or evaluative thinking was not fully utilized.

CLT posits that when extraneous load decreases below an optimal level, learners may enter an under-challenged state that inhibits schema formation and higher-order reasoning. In this context, automation alleviated unnecessary operational effort but, at the same time, reduced opportunities for reflective engagement. Such engagement involves the deliberate evaluation and reinterpretation that transform procedural efficiency into creative insight.

Idea generation was perceived as easier with GenAI (_M_ = 3.06 vs. 2.53; _t_ = 2.403, _p_ = .022), yet participants did not report a significant increase in the number of generated ideas (_M_ = 2.97 vs. 3.44; _t_ = –1.852, _p_ = .073). This suggests that while GenAI reduced the cognitive effort required to initiate ideas, it did not expand the overall diversity of conceptual outcomes. Participants frequently observed stylistic convergence: while the generated outputs maintained the intended concept, they often appeared as visually similar variations within the same aesthetic frame, lacking the broader diversity typically achieved through human-led experimentation. This pattern also corresponds closely to the functional characteristics of Firefly. The system tends to normalize stylistic features across outputs, producing variations that remain within a narrow aesthetic range. Because users have limited control over underlying parameters and cannot effectively direct the model toward more divergent stylistic options, the generative space becomes constrained. Consequently, participants generated ideas more quickly but did not achieve greater conceptual diversity.

Thus, although GenAI decreased the procedural demands of ideation, it appeared to introduce another form of cognitive constraint—conceptual fixation shaped by model regularities and limited output diversity.

For design engagement, no statistically significant difference was found between the two conditions (_t_ = –1.158, _p_ = .255), indicating that the cognitive resources freed from procedural operations were not automatically redirected toward deeper analytical reasoning or affective engagement during the design process.

The perceived total workload was significantly lower under the AI-assisted condition (_M_ = 2.15, _SD_ = 1.077) than under the conventional condition (_M_ = 4.21, _SD_ = .770), _t_ = –8.496, _p_< .001. This result indicates a broad reduction in cognitive burden, reflecting the combined effect of lower extraneous and intrinsic demands. However, according to CLT, reduced effort does not necessarily equate to enhanced cognitive elaboration. When total load decreases beyond an optimal level, learners may fail to engage in the reflective and integrative processes required for meaningful schema construction and creative reasoning. In this context, GenAI optimized procedural fluency but risked fostering a state of cognitive passivity—where tasks are completed efficiently, yet with limited reflective depth or conceptual integration.

Outcome evaluations followed this cognitive pattern. Conventional designs were rated higher in perceived creativity and originality (_M_ = 3.94 vs. 2.68; _t_ = –7.200, _p_< .001), aesthetic value (_M_ = 4.09 vs. 2.74; _t_ = –5.588, _p_< .001), satisfaction (_M_ = 3.91 vs. 2.26; _t_ = –6.513, _p_< .001), and goal fulfillment (_M_ = 4.03 vs. 2.00; _t_ = –8.706, _p_< .001).

A key factor that may help explain these lower evaluations is the limited refinement control available in Firefly during later stages of development. Several participants noted that even when the initial outputs captured the overarching concept with reasonable accuracy, they still lacked the ability to guide the design toward more specific stylistic, proportional, or structural intentions. Attempts to adjust composition, emphasis, or motif organization frequently exceeded what could be achieved through additional prompts or parameter adjustments, making manual reconstruction in Illustrator the only viable option. This discontinuity between AI-generated drafts and subsequent refinement disrupted the iterative design rhythm and reduced the functional utility of the outputs for continued development. The resulting gap between conceptual alignment and insufficient refinement flexibility provides a clear explanation for the diminished ratings in originality, aesthetic quality, and goal fulfillment in the AI-assisted condition.

The results also mirror the cognitive redistribution identified earlier: while procedural ease improved, the creative originality, aesthetic refinement, and overall fulfillment of the outcomes were diminished. Within the CLT–CSI perspective, reductions in extraneous load may have enhanced procedural fluency but concurrently weakened expressiveness and immersive engagement. These results suggest that automation reshaped cognitive processing from generative construction toward evaluative selection, reflecting a persistent tension between efficiency and creative fulfillment in AI-assisted design workflows.

### Reflections on AI-assisted design

As shown in Table[5](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40691-026-00459-w#Tab5), the results of interviews revealed four core themes: (1) erosion of creative autonomy, (2) reduced design immersion, (3) cognitive barriers, and (4) perceived limitations and benefits of AI. These themes offer interpretive depth to the patterns observed in the quantitative results.

**Table 5 Thematic summary of reflections on GenAI vs. conventional design workflows**

[Full size table](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40691-026-00459-w/tables/5)

Participants consistently reported that GenAI constrained their control over the design process, consistent with the quantitative decrease observed in personal style articulation (_M_ = 1.53 vs. 4.24; _t_ = –13.212, _p_< .001). Many students (_n_ = 16) described that the AI “decided everything,” generating outcomes that diverged from their original intent. This perceived automation of creative judgment diminished their sense of authorship, as participants increasingly viewed themselves as curators rather than creators. Such psychological distancing aligns with Sweller’s ([1988](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40691-026-00459-w#ref-CR40 "Sweller, J. (1988). Cognitive load during problem solving: Effects on learning. Cognitive Science, 12(2), 257–285. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1207/s15516709cog1202_4
                  
                ")) notion that reduced opportunities for direct manipulation can reduce cognitive investment and authorship of outcomes. Several participants (_n_ = 12) reported spending additional time on post-generation editing to “make the design mine again,” employing this as a compensatory strategy to reclaim agency and reflective authorship. These behaviors illustrate that the erosion of autonomy was not characterized by passivity but by an active negotiation of control within constrained creative systems (Gmeiner et al., [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40691-026-00459-w#ref-CR14 "Gmeiner, F., Yang, H., Yao, L., Holstein, K., & Martelaro, N. (2023). Exploring challenges and opportunities to support designers in learning to co-create with AI-based manufacturing design tools. In Proceedings of the CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (Article 580, pp. 1–20). ACM. 
                  https://doi.org/10.1145/3544548.3580999
                  
                ")).

Although GenAI accelerated task completion, mirroring the lower perceived workload (_M_ = 2.15 vs. 4.21; _t_ = –8.496, _p_< .001), participants repeatedly reported a loss of emotional engagement. Quantitative ratings for design engagement showed no significant difference between conditions (_M_ = 3.50 vs. 3.71; _t_ = –1.158, _p_ = .255), suggesting that participants invested comparable levels of effort to produce quality outcomes in both workflows. However, qualitative accounts revealed a marked divergence in the experiential quality of that involvement. The survey item measuring engagement likely captured effortful task investment—participants’ deliberate commitment to achieving design goals—rather than the spontaneous absorption and enjoyment associated with creative immersion. Descriptions such as “I skipped the fun part” or “I didn’t feel connected” indicate that intentional effort did not translate into affective immersion. Within the CLT framework, this pattern suggests an imbalance between cognitive challenge and skill level. As procedural demands decreased, participants maintained goal-directed effort but did not experience the intrinsic motivation and immersion typically associated with optimal challenge (Paas et al., [2010](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1186/s40691-026-00459-w#ref-CR33 "Paas, F.,

**Article Title:** From designer to curator: cognitive and creative trade-offs in GenAI-assisted design

**Published:** March 4, 2026, in *Fashion and Textiles*, Volume 13, Article 12 (Open Access)

**Author:** Shin Young Jang (South Korean university)

**Purpose:** This study investigates how Generative AI (GenAI) reshapes creative workflow in digital textile design, comparing GenAI-assisted workflows to conventional vector-based tools in Adobe Illustrator.

**Methods:**
- 34 undergraduate fashion design students (26 female, 8 male) completed matched pattern design tasks under both conditions (conventional and GenAI-assisted) using a within-subject experimental design.
- Each student created 20 total designs (4 per product across 5 categories: ball caps, eco-bags, blankets, scarves, sweatshirts).
- Mixed-methods: post-task surveys (12 core items on 5-point Likert scale) and semi-structured interviews with 18 participants.
- Theoretical framework: Cognitive Load Theory (CLT) and Creativity Support Index (CSI).

**Key Quantitative Results:**
- GenAI significantly reduced perceived task difficulty (M=2.09 vs 3.68, p<.001) and total workload (M=2.15 vs 4.21, p<.001).
- GenAI increased procedural efficiency (M=4.06 vs 2.29, p<.001).
- However, GenAI resulted in lower editability (M=2.47 vs 3.91, p<.001), weaker personal style articulation (M=1.53 vs 4.24, p<.001), and lower ratings for creativity (M=2.68 vs 3.94), aesthetic value (M=2.74 vs 4.09), satisfaction (M=2.26 vs 3.91), and goal fulfillment (M=2.00 vs 4.03) — all p<.001.
- Idea generation felt easier with GenAI (M=3.06 vs 2.53, p=.022), but the number of distinct ideas did not increase significantly, suggesting stylistic convergence rather than divergent exploration.

**Qualitative Themes (from interviews):**
1. Erosion of creative autonomy — students felt like "curators" rather than "creators"; AI "decided everything"
2. Reduced design immersion — "I skipped the fun part"; intentional effort did not translate to affective engagement
3. Cognitive barriers — limited refinement control; AI outputs were "editable in theory but not in practice"
4. Perceived limitations and benefits of AI — trade-off between efficiency and expressive control

**Key Conclusions:**
- GenAI has a dual effect: enhancing procedural fluency while diminishing authorship and creative fulfillment.
- Automation redistributed cognitive effort from generative construction toward evaluative selection.
- The study proposes structuring AI-integrated design education into three phases: exploration, refinement, and reflection, accompanied by assessment that documents prompts, decision histories, and human re-authoring of AI results.
- Firefly's tendency to normalize stylistic features across outputs constrained conceptual diversity.
- Reduced cognitive load may foster "cognitive passivity" rather than deeper schema formation.

Understanding Fashion Designers’ Behavior Using Generative AI for Early-Stage Concept Ideation and Revision

* Yu Jin : *Department of Design, PhD Candidate, Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology, Ulsan, Korea*
* Juhyeok Yoon : *Department of Design, Research Assistant, Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology, Ulsan, Korea*
* James Self : *Department of Design, Associate Professor, Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology, Ulsan, Korea*
* Kyungho Lee : *Department of Design, Assistant Professor, Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology, Ulsan, Korea*

**Background** Generative AI has emerged as a powerful tool in fashion design, supporting activities such as ideation, sketching, and creativity enhancement. This study explores how commercial generative AI tools like Bing, Midjourney, and DALL-E can augment the creative processes of professional fashion designers during the early stages of concept ideation and revision.

**Methods** A mixed-methods approach was employed, involving a pilot study, sketch experiment interviews, and a focus group discussion. 19 participants, including design students and professionals, used AI tools Midjourney and DALL-E for concept ideation and revision. Data were analyzed using thematic analysis, focusing on understanding designers’ behavior and decision-making processes while using generative AI tools.

**Results** Generative AI tools significantly enhanced the early stages of fashion design by providing diverse and rapid visual stimuli. Designers interacted with AI tools through text prompts, refining hand-drawn sketches, and enhancing digital sketches, which facilitated creativity and decision-making. Challenges identified included biases in AI outputs, intellectual property concerns, and usability issues.

**Conclusions** The study highlights the potential of generative AI to enhance the fashion design process by providing diverse visual stimuli and accelerating concept ideation and revision. The study identifies key challenges such as biases, intellectual property concerns, and gaps between designer intentions and AI realizations. Future research should explore a broader range of AI tools, long-term impacts, and ethical implications, underscoring AI’s role in augmenting and co-creating, rather than replacing, human creativity in fashion design.

Keywords:

Generative AI, Fashion, Design, Human-AI Co-Creation, Concept Design.

1. Introduction

The integration of intelligent tools into design processes is becoming increasingly common, supporting activities such as ideation, sketching, and fostering creativity ([Tholander & Jonsson, 2023](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B53)). Tools such as ChatGPT[1)](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_X001) enable natural language interactions with AI, significantly impacting various creative domains ([Kirmani, 2022](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B27)). Text-to-image generators like DALL-E[2)](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_X002), Midjourney[3)](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_X003), and Stable Diffusion[4)](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_X004) have revolutionized the creation of realistic images and artworks from textual descriptions, with applications in fields such as poetry, music, animation, and especially fashion design ([Gero & Chilton, 2019](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B14); [Huang et al., 2020](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B20); [Jeon et al., 2021](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B23); [Mazzone & Elgammal, 2019](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B40)). These tools democratize access to high-quality creative content generation ([Lawton & Ibarrola, 2023](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B32); [Louie et al., 2020](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B37)) and streamline the creative process for professionals ([Desai et al., 2019](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B9); [Grabe & Zhu, 2023](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B16); [Shin et al., 2023](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B50); [Tholander & Jonsson, 2023](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B53); [Verheijden & Funk, 2023](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B54)).

With the recent advancement, generative AI’s role in the fashion industry has gained momentum, focusing on improving design processes. Applications include Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) for apparel design ([Cui et al., 2018](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B5); [Kato et al., 2019](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B24)) and AI systems like DeepVogue by DeepBlue Technology (Jain, 2019), which use deep generative modeling to support creative efforts ([Davis et al., 2023](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B7)). Recent advancements such as CrossGAI ([Deng et al., 2024](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B8)) and the work by [Yan et al. (2022)](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B57) have developed tools for AI-enhanced sketching and rendering.

Despite advancements in recommendation systems and the generation of fashion images, there remains a knowledge gap regarding how commercial generative AI tools like Bing[5)](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_X005), Midjourney, and DALL-E can be integrated into traditional fashion design processes to augment and accelerate creativity. Understanding these gaps is crucial for designing effective creativity support tools that enhance human creativity in the early stages of design ideation and revision. For instance, the extensive process of image collection for inspiration involves shopping trips, catwalk visits, trade shows, and desk research ([Mete, 2006](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B42)). AI’s core function of image generation is well-suited to support the transition from concept development to design development, as shown in [Figure 1](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_F1).

![](ADR_2024_v37n3_25_f001.jpg)   
Figure 1 Conventional fashion design process in six steps

Considering the traditional process, there are three key knowledge gaps in applying current generative AI tools to the early stages of the fashion design process. First, user behavior and requirements: Fashion designers have unique needs that influence how they collect and create inspiration. Without a clear understanding of these needs, it is challenging to design user-friendly ([Oppenlaender, 2022](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B44)) and effective AI systems ([Zamfirescu et al., 2023](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B59)). Research should identify the specific outputs designers find useful, the control they need over AI, and the most helpful types of feedback. Second, understanding designer-AI interaction: Limited research exists on how professional fashion designers interact with generative AI tools. Understanding how designers use these tools to generate and refine concepts ([Oppenlaender, 2022](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B44)), the challenges they face, and how they incorporate AI outputs into their decision-making is essential for tailoring AI tools to fit seamlessly into the design process. Third, impact on creativity and workflow: The impact of generative AI on the creativity and workflow of fashion designers is not well understood. Research is needed to explore how AI tools influence the creative process, from idea generation to concept refinement ([Zamfirescu et al., 2023](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B59)), and whether they enhance or limit creativity by steering designers toward specific solutions. Additionally, ethical and practical concerns, such as authorship, intellectual property, data privacy, and bias in AI-generated designs, are critical for broader AI tool acceptance in fashion design. Addressing these concerns is essential for integrating AI responsibly and effectively.

This study aims to bridge these gaps by exploring how fashion designers use generative AI for early-stage concept ideation and revision, focusing on tools like Bing, Midjourney, and DALL-E. Through detailed interviews and experiments with fashion experts, the research provides empirical insights into how these tools support and augment the creative processes of professional fashion designers, highlighting the benefits, challenges, and ethical considerations associated with AI in fashion design.

The research addresses three key questions:

* 1) How does generative AI impact the creativity of fashion designers during the early stage of the design process for ideation and revision?
* 2) What are the interactions between human designers and AI-generated sketches, and how do these interactions influence design decisions?
* 3) What ethical issues and biases arise from the use of generative AI in fashion design, and how can they be mitigated?

To explore these questions, we used a mixed-methods approach that included a pilot study, sketch experiment interviews, and a focus group discussion. 19 participants, including design students for the pilot study and professionals, used the AI tools Midjourney and DALL-E to generate fashion sketches for data collection. Data were analyzed using thematic analysis, focusing on the evaluation of AI-generated sketches and the decision-making processes of professional designers.

By integrating interviews and experiments with fashion experts, this study provides a rare exploration of AI-generated design in the fashion industry. The findings provide valuable recommendations on how to better utilize AI as a tool for fashion designers, how to integrate AI-based design tools and workflows, and how to develop AI-based fashion platforms for future applications, especially in the early stages of the design process. This research represents a pioneering effort to understand the intersection of AI and fashion design, providing a comprehensive analysis that benefits both academia and industry.

2. Related Work

By understanding the nuances of fashion design processes, the role of inspiration, the opportunities and challenges of using current AI applications, and ethical considerations, we can design a user study that effectively explores how generative AI impacts creativity, designer interactions, and ethical issues in the early stages of fashion design. These insights ensured that our research is grounded in existing knowledge while pushing the boundaries to develop more effective and responsible AI tools for the fashion design process.

2. 1. The Process of Fashion Design

The fashion design process includes various stages, from trend research and initial concept development to final product readiness for the market ([Harreis et al., 2023](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B17)) as shown in [Figure 1](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_F1). Researchers have identified different models, such as the seven-stage model: accept, analyze, define, ideate, select, implement, and evaluate ([Jeon et al., 2021](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B23); [Koberg & Bagnall, 1974](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B28); [Munasinghe et al., 2021](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B43); [Watkins, 1988](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B56)), and a six-step model: trend research, trend pack development, design development, prototype development, finalization of range, and approval ([Fung & Choi, 2018](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B13)). This process can be condensed into three main phases: idea generation, product development, and production ([ElShishtawy et al., 2022](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B11); [LaBat & Sokolowski, 1999](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B31); [Kincade et al., 2007](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B26)). Understanding these steps helped us explore how generative AI tools can be integrated at various stages, particularly during ideation and concept development, to enhance creativity and efficiency.

2. 2. Generative AI in Use for Fashion Idea Generation

Idea generation in fashion design involves collecting and synthesizing inspiration to create new design concepts, a critical process for fostering creativity and innovation ([Plucker et al., 2004](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B46)). Creativity in fashion design is influenced by factors like visual thinking and the continuous search for inspiration from diverse sources such as nature, artwork, history, music, and technology ([Mete, 2006](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B42); [McKim, 1980](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B41)). Traditional tools like sketches, collages, and mock-ups help transform tacit knowledge into tangible designs designs ([Sarmakari & Vanska, 2022](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B48); [Keller, 2005](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B25)). While AI can assist in discovering inspirational stimuli, it may also lead to design fixation and inhibit divergent thinking ([Wadinambiarachchi et al., 2024](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B55); [Cai et al., 2023](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B2)). These insights informed our exploration of how generative AI tools impact design activities, assessing whether they enhance or hinder creative thinking, as [Kwon et al. (2023)](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B30) noted, and how they influence interactions between designers and AI-generated sketches.

Recent research on AI in fashion design has focused on enhancing creativity, personalizing fashion recommendations, optimizing supply chain management, and improving sustainability ([Bhattacharya et al., 2022](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B1); [Dong et al., 2019](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B10); [Hidayati et al., 2018](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B18); [Hou et al., 2021](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B19)). Advanced tools like DMGAN, CLIP, VQGAN+CLIP, and CLIP-guided GAN have proven beneficial in accelerating the design process by providing detailed and diverse design options quickly ([Zhu et al., 2019](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B61); [Radford et al., 2021](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B47); [Crowson et al., 2022](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B4); [Smith & Colton, 2021](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B51)). These tools enable designers to explore various possibilities with fewer resources, representing a new approach to design thinking ([Lee & Lin, 2023](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B33)). Understanding these capabilities and limitations helped us investigate how AI impacts designers’ decision-making processes and interactions with AI-generated outputs, providing a benchmark for evaluating the effectiveness of AI tools.

2. 3. Potential Limitations of Generative AI for Fashion Design

Generative AI faces several ethical and technical challenges, such as bias in training data, intellectual property concerns, and the tendency to produce designs reflecting existing dominant styles ([Flick & Worrall, 2022](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B12)). For example, the fashion label Acne Studios’ approach of incorporating GAN generations into their Fall 2020 Menswear Collection ([Helen, 2020](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B45)). Also, these tools could inadvertently marginalize minority groups ([Flick & Worrall, 2022](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B12); [Lawton et al., 2023](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B32)) and lack the novelty needed for truly innovative designs ([Grabe & Zhu, 2023](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B16)). These tools can inadvertently marginalize minority groups and lack the novelty needed for truly innovative designs ([Grabe & Zhu, 2023](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B16)). Also, it is suggested that AI-generated designs often overlook the specific needs of minority groups, including designs for larger individuals, people with disabilities, and those with atypical body shapes ([Flick & Worrall, 2022](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B12)). The subjective and intuitive nature of inspiration in fashion design poses additional challenges for AI integration ([Mete, 2006](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B42); [Stappers & Hennessey, 1999](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B52)). Understanding these limitations is essential for addressing the ethical issues and biases arising from the use of generative AI in fashion design. Identifying these challenges helped us develop strategies to ensure responsible and inclusive use of AI, directly addressing the third research question on ethical issues and biases.

3. Methods

3. 1. Pilot Study

Prior to the main study, a pilot study was conducted to test the experimental design and ensure the feasibility of the proposed methods. Seven design students from the (UNIST) participated in this preliminary phase. The pilot study involved a simplified version of the main experiment, where participants engaged with AI tools to create fashion sketches. Feedback from this pilot informed refinements to the experimental design, ensuring that the tasks were clear and that the tools used were appropriate for eliciting meaningful data. We built on our research methods from ([Gmeiner et al., 2023](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B15); [Yildirim et al., 2022](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B58); [Koch et al., 2019](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B29)) that they conducted a similar research experiment, but in product design and UX/UI design topic. We tailored the the experiment into fashion design filed by modifying the design task into a fashion topic.

3. 2. Participant Recruitment

Participants for the main study were recruited using a snowball sampling method, ensuring a diverse range of fashion design professionals. Initial contacts were made through a known fashion designer, who then recommended additional participants. This method was chosen to include designers with varying levels of experience and expertise, ensuring a comprehensive understanding of how different professionals interact with AI tools. In total, 19 participants were recruited, comprising a mix of students, industry professionals, and researchers in fashion design. 3. 3. Experimental Tools

The primary AI tools used in the study were Midjourney and DALL-E, both of which are text-to-image generators capable of producing high-quality fashion sketches from textual descriptions. The choice of tools was influenced by feedback from the pilot study, where participants preferred Midjourney for its user-friendliness and superior output quality compared to other tools like Stable Diffusion. Each participant was provided with access to these tools during the experiment, ensuring consistency in the AI-generated outputs.

3. 4. Main Study Designs

The main study consisted of two components: (1) sketch experiment interviews and an (2) expert focus group discussion.

(1) Sketch Experiment Interviews

Eight fashion designers participated in the sketch experiment interviews, conducted via Zoom. The sessions were structured into three phases:

* • Warm-Up Exercises (10 minutes): Participants engaged in basic tasks to familiarize themselves with the AI tools. This phase aimed to reduce any initial hesitation and ensure participants were comfortable using the technology.
* • AI Sketches Drawing Session (5-40 minutes): Participants were tasked with creating one to two fashion sketches for their company’s new season development using the AI tools. They were encouraged to base their prompts on recent real projects, making the experiment more realistic and relevant to their professional work. Participants were allowed to choose, revise, and iterate on their prompts independently, simulating a quasi-real design environment.
* • In-Depth Interviews (20 minutes): After the sketching session, participants engaged in a detailed interview where they discussed their experiences using the AI tools. These interviews were recorded and transcribed for further analysis. Participants were asked to evaluate the AI-generated sketches using a five-point rating scale across five criteria: Visual Fidelity and Realism, Originality and Creativity, Aesthetics and Composition, Practicality and Wearability, and Designer Input and Customization.

(2) Expert Focus Group Discussion

A two-hour online focus group discussion was conducted with 11 fashion practitioners. This session aimed to explore the broader implications of AI-generated designs in the fashion industry. Topics included the strengths and weaknesses of AI in creative processes, the potential impact on traditional design practices, and the opportunities AI presents for future design work. The focus group provided a platform for participants to share their diverse perspectives and experiences, enriching the study’s findings.

3. 5. Data Analysis

The data collected from the sketch experiment interviews and the focus group discussion were analyzed using thematic analysis. This method involves coding the data to identify recurring themes and patterns, providing a structured approach to understanding the qualitative insights gathered from participants as shown in [Figure 2](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_F2). The coding process was facilitated by ATLAS.ti, ensuring systematic and rigorous analysis through triangulation.

3. 6. Evaluation Criteria

The evaluation of AI-generated sketches was based on a six-question form, focusing on multiple criteria to assess the quality, creativity, and practicality of the designs based on ([Lupton, E., & Phillips, J. C., 2015](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B38)), ([Leborg, C., 2006](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B34)), and ([Culpepper, M. K., 2013](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B6)). We interpret and revise the categories to fit the fashion design field. The criteria were:

* • Visual Fidelity and Realism: Assessing the accuracy and detail of the AI-generated images.
* • Originality and Creativity: Evaluating the uniqueness and innovative aspects of the designs.
* • Aesthetics and Composition: Considering the overall visual appeal and layout of the sketches.
* • Practicality and Wearability: Determining the feasibility of producing and wearing the designs.
* • Designer Input and Customization: Measuring the extent to which designers could influence and personalize the AI-generated outputs.

Participants rated these criteria on a five-point scale and provided qualitative feedback, highlighting the strengths and limitations of the AI tools in their creative processes.

As for the visualization materials, we output all the AI-generated images and their prompts from the sketch experiments and uploaded them to Figma. We then organized them by participant and by time, and analyzed each participant’s iteration process as shown in [Figure 3](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_F3). This figure represents a workflow map of participant S6, who uses Midjourney as a tool during his design process. These results could provide a comprehensive understanding of the generative design tools in enhancing the ideation process and creating new meanings and experiences for fashion designers.

![](ADR_2024_v37n3_25_f003.jpg)   
Figure 3 A workflow map of participant S6 who utilizes Midjourney as a tool during their ideation and revision process.

3. 7. Ethical Considerations

We obtained approval from the Institutional Review Board (IRB) at our institution to ensure that all aspects of our experiment met ethical standards. All participants gave informed consent. Their confidentiality and privacy were strictly maintained throughout the study.

4. Results

The results of this study provide critical insights into how generative AI tools can support and augment the creative processes in the early stages of fashion design, the nature of designers’ interactions with AI-generated sketches, and the challenges and ethical considerations associated with using these tools.

4. 1. The designers’ evaluation of AI-generated fashion sketches

Participants rated AI-generated fashion sketches based on Visual Fidelity and Realism, Originality and Creativity, Aesthetics and Composition, Practicality and Wearability, and Designer Input and Customization. Designers rated Visual Fidelity and Realism the highest, while Designer Input and Customization received the lowest scores as shown in [Table 3](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_T3). However, designers considered Designer Input and Customization to be the most important category, highlighting a significant gap between AI capabilities and designer needs. Originality and creativity, while considered critical, were also areas where AI performed poorly. These findings suggest that future AI development should focus on improving customization and creativity to better meet the needs of fashion designers.

4. 2. Human designers and AI-generated tools interaction in creative decision-making

4. 2. 1. Modes of AI usage by fashion designers

Fashion designers utilized AI tools in three primary modes:

Text-to-Sketch for Rapid Concept Realization: Designers use text prompts to generate initial sketches when they have vague concepts in mind as shown in [Figure 4](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_F4). This method provides a tangible representation of their ideas, boosting confidence (Participant S6).

Hand-Drawn Sketch Enhancement: Designers input hand-drawn sketches into AI tools to add more detailed designs as showan in [Figure 5](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_F5). This is particularly helpful for those with weaker digital sketching skills (Participant S3).

Software-Assisted Sketch Enhancement: Designers use AI to enhance sketches created with computer software like Adobe Illustrator as shown [Figure 6](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_F6), aiming to visualize fabrics and techniques realistically without creating 3D simulation samples (Participant S5).

These modes highlight the diverse ways in which AI tools can be integrated into the design process, enhancing different aspects of creative decision-making. Understanding these interactions helps tailor AI tools to better support designers’ workflows.

4. 2. 2. AI tools as a bridge

Some participants emphasized that AI-generated images can provide inspiration and new directions when creativity or artistic skills are lacking. They suggested that AI tools can provide inspiration and new directions when designers face creative blocks. These tools can help visualize and expand conceptual ideas, which can help with brand planning and visual aesthetics ([Zhang et al., 2023](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B60)). They also suggested that AI can combine knowledge from different fields, generating unique design ideas that go beyond individual inspiration. This interdisciplinary approach enriches the creative process, as seen in designs that combine Issey Miyake’s style with other elements ([Hwang, 2022](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B21); Participant F2). AI’s ability to serve as a bridge and blender underscores its role in enhancing creativity and helping designers explore different styles and concepts.

4. 2. 3. Iterative Use of AI to Meet Their Goals

Designers iteratively refine AI-generated images by modifying prompts to align outputs with their vision. Experienced users create more accurate prompts, resulting in outputs that closely match their intentions (Participants S1, S2, S4, S5, S7). However, a richer experience did not necessarily translate into faster task completion ([Figure 7](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_F7)). AI provides designers with endless ideas and experimentation ([Figure 8](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_F8)). However, S5 also noted that if designers do not have a firm grasp of the intended topic and rely too heavily on AI, they risk being influenced by AI and deviating from their original design intent. Therefore, the iterative nature of using AI tools reflects their potential to enhance design accuracy and creativity. The need for clear design concepts and frameworks remains critical to prevent over-reliance on AI and ensure human-centered design outcomes, as suggested by [Liu (2023)](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B36).

4. 3. Challenges, biases, and ethical considerations in fashion design

4. 3. 1. Efficiency generation can inhibit deep thinking.

Participants expressed concerns that AI might inhibit deep thinking by providing straightforward design outcomes lacking reflective dialogue between designers and their media ([Maher & Poon, 1996](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B39); [Schon, 1983](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B49)). AI-generated images are often perceived as less valuable than designers’ original ideas (Participant S5). There is also a lack of comprehensive copyright laws addressing ownership of AI-generated materials.

4. 3. 2. Understanding issues with AI

AI-generated designs can exhibit randomness, leading to misalignment with designers’ intentions ([Verheijden & Funk, 2023](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B54)). Translating ideas into AI prompts often results in less rich or accurate images due to the characteristics of generative AI’s image synthesis mechanism. Enhancing designers’ knowledge of AI prompts and improving AI’s understanding of design terminology is critical for better alignment between AI outputs and creative visions as [Figure 9](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_F9) illustrated. These challenges emphasize the importance of building designers’ knowledge of AI prompts and descriptive logic to improve alignment between AI outputs and their creative visions. Enhancing AI’s understanding of design terminology is also critical.

![](ADR_2024_v37n3_25_f009.jpg)   
Figure 9 We observed this inequality during the inspiration phase. AI may enrich the designer's idea, diminish it, or, very rarely, match it exactly due to the characteristics of the generative AI using latent space.

4. 3. 3. Limitations of AI Sketches for Novelty and Uniqueness

AI-generated designs can exhibit randomness, leading to misalignment with designers’ intentions. The complexity of translating ideas into AI prompts often results in less rich or accurate images ([Verheijden & Funk, 2023](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B54)). Misinterpretation of fashion design terminology further complicates the process (Participant S5). Participants believed that AI had a limited understanding of some very novel ideas and unique styles, or ideas that did not follow the existing logic. An example is from S6*“We found that the AI didn’t understand the concept fully and generated mostly images of people wearing traditional coats. We attempted to provide a similar image to guide its generation, but the result still didn’t match our mental image... it operates based on existing content and doesn’t conform to uncommon design principles”*. AI also have a limited understanding of design principles and human aesthetics. For instance, S1 mentioned that AI is struggling to grasp the reasonable distribution of muscles and appropriate balance. Moreover, F8 explained: *“AI is great for creativity and concepts, but clothing needs physical representation, and this intermediate process depends on many factors”*. AI has limitations in comprehending unconventional or highly original ideas that defy standard logic. Recognizing these limitations is crucial for developing AI tools that better support the unique and innovative aspects of fashion design. AI should be seen as a complementary tool rather than a replacement for human creativity and detailed craftsmanship.

4. 4. Impact on transforming the fashion design process with generative AI

4. 4. 1. AI tools serve as a starting point.

Participants highlighted the role of generative AI in enhancing efficiency and inspiring creativity during the initial stages of design as [Tholander & Jonsson (2023)](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B53) and [Verheijden & Funk (2023)](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B54) suggested. AI-generated designs are better suited for inspiration rather than final products, aiding in brand planning and image searches but requiring human intervention for execution and detailed design (Participants S1, S2, S4); this confirms ([Tholander & Jonsson, 2023](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B53); [Zhang et al., 2023](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B60))’s results. These insights suggest that AI tools should be viewed as starting points for creativity, complemented by human expertise for practical implementation.

4. 4. 2. Fashion designers need customized AI.

Participants identified a gap in the market for AI generative design platforms specifically tailored to fashion design. While platforms like AiDLab[6)](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_X006), Fabrie12[7)](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_X007), and Zhiyi Tech[8)](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_X008)’s Fashion Diffusion Beta exist, they do not fully meet the specific needs of clothing design. Developing specialized AI tools with tailored functionalities, detailed instructions, and advanced search capabilities can better support designers’ creative processes as [Chiou et al. (2023)](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B3) and [Yildirim et al. (2022)](#ADR_2024_v37n3_25_B58) noted.

4. 4. 3. Fashion designers’ roles and responsibilities in the future.

The integration of AI in fashion design is creating new roles and responsibilities for designers. However, there is a disparity between the demand for AI skills and the availability of training and real project opportunities. To bridge this gap, fashion companies need to provide more structured training and project opportunities for designers to develop AI skills. Fashion education programs should also incorporate AI training to prepare future designers for effective collaboration with these technologies (Participants S3, S4, F7).

5. Discussion

The results of this study provide substantial insights into the role and impact of generative AI tools in the early stages of fashion design, highlighting both the potential benefits and the challenges of existing tools. The findings suggest the importance of customization, interaction dynamics, and ethical considerations for the future creative workflow of fashion designers.

5. 1. Impact of generative AI on the early design activities in Fashion Design

The evaluation of AI-generated fashion sketches reveals that while AI excels in visual fidelity and realism, it falls short in originality, creativity, and customization. This disparity points to a crucial area for improvement in AI tools. For AI to genuinely augment the creative process, it must offer greater flexibility and customization options that align more closely with designers’ needs. The true value of AI lies in its capacity to inspire and foster unique, original ideas. Future AI development should prioritize enhancing creative functionalities and providing more sophisticated customization features to support the ideation phase more effectively.

5. 2. Interactions between designers and AI-generated sketches

The study highlights diverse modes of interaction between human designers and AI tools, including text-to-sketch generation, hand-drawn sketch enhancement, and software-assisted sketch refinement. These interactions illustrate how AI can be integrated into different stages of the design process, enhancing creativity and decision-making. Using text prompts to quickly visualize vague concepts boosts designers’ confidence, while enhancing hand-drawn sketches with AI helps refine ideas more efficiently. AI tools act as bridges, providing inspiration and new directions when designers face creative blocks. This cross-disciplinary blending of ideas enriches the creative process by enabling designers to explore a broader range of styles and concepts. However, the iterative use of AI, where designers refine outputs through repeated prompt modifications, highlights a potential dependency risk. While AI can offer endless ideas and experimentation opportunities, there is a risk of designers deviating from their original intent if they overly rely on AI-generated suggestions. Designers need to maintain a clear framework and design concept to ensure AI complements rather than overshadows their creative vision.

5. 3. Ethical issues in data and biases in visual materials generated

The study identifies several ethical concerns and biases associated with AI-generated designs. Participants expressed worries about AI inhibiting deep, reflective thinking, as the straightforward design outcomes provided by AI can lack the nuanced dialogue between designer and media essential for creativity. The perception that AI-generated images are less valuable than original ideas also highlights a significant challenge in integrating AI into creative processes. Additionally, the lack of comprehensive copyright laws for AI-generated materials poses a legal and ethical dilemma, emphasizing the need for clearer regulations to protect designers’ intellectual property.

Understanding issues with AI, such as the randomness and misalignment of AI-generated designs with designers’ intentions, complicates the integration of AI in fashion design. Translating ideas into AI prompts often results in less rich or accurate images, highlighting the importance of building designers’ knowledge of AI prompts and improving AI’s understanding of design terminology. Enhancing AI’s ability to accurately interpret and generate designs based on specific fashion terminology is critical for better alignment with designers’ creative visions.

5. 4. Practical and ethical implications

To fully leverage the benefits of generative AI in fashion design, developers need to focus on enhancing the customization and creative capabilities of AI tools. Providing designers with more control over AI-generated outputs and integrating advanced customization options will help align these tools with the specific needs of the fashion industry. Ethically, it is crucial to address the biases and limitations of AI-generated designs. Ensuring that AI tools do not perpetuate existing biases or marginalize minority groups is essential for creating inclusive and diverse fashion designs. Developing clearer guidelines and regulations regarding the ownership and copyright of AI-generated designs will help protect designers’ intellectual property and foster a more ethical integration of AI in fashion design.

6. Conclusion

This study provides substantial insights into the role of generative AI tools in the early stages of fashion design, highlighting their potential to enhance creativity and streamline the design process. AI tools like Midjourney, DALL-E, and Bing can significantly augment the creative processes of fashion designers by providing rapid, diverse visual stimuli. However, the findings reveal that while AI excels in generating visually realistic and detailed images, it falls short in originality, creativity, and customization. To genuinely augment the creative process, future AI development must prioritize enhancing these creative functionalities and offering more sophisticated customization options.

Interactions between designers and AI tools are diverse, ranging from text-to-sketch generation to hand-drawn and software-assisted sketch enhancements. These interactions help integrate AI into different stages of the design process, enhancing creativity and decision-making. Nevertheless, the iterative use of AI highlights a potential dependency risk, underscoring the need for designers to maintain a clear framework and design concept to ensure AI complements rather than overshadows their creative vision.

Ethical concerns and biases in AI-generated designs present significant challenges. Issues such as inhibiting deep reflective thinking, perceived lower value of AI-generated images, and the lack of comprehensive copyright laws for AI-generated materials highlight the need for ethical guidelines and clearer regulations. Addressing these concerns is crucial for the responsible and inclusive use of AI in fashion design.

Despite its contributions, this study has several limitations. The relatively small sample size and the specific demographic of participants may limit the generalizability of the findings. The study also primarily utilized Midjourney and DALL-E, which, while effective, represent only a subset of available AI tools, and the design tasks in this study were limited to initial ideation and sketching. Lastly, this study did not address into the long-term impact of generative AI on the fashion design process and desginers’ reliance.

Future research should explore a broader range of AI tools and their long-term impacts on the fashion design process. Investigating how AI can be tailored to support specific design needs and preferences will be crucial. Furthermore, addressing ethical concerns and biases through comprehensive studies will help develop clearer guidelines and regulations for AI integration in fashion design. Expanding the scope to include the later stages of the design process will provide a more holistic understanding of AI’s role in the fashion industry. Finally, future work should consider larger, more diverse sample sizes to validate and extend the findings of this study.

# Summary: Understanding Fashion Designers' Behavior Using Generative AI for Early-Stage Concept Ideation and Revision

## Publication Details
- **Authors:** Yu Jin, Juhyeok Yoon, James Self, Kyungho Lee (Ulsan National Institute of Science and Technology, Korea)
- **Journal:** Archives of Design Research, Vol. 37, No. 3, July 2024, pp. 25-45
- **DOI:** https://doi.org/10.15187/adr.2024.07.37.3.25

## Objective
This study explores how commercial generative AI tools (Bing, Midjourney, DALL-E) can augment the creative processes of professional fashion designers during early-stage concept ideation and revision.

## Methodology
- **Mixed-methods approach** including: pilot study, sketch experiment interviews, and focus group discussion
- **19 participants total:** 8 in sketch experiment interviews (fashion designers, researchers, students) + 11 in focus group discussion (fashion practitioners)
- **AI tools used:** Midjourney and DALL-E (text-to-image generators)
- **Data analysis:** Thematic analysis using ATLAS.ti, with evaluation across five criteria: Visual Fidelity and Realism, Originality and Creativity, Aesthetics and Composition, Practicality and Wearability, and Designer Input and Customization
- **Three research questions:** (1) How does generative AI impact creativity during ideation/revision? (2) What are designer-AI interactions and how do they influence decisions? (3) What ethical issues and biases arise?

## Key Findings

### Evaluation of AI-Generated Sketches
| Criteria | Mean Rating | Rank |
|---|---|---|
| Visual Fidelity and Realism | 4.25 | 1st |
| Aesthetics and Composition | 3.88 | 2nd |
| Practicality and Wearability | 3.50 | 2nd |
| Originality and Creativity | 3.25 | 4th |
| Designer Input and Customization | 3.13 | 5th |

Designers rated **Designer Input and Customization** as the most important category but AI performed worst here, highlighting a significant gap between AI capabilities and designer needs.

### Three Modes of AI Usage by Designers
1. **Text-to-Sketch** for rapid concept realization from vague ideas
2. **Hand-Drawn Sketch Enhancement** — inputting hand-drawn sketches into AI for detailed refinement
3. **Software-Assisted Sketch Enhancement** — using AI to enhance digital sketches (e.g., Adobe Illustrator) to visualize fabrics without 3D simulation

### AI as a Bridge and Blender
AI tools provide inspiration and new directions when designers face creative blocks, combining knowledge from different fields to generate unique ideas.

### Iterative Use
Designers iteratively refine AI-generated images by modifying prompts. Experienced users create more accurate prompts, but richer experience did not necessarily translate into faster task completion.

## Challenges Identified
1. **Efficiency generation may inhibit deep thinking** — AI provides straightforward outcomes lacking reflective dialogue
2. **Understanding issues with AI** — randomness and misalignment between designer intentions and AI outputs; AI struggles with fashion design terminology and unconventional ideas
3. **Limitations for novelty** — AI operates based on existing content and doesn't conform to uncommon design principles
4. **Bias in training data** — AI may marginalize minority groups, overlook needs for larger individuals, people with disabilities, atypical body shapes
5. **Intellectual property concerns** — lack of comprehensive copyright laws for AI-generated materials
6. **Risk of over-reliance** — designers may deviate from original intent if too dependent on AI suggestions

## Conclusions
- Generative AI significantly enhances early-stage fashion design by providing rapid, diverse visual stimuli
- AI should be viewed as a **starting point for inspiration** and a **complementary tool** rather than replacement for human creativity
- Need for **customized AI platforms** specifically tailored to fashion design
- **Fashion education programs** should incorporate AI training
- Future research should explore broader range of AI tools, long-term impacts, and ethical implications

## Funding
Supported by Korea Institute for Advancement of Technology (KIAT) and Ministry of Trade, Industry & Energy (MOTIE, Korea).
