# Copyright uses for AI training go beyond the scope of the text and data mining exception: Several EU member states agree

[All CCS and Cross-sectoral](https://creativesunite.eu/theme/all-ccs-and-cross-sectoral/) [Music](https://creativesunite.eu/theme/music/) [Performing Arts](https://creativesunite.eu/theme/performing-arts/) [Visual Arts](https://creativesunite.eu/theme/visual-arts/) [Literature & Books](https://creativesunite.eu/theme/literature-books/) [Media & Press](https://creativesunite.eu/theme/media-press/) [Audiovisual - Film, TV & Radio](https://creativesunite.eu/theme/audiovisual-film-tv-radio/) [Video Games & Multi-media](https://creativesunite.eu/theme/video-games-multi-media/) [Design & Fashion](https://creativesunite.eu/theme/design-fashion/) [Architecture](https://creativesunite.eu/theme/architecture/) [Research / Surveys](https://creativesunite.eu/theme/research-surveys/) [Artificial Intelligence](https://creativesunite.eu/theme/artificial-intelligence/)

![](https://creativesunite.eu/images/900px-Artificial_Intelligence___AI___Machine_Learning.jpg)

This acknowledgment reinforces the arguments of the authors' coalition, which points to a problematic application of the Directive that allows AI models to be trained on copyrighted content without the permission of the creators.

 By Ilias Maroutsis   
January 21, 2025

![](images/logos/file_document.svg)

[Save as PDF](generate_pdf.php?slug=copyright-uses-for-ai-training-go-beyond-the-scope-of-the-text-and-data-mining-exception-several-eu-member-states-agree)

You can download this article in PDF format here!

Find out more here:

Unclarities regarding the applicability of the Text and Data Mining (TDM) exception to AI training admit many Member States of the European Union as shown by their responses to a questionnaire on the relationship between generative artificial intelligence and copyright.   
  
The questionnaire was circulated to the 27 Member States last summer by the Hungarian Presidency of the Council of Europe, recognising that the increasing prevalence of AI-generated content poses significant challenges to the creative industries. The Member States were invited to submit proposals on seven different topics related to AI and copyright.  
  
The insights from the recently published Member States' replies seem to support the claims of the [Coalition of Creators](https://composeralliance.org/media/1748-joint-letter-on-ai-to-executive-vp-virkkunen-and-commissioner-micallef.pdf), who sent an open letter to the relevant EU Commissioners in December, pointing to the problematic reality regarding AI and authors' rights that has resulted from a misinterpretation of the 2019 Directive on the TDM exception.  
  
The signatories of the open letter claimed that all generative AI models in existence today are trained in complete opacity on vast amounts of copyrighted content and personal data, scraped and copied from the internet without permission or compensation to the creators. This is because the relevant EU directive of 2019 introduced an exception to copyright for text and data mining (TDM), unless creators and other rights holders have expressly reserved their rights (Article 4 of the CDSM Directive). According to the coalition of creators although Article 4 was adopted years before the sudden emergence of generative AI technologies and does not mention or define "artificial intelligence" and "generative AI", the European Commission appears to have retrospectively interpreted this exception broadly to cover the systematic and extensive use of creators' protected works and performances without any authorisation. 

#### The responses of the Member States

Based on the responses to the questionnaire, it is clear that the relationship between AI and copyright is at the centre of attention and that several activities are taking place in the Member States to analyse the links between AI and copyright.  
  
While most of the Member States' contributions showed that the current EU legal framework is sufficient to address the issues that arise, the majority of Member States raised practical issues where, in their view, more clarity and certainty would be needed to better implement the existing EU acquis.  
  
According to the report, the most frequently raised issue in this context was the applicability of the text and data mining (TDM) exception and its opt-out mechanism, introduced by Directive (EU) 2019/790 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 17 April 2019 on copyright and related rights in the digital single market (hereinafter: the DSM Directive), to the AI training process. According to a significant number of contributions, there are certain uncertainties regarding the applicability of the TDM exception to AI training. This was reflected in a number of national positions and many stakeholder views. In this context, several Member States considered that copyright uses for AI training go beyond the scope of the TDM exception.  
However, Member States agreed that there is no need to provide new or additional copyright-related protection. Several Member States expressed the view that the existing legal framework, including the current opt-out provision of Article 4(3) of the DSM Directive, combined with the AI Act's transparency obligation with respect to training data, should be sufficient to encourage the conclusion of licences between rightholders and AI companies. In their view, however, it is crucial that these provisions are properly implemented and enforced.   
  
A significant number of Member States and stakeholders considered that the mass scale of AI-related copyright uses and the practical challenges for rightholders in policing them both underline the importance of collective management in this area. Many Member States reflected the views of their stakeholders, who supported the individual licensing approach and licence-based education for generative AI.  
  
With regard to further measures that could be taken at EU level to facilitate the conclusion of licences between right holders and AI developers, there were diverging views on the possible establishment of a remuneration scheme for generative AI activities.

# The New Copyright Directive: Text and Data Mining (Articles 3 and 4)

[P. Bernt Hugenholtz](https://legalblogs.wolterskluwer.com/copyright-blog/author/bernthugenholtz/) [(Institute for Information Law (IViR))](http://www.ivir.nl/)

July 24, 2019

![search-result-placeholder-16-9.jpg](https://legalblogs.wolterskluwer.com/copyright-blog/themes/custom/kli_blogs_theme/images/search-result-placeholder-16-9.jpg)

Image

![copyright-40632_1280-2](/copyright-blog/uploads/sites/49/styles/large/public/2019/06/copyright-40632_1280.png.webp?itok=yYhH7erD "copyright-40632_1280")

Art. 2(2) of the DSM Directive defines ‘text and data mining’ as “any automated analytical technique aimed at analysing text and data in digital form in order to generate information which includes but is not limited to patterns, trends and correlations”. [Text and data mining](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Data_mining) (TDM) generally refers to the computer-based analysis of large bodies of data in order to gain knowledge.

With the increasing powers of computer processing and the omnipresence of vast amounts of minable text and data on the Internet, TDM has become a hugely important research tool in science and many other domains. For example, in linguistics TDM can be used [to analyze large bodies of text to extract syntactic or grammatical patterns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Text_mining). TDM is also applied in numerous other scientific domains, ranging from astronomy to musicology to the social sciences. Outside the world of science proper, data mining plays a growing role in the arts, as the spectacular [Next Rembrandt](https://www.google.com/url?sa=t&rct=j&q=&esrc=s&source=web&cd=1&cad=rja&uact=8&ved=2ahUKEwj5m6yamcHjAhVGDewKHUXWDwAQFjAAegQIARAB&url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.nextrembrandt.com%2F&usg=AOvVaw2kS10Amm4mdjVIpNmnrXuv) project that produced an amazing Rembrandt-like portrait based on mining Rembrandt’s oeuvre, reveals.

In the industrial and commercial realm TDM has become even more pervasive. Text and data mining is nowadays standard practice in pharmaceutical research, journalism, information retrieval, search, and consumer information – to name just a few areas. TDM is also an essential tool in developing intelligent applications that require vast volumes of raw text and data to ‘self-learn’ complex tasks such as translation or speech recognition. [Much of the current and future development in artificial intelligence, therefore, depends on TDM](https://www.leru.org/news/better-rules-on-text-and-data-mining-are-needed-to-maximise-the-potential-of-artificial-intelligence-in-europe).

With the InfoSoc Directive’s all-inclusive reproduction right extending to every “direct or indirect, temporary or permanent reproduction by any means and in any form, in whole or in part” (Art. 2 InfoSoc Directive), TDM creates potential conflicts with copyright law when copyright protected content is mined. Similarly, the sui generis database right may also be implicated. Whereas [some scholars](http://copyrightblog.kluweriplaw.com/2019/03/19/limitations-to-text-and-data-mining-and-consumer-empowerment-making-the-case-for-a-right-to-machine-legibility/) have advocated a normative interpretation of the reproduction right, which would restrict its scope to exploitative uses “of the work as the work”, and would [rule out non-exploitative uses such as mining](https://www.ivir.nl/new-book-in-information-law-series-copyright-reconstructed/), the EU legislature assumed that an express TDM exception was required for reasons of legal certainty (see [EC, Impact Assessment](https://ec.europa.eu/digital-single-market/en/news/impact-assessment-modernisation-eu-copyright-rules), p. 104-105; see [recital 8 DSM)](https://eur-lex.europa.eu/eli/dir/2019/790/oj).

While the need to ensure broad TDM freedoms in science was always self-evident, the EU’s approach towards text and data mining in the commercial realm is more ambivalent. The European Commission’s draft DSM Directive merely proposed a mandatory TDM exception for the benefit of non-commercial research organizations and cultural heritage institutions. During the discussions in the Council Working Group, following a proposal by the Dutch delegation, an optional exception was added that conditionally permitted TDM for commercial purposes. In the end, the European Parliament gave mandatory status to that exception as well. Consequently, the DSM Directive now comprises two obligatory DSM provisions: Articles 3 and 4. The two exceptions are not, however, equally robust.

Art. 3 exempts acts of reproduction and extraction committed by “research organisations and cultural heritage institutions”. Art. 2(3) defines a ‘cultural heritage institution’ as “a publicly accessible library or museum, an archive or a film or audio heritage institution”. According to Art. 2(1), a ‘research organisation’ is either a not-for-profit entity or an entity tasked by a Member State with a public service research mission. Public broadcasting organizations and commercial research institutes, for example, are therefore excluded from the scope of Art. 3, but might still find solace in Art. 4.

In addition to permitting mining activities per se, Art. 3(2) allows the secure storage and retention of copies of mined works and other subject matter “for the purposes of scientific research, including for the verification of research results”.  This is important because empirical scientific research generally requires research data to remain available for corroboration purposes. Nevertheless, Art. 3 permits TDM only in respect of works or other subject matter (e.g. databases) to which beneficiary organizations “have lawful access”. According to Recital 14, ‘lawful access’ covers access to content pursuant to contractual arrangements (e.g. subscriptions or open access licenses), as well as to “content that is freely available online”. The requirement of ‘lawful access’ does not however imply that rightholders may contractually rule out text and data mining in their terms of agreement. Article 7 expressly provides that any contractual provision contrary to Article 5 is unenforceable. Note as well that the option to ‘opt out’ out of the TDM exemption is provided only in respect of the non-research uses governed by Art. 4.

Rightholders do remain free to “apply measures to ensure the security and integrity of the networks and databases where the works or other subject matter are hosted. Such measures shall not go beyond what is necessary to achieve that objective” (Art. 3(3)). As Recital 16 clarifies, such measures are justifiable only for reasons of systems or database security and integrity (e.g. “in view of a potentially high number of access requests to, and downloads of, their works or other subject matter”), not for purely commercial reasons.  Given the limited potential harm (if any) that right holders might suffer from this exemption, Member States need not provide for financial compensation (Recital 17).

The Directive’s second TDM exception encompasses a much broader class of users, but is considerably narrower in scope. Art. 4(1) generally allows acts of reproduction and extraction “for the purposes of text and data mining”, and reproductions and extractions may be retained for the same purpose. The provision thus permits TDM for all imaginable purposes, regardless of any underlying commercial motive. Art. 4 does, however, allow rightholders to opt out of the exemption. Art. 4(3) applies only on condition that right holders have not expressly reserved their rights “in an appropriate manner, such as machine-readable means in the case of content made publicly available online”. According to Recital 18, “it should only be considered appropriate to reserve those rights by the use of machine-readable means, including metadata and terms and conditions of a website or a service. […] In other cases, it can be appropriate to reserve the rights by other means, such as contractual agreements or a unilateral declaration.” In other words, Art. 4 right holders may effectively prohibit text and data mining for commercial uses by adding robot.txt type metadata to their content online.

As a result, the Directive effectively creates and legitimizes a derivative market for text and data mining, which right holders may wish to control, license or even entirely prohibit.  While most content owners will have no incentive to prohibit or monetize data mining, some right holders will. Scientific publishers, for example, are well aware that their publishing portfolios have informational value beyond the published articles they have aggregated. Indeed, some publishers already offer paid-for text and data mining as value-added services, and will be reluctant to grant TDM licenses to third parties. Other publishers are still in the process of developing licensing strategies to capitalize on this emerging market (see report [here](https://pure.uva.nl/ws/files/8885048/FutureTDM_D3.3_Baseline_Report_of_Policies_and_Barriers_of_TDM_in_Europe.pdf)).

In conclusion, the TDM provisions of the DSM Directive secure considerably less freedom to text and data mine than they initially appear to do. The opt-out clause of Art. 4, in particular, leaves for-profit miners in the EU at the mercy of the content owners. This puts AI developers, journalists, commercial research labs, and other innovators at a competitive disadvantage [in comparison with the United States](http://copyrightblog.kluweriplaw.com/2018/07/12/eus-controversial-digital-single-market-directive-part-ii-proposed-mandatory-text-data-mining-exception-restrictive/), where text and data mining is deemed fair use, even if it is done for profit. One may wonder if innovation in Europe would not have been better served without any of the TDM exceptions in the new Directive.

*This post is part of a series on the new Directive (EU) 2019/790 on copyright and related rights in the Digital Single Market (CDSM Directive):*

[The New Copyright Directive: A tour d'horizon - Part II (of press publishers, upload filters and the real value gap)](http://copyrightblog.kluweriplaw.com/2019/06/17/the-new-copyright-directive-a-tour-dhorizon-part-ii-of-press-publishers-upload-filters-and-the-real-value-gap/) by João Pedro Quintais

[The New Copyright Directive: Collective licensing as a way to strike a fair balance between creator and user interests in copyright legislation (Article 12)](http://copyrightblog.kluweriplaw.com/2019/06/25/the-new-copyright-directive-collective-licensing-as-a-way-to-strike-a-fair-balance-between-creator-and-user-interests-in-copyright-legislation-article-12/) by Johan Axhamn

Note as well that the option to 'opt out' out of the TDM exemption is provided only in respect of the non-research uses governed by Art. 4.", "Art. 4(3) applies only on condition that right holders have not expressly reserved their rights 'in an appropriate manner, such as machine-readable means in the case of content made publicly available online'.", "In conclusion, the TDM provisions of the DSM Directive secure considerably less freedom to text and data mine than they initially appear to do. The opt-out clause of Art. 4, in particular, leaves for-profit miners in the EU at the mercy of the content owners."
args.summary:
This blog post by P. Bernt Hugenholtz (Institute for Information Law, IViR), published July 24, 2019, analyzes Articles 3 and 4 of the EU DSM Directive (2019/790) concerning Text and Data Mining (TDM) exceptions.

The post defines TDM as "any automated analytical technique aimed at analysing text and data in digital form in order to generate information which includes but is not limited to patterns, trends and correlations." It notes TDM is critical for scientific research, AI development, and commercial applications, but conflicts with copyright law's broad reproduction right.

**Article 3** creates a mandatory TDM exception for "research organisations and cultural heritage institutions" (non-profit entities or those with public service research missions). It permits reproduction and extraction of lawfully accessed content, allows secure storage for scientific research verification, and prohibits contractual override of the exception. Rightholders may apply security measures for network/database integrity but not for commercial reasons. No financial compensation is required.

**Article 4** applies to all users (including commercial entities) but allows rightholders to opt out by expressly reserving their rights "in an appropriate manner, such as machine-readable means" (e.g., robot.txt-type metadata). This effectively creates a derivative market for TDM licensing.

The author concludes that the TDM provisions secure "considerably less freedom to text and data mine than they initially appear to do," putting EU commercial miners (AI developers, journalists, research labs) at a competitive disadvantage compared to the US, where TDM is deemed fair use even for profit.

<webpage_content>
![Norton Rose Fulbright logo](https://www.nortonrosefulbright.com/-/media/nrf/modules/header/logo.svg?iar=0&revision=9457b274-88a1-464c-b861-61d519df49c5,5248331205337387904&hash=874D231970B1E4FE87E1B5EFF6CDB1BA)

# AI in litigation series: An update on AI copyright cases in 2026

## 

Authors:

United States | 
Publication | 
March 2026

As [artificial intelligence](https://www.nortonrosefulbright.com/en/services/71588072/artificial-intelligence) (AI) continues to expand its breadth of capabilities and scope of use, it continues to challenge existing legal principles in new and varied ways. [Copyright](https://www.nortonrosefulbright.com/en/services/eb4f91e2/copyright-law) issues are at the forefront of these challenges and have seen significant [litigation](https://www.nortonrosefulbright.com/en/services/3f9af3de/litigation-and-disputes) related to the use of AI and ownership of the end products created.

In general, copyright law covers and protects “original works of authorship fixed in any tangible medium of expression.”[1](#1) An original work of authorship is a work that is independently created by a human author and possesses at least some minimal degree of creativity. A work is “fixed” when it is captured, either by or under the authority of an author, in a sufficiently permanent medium such that the work can be perceived, reproduced or communicated for more than a short time. Simply put, copyright protects the *expression*, not the *idea*.

The [US Copyright Office](https://www.copyright.gov/) recognized AI’s potential disruption to copyright law years ago and in 2023 launched its official initiative on AI to examine AI’s impact to copyright law more closely. To that end, the US Copyright Office has released two reports on AI’s impact already, the second of which was focused on the “copyrightability” of material created with or while using AI. The report noted that, generally, “copyright protection in the United States requires human authorship. This foundational principle is based on the Copyright Clause in the Constitution and the language of the Copyright Act as interpreted by the courts. The Copyright Clause grants Congress the authority to “secur[e] for limited times to authors . . . the exclusive right to their . . . writings.” As the Supreme Court has explained, “the author [of a copyrighted work] is . . . the person who translates an idea into a fixed, tangible expression entitled to copyright protection.” No court has recognized copyright in material created by non-humans, and those that have spoken on this issue have rejected the possibility.[2](#2) In the context of generative AI, in the US at least, copyright law does not currently protect AI outputs.

These principles have been tested recently, with numerous copyright infringement cases filed in the US against AI model providers and users. Many of these cases raise fundamental questions about whether training AI on copyrighted works constitutes fair use, whether AI-generated outputs infringe copyrights or are copyrightable and who bears liability for potentially infringing outputs. Some of these cases are still pending, while others have settled.

Here, we analyze six of the most notable AI-related copyright cases and discuss their effects on copyright law and AI usage. Namely, (1) *Thaler v. Perlmutte*r[3](#3); (2) *Thomson Reuters v. Ross Intelligence*;[4](#4) (3) *Bartz et al. v. Anthropic*;[5](#5) (4) *Kadrey et al. v. Meta Platforms Inc.*;[6](#6) (5) *In Re OpenAI, Inc. Copyright Infringement Litigation*[7](#7); and (6) *Disney et al. v. Midjourney*.[8](file:///C:/Users/nd62103/Downloads/2026.03.10_Client%20Alert_AI%20Litigation%20Series_Copyright%20Cases_FINAL%20DRAFT_Comms.docx#_ftn8)

Summary of the cases

### *Thaler v. Perlmutter*

Dr. Stephen Thaler, a computer scientist, developed a generative AI system called the "Creativity Machine.” This system created an artwork titled “A Recent Entrance to Paradise,” shown below:[10](#10)

![Norton Rose Fulbright | AI in litigation series: An update on AI copyright cases in 2026](https://www.nortonrosefulbright.com/-/media/images/nrf/thought-leadership/us/2026/ai-in-litigation-series-an-update-on-ai-copyright-cases-in-2026_image-1.jpg?revision=5250774643747387904&h=191&w=257&hash=80C3FD55C45A4F024F88840E779C25E3)

![Norton Rose Fulbright | AI in litigation series: An update on AI copyright cases in 2026](https://www.nortonrosefulbright.com/-/media/images/nrf/thought-leadership/us/2026/ai-in-litigation-series-an-update-on-ai-copyright-cases-in-2026_image-1.jpg?revision=5250774643747387904&h=191&w=257&hash=80C3FD55C45A4F024F88840E779C25E3)

In 2018, Dr. Thaler filed a copyright application with the US Copyright Office for the artwork. On the application, he identified the Creativity Machine as the sole author and himself as the owner, acknowledging that the work lacks traditional human authorship. The Copyright Office denied the registration, relying on its longstanding human authorship requirement under the Copyright Act.

Dr. Thaler then sought judicial review in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia, arguing the Copyright Office’s decision was wrong on constitutional, statutory and policy grounds and asserting ownership under the work-for-hire doctrine. Both parties moved for summary judgment. Judge Beryl Howell granted summary judgment in favor of the Copyright Office, holding that human authorship is a “bedrock requirement of copyright.”[11](#11) The court also held that Dr. Thaler could not rely on the work-for-hire statute because that provision “presuppose[s] that an interest exists to be claimed.”[12](#12) The “image autonomously generated” by the Creativity Machine was not such an interest because it “was never eligible for copyright,” so there was no copyright to transfer to Dr. Thaler even if he were the Creativity Machine’s employer.[13](#13) Finally, the court found that Dr. Thaler waived his argument that he should own the copyright because he created and used the Creativity Machine. Dr. Thaler subsequently appealed to the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit. On March 18, 2025, the panel affirmed Judge Howell’s ruling. The court explained that although the Copyright Act does not explicitly define “author,” multiple provisions make clear that authors must be human. The court further noted that Congress adopted the Copyright Office’s human authorship requirement when enacting the Copyright Act. The panel also rejected Dr. Thaler’s alternative arguments based on the work-for-hire doctrine, reasoning that this provision requires the underlying work to be eligible for copyright protection in the first instance. Finally, the court found that Dr. Thaler had waived his argument that he should be recognized as the author by virtue of creating the AI platform, as he failed to raise this claim during administrative proceedings.

On October 9, 2025, Dr. Thaler petitioned for a writ of certiorari to the United States Supreme Court, arguing that the lower courts’ decisions have created a “chilling effect on anyone else considering using AI creatively.”[14](#14) In response, the Solicitor General, on behalf of the Copyright Office, contended that Dr. Thaler had consistently disclaimed any human contributions to the work and thus the work should not be copyrightable. The US Supreme Court denied certiorari on March 2, 2026, thereby reaffirming human authorship as a foundational requirement of US copyright law, even in this era of rapid AI advancement.

To be clear, this case does not necessarily prohibit copyright protection for works created with AI *assistance*; human contributions with AI assistive use may be protectable. Here, Dr. Thaler explicitly and repeatedly disclaimed any human creative input, so the court did not address how much human involvement is necessary to support copyright registration for AI-assisted works. That issue is still ripe for resolution.

### *Thomson Reuters v. Ross Intelligence*

Thomson Reuters Enterprise Centre GmbH sued Ross Intelligence Inc. in Delaware, alleging that Ross Intelligence—via a vendor—infringed Thomson Reuters' copyrights in its Westlaw headnotes and by actually copying and using them to train its competing AI-powered legal research tool.

In late 2023, the court denied cross summary judgment motions in this case. But as the case was progressing to trial, the court invited the parties to resubmit those motions. On February 11, 2025, the court granted partial summary judgment in favor of Thomson Reuters, finding that (1) Thomson Reuters’ Westlaw's headnotes and Key Number System were original and protected by copyright, and (2) Ross Intelligence's actual copying of the headnotes was not fair use. Specifically, its vendor was contracted to create training data in the form of “Bulk Memos,” which were compilations of legal questions created by lawyers with good and bad answers to help train the platform. Its vendor created these Bulk Memos using Westlaw headnotes. To reach its decision, the court reviewed the thousands of Bulk Memos at issue and compared them against the headnotes and the underlying case opinions; after doing so, the court concluded that the headnotes are sufficiently original, and that Ross did copy them.

In fact, the court found that the 2,243 headnotes at issue matched content so closely that "no reasonable jury could find otherwise"[15](#15) that actual copying occurred. Ross's defenses of innocent infringement, merger, scènes à faire and copyright misuse were all rejected. As for the Key Number System, the court indicated it was not clear if or how those were used, and so actual copying on those was left to the jury to decide.

When the court analyzed the four fair use factors, it found that Ross's use was commercial and not transformative because it created a competitive tool with the same function as Westlaw. Critically, the court emphasized that Ross's tool is not generative AI, finding that it does not write legal research memos or opinions and that it is merely a search tool that identifies cases in response to the user's legal research questions. The factors regarding the nature of the work and the amount used weighed in Ross's favor, given the narrow scope of protection afforded the headnotes and the fact that they did not appear to Ross’s end users. However, the effect on the market heavily favored Thomson Reuters, as Ross's tool was directly competitive and undercut Westlaw's market.

On May 23, 2025, the court granted Ross Intelligence's motion for interlocutory appeal and stay pending appeal, noting that "the questions here are hard."[16](#16) In its appeal brief filed in September 2025, Ross Intelligence argued that if the decision stands, it will have "sweeping consequences for innovation"[17](#17) in both legal research and artificial intelligence. The issues on appeal include whether headnotes and Key Numbers are copyrightable and whether Ross Intelligence’s use was fair. That appeal is still pending.

### *Bartz et al. v. Anthropic*

This class action, which ultimately included nearly half a million authors, was filed in August 2024 by authors Andrea Bartz, Charles Graeber and Kirk Wallace Johnson against Anthropic. The authors challenged Anthropic's use of their books (both lawfully acquired and pirated) to train its Claude LLM and to keep in its “central library” for undisclosed future purposes. The plaintiffs alleged that Anthropic illegally downloaded over seven million copyrighted books from "shadow libraries" like LibGen, and then ultimately changed course and acquired the books legally. Notably, the claims did not assert that Claude’s outputs were infringing; the case’s focus was on training and retention in the “central library.”

On June 23, 2025, the court found that Anthropic’s training was fair use, but that storing pirated copies was not. The decision stopped short of explicitly addressing whether training conducted with pirated source copies is fair use. However, the court expressed skepticism that "any subsequent fair use” could ever justify pirated downloads.[18](#18) This skepticism suggests a doctrinal tension: while the fair‑use holding did not depend on lawful acquisition, the decision intimates that obtaining copies from piracy sites may erode the defense, even in a training context.

The court’s fair use analysis concluded that training data was ”transformative—spectacularly so.”[19](#19) and “among the most transformative many of us will see in our lifetimes.”[20](#20) Training an LLM involves feeding it billions of words or “tokens,” and the model converts those tokens into numbers, then repeatedly adjusts its internal parameters, known as weights, so it gets better and better at predicting the next token. The more material and the higher quality of material used to train the LLM, the better it will learn language and be able to generate content and complete tasks. The court likened this training process to reading books to learn human language: "To make anyone pay specifically for the use of a book each time they read it, each time they recall it from memory, each time they later draw upon it when writing new things in new ways would be unthinkable."[21](#21)

Because the works at issue here were novels and other long-form books, the court found that the second factor looking at the nature of the works favored the authors. However, that factor is typically given little weight. The court also concluded that copying entire works was "reasonably necessary" to train an LLM. Critically, the court also found that since the training data is never shown to users and doesn't replace the market for the original books, the market-effect factor favored Anthropic. In the court’s view, the fourth fair use factor protects against *replacement*, not competition. It was critical to the court’s decision that the plaintiffs did not allege that Claude would replicate significant amounts of text that it was trained on, and Anthropic had incorporated safeguards to prevent this from happening. The court also noted that authors are not entitled to licensing revenue for training *because* it is a fair use, and that a market for licensing training data is not one the Copyright Act entitles authors to exploit.

However, the court went on to find that Anthropic's acquisition and storage of over seven million pirated books was not protected by fair use, as obtaining and storing pirated books was not necessary to train the LLM. Further, Anthropic's subsequent decision not to train Claude on pirated copies did not absolve its liability for storing the works in the first place. There was no “get out of jail free” card for downloading pirated copies simply because the intended end use might be transformative.

The case later settled for a total of US$1.5 billion. The settlement terms include the destruction of Anthropic's pirated dataset and are limited to past use of training data, not outputs. Based on this value, authors in the class are estimated to receive a payout of approximately US$3,000 per work before fees and costs. The class's attorneys have requested US$300 million (20 percent) in fees and US$2 million in expenses.

The settlement halted a trial that might have tested the boundaries of copyright statutory damages. Because statutory copyright damages can reach US$150,000 per infringed work, Anthropic’s exposure theoretically extended into the hundreds of billions of dollars, raising existential risk for the company. The effects will likely resonate well beyond a single suit. In fact, another group of plaintiffs—music publishers—subsequently moved to amend their complaint against Anthropic to add piracy claims similar to what the plaintiffs alleged here. We may see other AI platforms settle with creators as cases get closer to trial to avoid potentially astronomical damages.

### *Kadrey et al. v. Meta Platforms Inc.*

In this case, filed in 2023, the plaintiffs (another group of authors including Richard Kadrey, Sarah Silverman and Junot Diaz) alleged that Meta infringed the authors' copyrights by training its AI LLM (Llama) models on their books. This suit also includes allegations that the books were pirated from “shadow libraries.” Importantly, in this suit, the allegations specifically include that Meta downloaded the books via torrenting.

Similar to the *Bartz* court, on June 25, 2025, this court granted partial dismissal in Meta’s favor on the basis of fair use, finding that the training was transformative. However, the court differed from the *Bartz* court’s opinion on the fourth fair-use factor—market harm—criticizing the plaintiffs’ "half-hearted" arguments of market harm.[22](#22) It also diverged from the *Bartz* court in how it treated training the model on pirated works, squarely holding that LLM training constitutes fair use regardless of whether the underlying materials were obtained from legitimate sources or not.

In a separate opinion, the court ruled in favor of Meta on the plaintiffs’ Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA) claims regarding the removal of copyright management information (CMI) in training Llama. The DMCA prohibits removal of CMI that will “induce, enable, facilitate, or conceal an infringement of any right under this title.” The court found that because the training was fair use, the removal of the information was not in furtherance of any infringement and so the DMCA claim fails.

The court had some strong criticisms in this opinion. Not only did the court call out the plaintiffs for failing—in the court’s view—to put forth any good arguments about the fourth fair use factor, but the court also explicitly disagreed with the *Bartz* court’s analysis on this factor, which this court considered to be the most important factor in the analysis. Of the plaintiffs’ arguments, the court wrote:

This . . . ruling only affects the rights of these thirteen authors—not the countless others whose works Meta used to train its models. And, as should now be clear, this ruling does not stand for the proposition that Meta’s use of copyrighted materials to train its language models is lawful. It stands only for the proposition that these plaintiffs made the wrong arguments and failed to develop a record in support of the right one.[23](#23)

To summarize, the authors focused their market harm arguments on two theories: either that the model could create substantially similar outputs to their books, or that Meta would usurp the market for licensing training materials. The court found both arguments unpersuasive. Llama is safeguarded against regurgitating the training materials and there was no evidence it had done so here. Similarly, regarding the potential market for licensing, the court found that this argument was circular. If harm from the loss of fees paid to license a work for a transformative purpose is actionable, the plaintiff would win every time.

However, the court did identify what it considered to be a potentially more persuasive argument: that AI models can flood the market with similar texts and stifle competition. In the court’s view, that could be exactly the sort of market harm the fair use analysis seeks to prevent. The court emphasized that the fact that books like the plaintiffs’ here make for better training data supports this argument; in essence, that training the LLM on books can make it better at diluting the market for those books. However, the court found that the plaintiffs here did not build any record to support this argument, so the court found in Meta’s favor.

There are still some claims that survived summary judgment. Specifically, there is a question of whether, during the torrenting process, Meta “seeded” the books, essentially meaning it may have distributed the pirated copies to third parties. On December 11, 2025, the authors moved to amend their lawsuit to add a contributory infringement claim related to this issue. The authors claim they "were in the dark about how Meta obtained plaintiffs' copyrighted works" and that their understanding of Meta's alleged "torrenting activities" has only recently "crystallized."[24](#24) They allege that new log data suggested that Meta engaged in large-scale torrenting, which prompted the authors to refine their class definition before discovery. Meta has opposed the plaintiffs’ motion and the parties have been engaged in cross-briefing as recently as last week. The parties’ latest arguments center on whether Meta belatedly asserted a new fair use defense regarding the “seeding” process and whether schedule adjustments and further discovery are needed.

In short, the case is far from closed on fair use for training data and demonstrates that courts—even those sitting in the same district—can reach different conclusions when confronted with similar facts. This will be an interesting case to monitor, and we might see other authors using the court’s decision here as a blueprint in their own complaints regarding the market harm factor. The fact that courts are splitting on this issue may also encourage the appellate courts to weigh in on whether training generative AI models on pirated works can ever be fair use.

### *In Re OpenAI, Inc. copyright infringement litigation*

In April 2025, the United States Judicial Panel on Multidistrict Litigation consolidated twelve cases against OpenAI and another defendant originating in the Southern District of New York and the Northern District of California. The MDL encompasses class actions originally filed in California by authors, New York suits brought by news organizations, DMCA-focused suits and a case brought by an online video creator. The panel found that these cases involve common questions of fact regarding the defendants' use of copyrighted works, without consent or compensation, to train their LLMs. The consolidated matter was assigned to the Southern District of New York and aims to streamline the infringement claims against OpenAI and provide some consistency in rulings.

In the MDL, the plaintiffs allege that the defendants infringed their copyrights by downloading and reproducing their works to train OpenAI's LLMs and to create infringing outputs through OpenAI's ChatGPT. The plaintiffs further claim that ChatGPT used these training datasets to generate comprehensive summaries and outlines of their copyrighted books, which they contend constitutes infringement. OpenAI generally denies the claims but admitted to several factual allegations concerning the datasets used to train its GPT‑2 and GPT‑3 models. OpenAI asserted numerous affirmative defenses, including failure to state a claim under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 12(b)(6), fair use, de minimis copying, invalid or nonexistent copyright ownership, and lack of provable injury. In its motion to dismiss, filed on July 14, 2025, OpenAI argued that the court cannot assess whether ChatGPT’s outputs are substantially similar to plaintiffs’ works because the consolidated complaint neither cites nor attaches examples of the allegedly infringing outputs. OpenAI also claimed that the outputs at issue are similar to the news‑article summaries that the court held were not substantially similar to copyrighted works in related litigations.

In an opinion dated October 27, 2025, the court held that “[i]t is sufficient to defeat OpenAI's motion to dismiss that plaintiffs have alleged some outputs that a reasonable jury could find are substantially similar to plaintiffs’ works.”[25](#25) Further, the court noted that nothing in its opinion “is intended to suggest a view on whether the allegedly infringing outputs are protected as fair uses of the original works.”[26](#26)

Most recently, on January 5, 2026, the court ordered OpenAI to produce all 20 million output logs noting that “OpenAI identifies no caselaw requiring a court to order the least burdensome discovery possible or to explain specifically why it rejects a party's discovery proposal.”[27](#27) And just earlier this week, on March 9, 2026, the Court granted the plaintiffs’ motion to compel and ordered OpenAI to produce “the reservoirs of 78 million and 10 million logs,” on top of the 20 million log sample that was already ordered to be produced.[28](#28) Discovery is ongoing.

### *Disney et al. v. Midjourney*

In this case, Disney and its subsidiaries, including Lucasfilm and Marvel, along with other studios, allege that Midjourney unlawfully copied their copyrighted works to train its AI image-generation service, and that it continues to infringe because it continues to reproduce, publicly display and distribute derivative images of the companies’ iconic characters. Below are some of the images generated by Midjourney highlighted in the plaintiffs' complaint:

The plaintiffs assert that Midjourney engaged in willful misconduct by ignoring cease-and-desist demands, failing to implement copyright safeguards and actively promoting infringing outputs as a feature to attract subscribers, thereby generating hundreds of millions of dollars in revenue. Accordingly, the plaintiffs seek injunctive relief, statutory or actual damages (up to US$150,000 per work for willful infringement), disgorgement of profits and attorneys' fees.

Notably, in a related development, Disney and OpenAI recently signed a deal allowing OpenAI's Sora to generate AI videos featuring Disney's iconic characters. Under the three-year deal, Sora can create short, user-prompted videos featuring over 200 characters from Disney’s most beloved franchises, along with costumes, props, vehicles and themed environments. As part of the agreement, Disney will invest US$1 billion in OpenAI and become a major customer, leveraging AI for new products and Disney+ experiences. Both companies pledged to uphold user safety and creator rights, with Disney emphasizing its goal of extending storytelling through generative AI while respecting and protecting creators and their works.

This development may spark a trend toward formal licensing of copyrighted material for generative AI use. Agreements like this may also have an impact on the fair use analysis as well. Licensing agreements of this nature could materially impact the fourth, market-harm factor by providing evidence of an active, remunerative licensing market for generative AI use. Put another way, big licensing deals like this one give concrete evidence of the potential market for creators and copyright holders to exploit their content in connection with training and AI content outputs. Unlicensed AI uses are more likely to be viewed as impairing a protected market, which could weigh against fair use.

## Summary of trends in AI-related copyright cases

Several key patterns and trends emerge from these AI-related copyright cases:

First, courts are grappling with fundamental questions about AI and copyright, including: (1) whether copyrighted works can be used to train AI models under fair use, and whether that answer depends on if the works were acquired legitimately or pirated; (2) whether AI-generated outputs constitute fair use or infringement; and (3) who owns and can copyright AI-generated or AI-assisted content.

Second, the fair use analysis in AI training cases is evolving, and different courts may reach varied conclusions. This revolutionary [technology](https://www.nortonrosefulbright.com/en/services/6ba18aea/technology) presents many issues of first impression, requiring courts to apply the law in new ways. For instance, the *Ross* court emphasized that Ross Intelligence's tool was not generative AI but a search tool, distinguishing its analysis from cases involving generative models. Even among generative AI cases, courts have diverged. The *Bartz* court found that AI training was fair use, but expressed skepticism that "any subsequent fair use" could justify pirated downloads.[29](#29) In contrast, the *Kadrey* court squarely held that LLM training constitutes fair use regardless of whether the underlying materials were obtained from legitimate sources. The judges also differed on the market harm factor. The *Kadrey* court left the door open for a different outcome in other LLM training cases based on market harm, in stark contrast to the *Bartz* court’s view on fair use. This emphasizes the fact that courts are reaching different conclusions when presented with similar claims and facts.

Third, courts have consistently found that the source of training data is significant. Courts may permit AI companies to train on copyrighted works if they obtained those works lawfully, as demonstrated by the *Bartz* court. However, as *Bartz* and *Kadrey* show, the retention and/or distribution of pirated copies can create separate liability independent of training.

Fourth, licensing is accelerating and emerging as a potential solution to these issues. The Disney-OpenAI agreement shows a trend towards formal licensing of copyrighted material for generative AI use, setting the stage for how entertainment companies monetize IP in AI-driven platforms. Such arrangements may become the industry standard for using copyrighted content in AI training in order to avoid costly and uncertain litigation.

Fifth, liability for outputs remains on the table. Cases such as *Disney* will test responsibility for infringing or look-alike AI outputs and marketing uses. The question of whether outputs infringe may depend on whether they reproduce protected expression or merely reflect learned patterns.

## Conclusion: Practical takeaways

More and more companies are rapidly investing in, using and planning to grow their use of GenAI. Given the widespread deployment of, and significant volume of information generated by, these tools, new litigation and claims will quickly arise as well. Companies seeking to utilize AI tools in a way that would impact their ability to protect materials under copyright laws should consider the following practical takeaways from these cases:

First, understand how the tools that are considered to be used will actually be used and ensure that before the company brings the same in for use that it conducts due diligence on AI tools and their training data sources, reviewing license rights and terms of service and assessing potential exposure from using AI-generated content.

Second, be proactive by implementing monitoring systems for AI-generated content, communicating clear policies regarding AI use, scanning outputs for potential infringement issues and training employees on copyright considerations when using AI tools.

Third, stay informed on all legal developments including related case law which generally moves quicker than regulation as courts continue to refine the application of fair use doctrine to AI training and outputs. The pending appeals in *Thomson Reuters* and ongoing litigation in other cases may significantly shape the legal landscape.

Fourth, consider licensing arrangements where appropriate, as the trend toward formal licensing agreements between content owners and AI companies may reduce litigation risk and provide clearer rights to use copyrighted materials.

args.summary:
This Norton Rose Fulbright publication (March 2026) provides a comprehensive update on six major AI copyright cases in the United States, analyzing their implications for copyright law and AI usage. The article begins by outlining foundational copyright principles—human authorship requirement, protection of expression not ideas—and the US Copyright Office's position that human authorship is required for copyright protection.

**Key Cases Summarized:**

1. **Thaler v. Perlmutter**: Dr. Thaler sought copyright for an AI-generated artwork ("A Recent Entrance to Paradise") created by his "Creativity Machine," listing the AI as sole author. The US Supreme Court denied certiorari on March 2, 2026, reaffirming that human authorship is a bedrock requirement of US copyright law. The case does not address how much human involvement is needed for AI-assisted works.

2. **Thomson Reuters v. Ross Intelligence**: Court found that Westlaw headnotes are copyrightable and that Ross Intelligence's copying of 2,243 headnotes to train its AI legal research tool was not fair use. Ross's tool was distinguished from generative AI as a search tool. Appeal is pending.

3. **Bartz et al. v. Anthropic**: Nearly half a million authors sued Anthropic for using books (including pirated copies from "shadow libraries") to train Claude LLM. Court found (June 23, 2025) that training was transformative fair use, but storing pirated copies was not. The case settled for US$1.5 billion, with authors estimated to receive ~US$3,000 per work.

4. **Kadrey et al. v. Meta Platforms Inc.**: Authors sued Meta for training Llama models on books obtained via torrenting from shadow libraries. Court (June 25, 2025) granted partial dismissal on fair use grounds, holding that LLM training constitutes fair use regardless of whether materials were obtained legitimately. The court criticized plaintiffs' weak market harm arguments but noted that stronger arguments (e.g., AI models flooding the market) could yield different results. Claims about Meta's "seeding" (distributing pirated copies via torrenting) survived.

5. **In Re OpenAI, Inc. Copyright Infringement Litigation**: MDL consolidating 12 cases against OpenAI, including claims from authors, news organizations, and creators. Court ordered OpenAI to produce millions of output logs. Discovery is ongoing as of March 2026.

6. **Disney et al. v. Midjourney**: Disney, Lucasfilm, and Marvel allege Midjourney unlawfully copied copyrighted works to train its AI image-generation service and continues to produce derivative images of iconic characters. Notably, Disney separately signed a deal with OpenAI's Sora (US$1 billion investment) for AI-generated video featuring Disney characters, signaling a trend toward formal licensing.

**Key Trends Identified:**
- Courts are grappling with fundamental questions about fair use for AI training, especially regarding pirated vs. lawfully acquired data
- Courts are reaching different conclusions on similar facts (e.g., Bartz vs. Kadrey on market harm and pirated training data)
- Source of training data matters significantly; pirated copies create separate liability
- Licensing is accelerating as a potential solution (e.g., Disney-OpenAI deal)
- Liability for AI outputs remains an open question

**Practical Takeaways:** Companies should conduct due diligence on AI tools and training data sources, implement monitoring systems for AI-generated content, stay informed on legal developments, and consider licensing arrangements to reduce litigation risk.

# The Art (and Legality) of Imitation:  Navigating the Murky Waters of Fair Use in AI Training

July 15, 2025

As generative AI technology advances, the legal battles over the use of copyrighted materials for training these models are heating up. In the first wave of lawsuits the courts have diverged in their approach to fair use as a defense to claims of copyright infringement. Other legal theories of protection—including the right of publicity and unfair competition under state and federal law—remain largely untested.

Fair use is a legal doctrine that allows limited use of copyrighted material without requiring permission from the rights holder. 17 U.S.C § 107. Courts consider four main factors to determine whether a use qualifies as fair use: (1) purpose and character of the use (commercial or noncommercial); (2) nature of the copyrighted work (factual or creative); (3) amount and substantiality of the portion used; and (4) effect of the use on the market.

In May of 2025, the Copyright Office released a third (pre-publication) [report](https://www.copyright.gov/ai/Copyright-and-Artificial-Intelligence-Part-3-Generative-AI-Training-Report-Pre-Publication-Version.pdf) that provided ample support for both sides on whether training AI with copyrighted works constitutes copyright infringement or fair use.

So far in 2025 four cases have directly analyzed the applicability of the fair use defense to AI model training. For the most part, each case put its own spin on the issue, confirming that the debate over AI and intellectual property is just beginning.

***Lehrman v. Lovo, Inc.,* No*.* 1:24-cv-03770 (S.D.N.Y. July 10, 2025)**

A class action filed in May 2024 by two voice actors in the Southern District of New York was one of the first to raise the issue [3]. The plaintiffs claim that Lovo, Inc., used AI-generated replicas of their voices without permission. Their 313-paragraph amended complaint brings 17 counts ranging from violations of New York statutes protecting the right of publicity to copyright infringement and various unfair competition and false advertising claims under the Lanham Act. Lovo moved to dismiss, arguing that the plaintiffs failed to state any actionable claim against it, including because the use of AI-generated voices is not copyright infringement and is not covered by relevant state laws. The court [held](https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.nysd.621575/gov.uscourts.nysd.621575.45.0_1.pdf) that the claims for copyright infringement and violation of state laws were sufficiently stated, but dismissed the claims based on the Lanham Act. The court also permitted the actors to amend their claim that Lovo’s AI training infringed their copyrights. Most critically for the plaintiffs, the class action claims in *Lovo* remain alive.

***Bartz v. Anthropic PBC,* No. 24-cv-05417 (N.D. Cal. June 23, 2025)**

Anthropic used millions of digital books to train its AI model, Claude. It scanned many printed books, but also downloaded others from pirate libraries. A group of authors sued Anthropic for copyright infringement, claiming that copying the books and using them to train Claude is unlawful. Anthropic has argued that its actions are fair use and asked for an early summary judgment ruling. The judge looked at three main activities separately and decided whether each was fair use:

* **Training**: The judge [held](https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.cand.415175/gov.uscourts.cand.415175.598.0_1.pdf) that training an AI model on lawfully obtained, copyrighted books constituted fair use, finding the use exceedingly transformative.
* **Library copies**: The judge also agreed that buying and digitizing books is transformative because “every purchased print copy was copied in order to save storage space and to enable searchability as a digital copy.” But the judge denied summary judgment on “copies made from central library copies but not used for training.”
* **Pirated library copies**: The judge denied summary judgment because while the use of these books for training was transformative, the creation and maintenance of a permanent, general-purpose digital library of pirated works was not protected by fair use.

***Kadrey v. Meta Platforms, Inc.,* No. 23-cv-03417 (N.D. Cal. June 25, 2025)**

A few days later, a different Northern District of California judge [granted](https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.cand.415175/gov.uscourts.cand.415175.601.0_2.pdf) Meta a significant victory in a copyright lawsuit brought by 13 authors who alleged that their books were improperly used to train Meta’s Llama AI model. The judge ruled that the use of the plaintiffs’ works in training the AI model qualified as fair use under copyright law—particularly because the training was found to be highly transformative, serving purposes like summarization and content generation that differ fundamentally from the original works. The judge added that the plaintiffs had not provided sufficient evidence of harm. The judge, however, emphasized that the court’s decision was narrowly decided—focused on the plaintiffs’ inadequate arguments—and does not establish a blanket legality for AI training practices. He cautioned that more compelling evidence in future cases could lead to different outcomes and that evidence of infringement or economic damage could succeed.

***Thomson Reuters Enter. Ctr. GMBH v. Ross Intel. Inc.*, 765 F. Supp. 3d 382 (D. Del. 2025) (on appeal before the 3rd Circuit)**

Contrary to the preceding cases is *Thomson Reuters Enter. Ctr. GMBH v. Ross Intel. Inc.*, where the District of Delaware held that fair use was an inapplicable defense when training AI models. Thomson Reuters alleged that Ross infringed its copyrights when Ross used Thomson Reuters’s Westlaw headnotes to train Ross’ new AI legal-research search engine. The court granted partial summary judgment for Thomson Reuters on its claims of direct infringement, while denying Ross’ defenses, including fair use. When evaluating Ross’ fair use defense, the court found that Ross use did not qualify as fair use in part because the use was “commercial” and not “transformative.” The decision is currently being appealed by Ross.

**So What Now?**

The legal landscape for artificial intelligence is still developing, and no outcome can yet be predicted with any sort of accuracy. While some courts appear poised to accept AI model training as transformative, other courts do not. As AI technology continues to advance, the legal system must adapt to address the unique challenges it presents. Meanwhile, businesses and creators navigating this uncertain terrain should stay informed about legal developments and consider proactive measures to mitigate risks. As we await further rulings and potential legislative action, one thing is clear: the conversation around AI and existing intellectual property protection is just beginning.

If you have questions about how statutes, regulations, or court rulings surrounding generative AI impact you or your business, contact your Miller Canfield attorney or one of the authors of this alert.

## [Fair Use and Artificial Intelligence 2026 Update](https://library.osu.edu/site/copyright/2026/03/20/fair-use-and-artificial-intelligence-2026-update/ "Fair Use and Artificial Intelligence 2026 Update")

[March 20, 2026](https://library.osu.edu/site/copyright/2026/03/20/fair-use-and-artificial-intelligence-2026-update/ "Fair Use and Artificial Intelligence 2026 Update")  /  [Landen Stafford](https://library.osu.edu/site/copyright/author/stafford-325osu-edu/ "Posts by Landen Stafford")  /  Comments Off on Fair Use and Artificial Intelligence 2026 Update

[*Fair Use Week*](https://www.fairuseweek.org/) *is an annual celebration of the legal doctrine of fair use, which plays an essential role in teaching, education, and scholarship. The*[*fair use*](https://library.osu.edu/copyright/fair-use)*doctrine allows for the use of copyrighted works in certain circumstances, which is determined using a four-factor test that considers the purpose of the use, the nature of the copyrighted work, the amount and substantiality used, and the effect of the use on the market for the copyrighted work.*

## **Fair Use in Current Artificial Intelligence Lawsuits**

A year ago, in recognition of Fair Use Week, Copyright Corner [wrote about the intersection of fair use and artificial intelligence](https://library.osu.edu/site/copyright/2025/02/24/fair-use-week-2025-fair-use-and-artificial-intelligence/) (AI). It explored how AI might interact with a four-factor fair use analysis, summarized guidance from Parts 1 and 2 of the U.S. Copyright Office’s [*Copyright and Artificial Intelligence*](https://www.copyright.gov/ai/) report, and provided an overview of some current AI lawsuits involving copyright. At the time, a new summary judgement ruling in [*Thomson Reuters v Ross Intelligence*](https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.ded.72109/gov.uscourts.ded.72109.770.0.pdf) had been recently released, giving an early look into how courts might rule on fair use in the context of AI. Since then, [*Part 3: Generative AI Training*](https://www.copyright.gov/ai/Copyright-and-Artificial-Intelligence-Part-3-Generative-AI-Training-Report-Pre-Publication-Version.pdf) of the U.S. Copyright Office’s AI report was published, and further rulings in current cases involving copyright and AI have been released, which both expand on how the standing legal frameworks in copyright law, and more specifically, fair use, may be applied to the unprecedented advances in AI technology. To keep up with how courts are applying established principles of the fair use doctrine to AI, let’s explore some of the key takeaways from recent decisions in [*Bartz v. Anthropic*](https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.cand.434709/gov.uscourts.cand.434709.231.0.pdf) and [*Kadrey v. Meta*](https://storage.courtlistener.com/recap/gov.uscourts.cand.415175/gov.uscourts.cand.415175.598.0.pdf).

In *Reuters v. Ross*, the court rejected a fair use defense in the use of copyrighted works for training of an AI legal search tool. Weighing the first factor, the court held that Ross was using the headnotes as AI data to create a competing legal research tool, which was not a transformative use. Additionally, under the fourth factor, the court found that Ross’s legal research tool served as a market substitute and also noted consideration for the effect of Ross’s use on a potential market for AI training data. Perhaps unsurprising to those familiar with fair use analyses, those same two factors—the first and the fourth—play a large role in the decisions in *Bartz* and *Kadrey*, which were released in the same week in June 2025, only two days apart. In both cases, lawsuits were brought against companies that used copyrighted works to train large language models without authorization from the copyright owners. Both defendants made fair use defenses, and in both cases, the judges ruled in favor of fair use, at least in part. There is much to be gathered, however, beyond a simple fair use finding from the analysis the judges provide in their opinions.

In *Bartz v. Anthropic*, while the court denied summary judgment for Anthropic’s use of pirated copies of copyrighted works to assemble a central library, it also found that training AI on copyrighted works is a fair use if the works are acquired legally. According to the judge, Anthropic’s use of legally acquired works to train AI models was “transformative—spectacularly so,”[[1]](#_ftn1) which supports a fair use finding under the first factor. When evaluating any potential market harm under the fourth factor, the judge found “copies used to train specific LLMs did not and will not displace demand for copies of Author’s works” because there is no evidence that the AI would produce exact copies of the works, meaning there is no direct substitution.[[2]](#_ftn2) The judge went on to analogize the plaintiff’s argument for potential market harm: “Authors’ complaint is no different than it would be if they complained that training school children to write well would result in an explosion of competing works.”[[3]](#_ftn3) Ultimately, the decision in *Bartz v. Anthropic* suggests that companies training AI on copyrighted works may be able to rely on fair use when those works they are using are lawfully acquired. For the issue of Anthropic’s use of pirated copies of works, notable developments in the case came in August and September 2025 when it was certified as a class action and preliminary approval of a $1.5 billion settlement was announced. Nearly half a million works have claims in this case through the certified class, meaning the potential statutory damages Anthropic could have faced had they lost were astronomical, so they decided to settle for a smaller amount to avert that risk.

The judge’s opinion in *Kadrey v. Meta*, despite an overall finding of fair use, proved to be more controversial. Similar to *Bartz*, the judge in *Kadrey* found the use of copyrighted works as training data for AI models to be transformative, noting that the original purpose of the works was to be “read for entertainment or education” and using the works in various AI functions was a sufficiently different purpose.[[4]](#_ftn4) Approaching the fourth factor, however, is where the *Kadrey* decisions differs significantly from the analysis in *Bartz*. The judge in *Kadrey* employs a novel “market dilution” theory, arguing that “[n]o other use…has anything near the potential to flood the market with competing works the way that LLM training does.”[[5]](#_ftn5) In the judge’s opinion, the competing works serve as indirect substitutes for the copyrighted works (instead of the typical direct substitutes that are considered under the fourth factor in a fair use analysis). The judge finds that even a transformative use can produce an indirect market substitute under the market dilution theory: “No matter how transformative LLM may be, it’s hard to imagine that it can be fair use to use copyrighted books to develop a tool to make billions or trillions of dollars while enabling the creation of a potentially endless stream of competing works that could significantly harm the market for those books.”[[6]](#_ftn6) The same analogy from *Bartz* about teaching children to write is addressed in *Kadrey*, with the judge arguing that “using books to teach children to write is not remotely like using books to create a product that a single individual could employ to generate countless competing works with a miniscule fraction of the time and creativity it would otherwise take.”[[7]](#_ftn7) Ultimately, the opinion in *Kadrey* emphasizes the unprecedented nature of AI technology and how it may affect a copyright owner’s ability capitalize on their work. Though the court ultimately grants summary judgement for Meta on its fair use defense,[[8]](#_ftn8) it outlines an analysis that may prove prohibitive for those relying on fair use to train AI models on copyrighted works.

It is important to remember that each fair use case is different and highly fact dependent, so results of fair use and AI cases will likely continue to vary based on the facts of a particular case, just as *Bartz* and *Kadrey* did, so it may be wise to hesitate from drawing generalizations from the results of only two cases. Hopefully, as courts perform more fair use analyses and subsequently release more opinions, a more clear and consistent thread of practices will become evident, giving a clearer picture on what is and is not fair use in the context of AI.

Anthropic, the court found training AI on copyrighted works is a fair use if the works are acquired legally, with the judge describing the use as 'transformative—spectacularly so.', The judge in Kadrey v. Meta employed a novel 'market dilution' theory, arguing that 'no other use…has anything near the potential to flood the market with competing works the way that LLM training does.', The judge in Bartz analogized: 'Authors' complaint is no different than it would be if they complained that training school children to write well would result in an explosion of competing works.', The judge in Kadrey countered: 'using books to teach children to write is not remotely like using books to create a product that a single individual could employ to generate countless competing works with a miniscule fraction of the time and creativity it would otherwise take.', 'It is important to remember that each fair use case is different and highly fact dependent, so results of fair use and AI cases will likely continue to vary based on the facts of a particular case.'
args.summary:
This Ohio State University Libraries Copyright Corner article (March 20, 2026) by Landen Stafford provides an update on fair use and artificial intelligence in the wake of recent court rulings. It revisits the intersection of fair use and AI, building on a 2025 article and incorporating new developments including Part 3 of the U.S. Copyright Office's AI report and recent rulings in Bartz v. Anthropic and Kadrey v. Meta.

Key case developments:

- **Thomson Reuters v. Ross Intelligence**: The court rejected fair use for AI training, finding Ross's use of copyrighted headnotes to train a competing legal research tool was not transformative and harmed the market.

- **Bartz v. Anthropic (June 2025)**: The court denied summary judgment for Anthropic's use of pirated copies but found training AI on legally acquired works to be fair use. The judge described the use as "transformative—spectacularly so" under the first factor. Under the fourth factor, the court found no direct market substitution since AI did not produce exact copies. Notably, in August/September 2025, the case was certified as a class action and a $1.5 billion settlement was preliminarily approved.

- **Kadrey v. Meta (June 2025)**: The court found fair use overall, with the judge deeming the use of copyrighted works as training data transformative. However, the judge introduced a novel "market dilution" theory, arguing that LLM training could flood the market with competing works serving as indirect substitutes. Despite this theory, summary judgment favored Meta's fair use defense because plaintiffs presented no meaningful evidence of market dilution.

The article emphasizes that fair use cases are highly fact-dependent and cautions against drawing broad generalizations from these two rulings. It notes that the first and fourth factors of the fair use analysis (purpose of use and market effect) continue to be decisive in AI-related cases.

# Copyright Law in 2025: Courts begin to draw lines around AI training, piracy, and market harm

By [Edward D. Lanquist](https://www.reuters.com/authors/edward-d-lanquist/) and [Benjamin West Janke](https://www.reuters.com/authors/benjamin-west-janke/)

March 16, 2026 3:05 PM UTC Updated March 16, 2026

![Image 3: Man works with a laptop at the airport in Hanoi](https://www.reuters.com/resizer/v2/ECH4IHHB7NJNXPEKJG6NOOSE54.jpg?auth=7eb38bc9a9bca3ac51a191a9cb6914ff4f3401f75f820a35aca76172ba0c2a95&width=1920&quality=80)

A man works with a laptop at the airport in Hanoi, Vietnam October 18, 2017. REUTERS/Kham [Purchase Licensing Rights, opens new tab](https://www.reutersagency.com/en/licensereuterscontent/?utm_medium=rcom-article-media&utm_campaign=rcom-rcp-lead)

March 16, 2026 - In 2025, U.S. courts issued the first substantive, merits-stage decisions addressing whether the use of copyrighted works to train generative artificial intelligence systems constitutes "fair use." Although these rulings do not settle all open questions — and in some respects highlight emerging judicial disagreements — they represent a significant inflection point in copyright law's response to large language models, image generators, and other foundation models.
