In 2017, the U.S. Supreme Court considered copyright’s “separability doctrine” in *Star Athletica, L.L.C. v. Varsity Brands, Inc.*, which involved copyright protection for cheerleader uniforms.

8580 U.S. 405; *see also* Peter Lee & Madhavi Sunder, *The Law of Look and Feel*, 90 S. Cal. L. Rev. 529 (2017).

 The Court held that the surface decorations on the uniforms, consisting of an “arrangement of colors, shapes, stripes, and chevrons,” were conceptually separable from the useful elements of the uniforms.

9*Star Athletica*, 580 U.S. at 417–18.

 In other words, the chevrons and lines could be drawn onto a canvas and enjoy copyright protection as art, and so, copyright protection was not forfeited simply because the designs were applied to a cheerleading uniform.

Since then, few courts have found infringement of copyrighted clothing designs. In *Puma SE v. Forever 21, Inc.*, the plaintiff sued for infringement of three shoe designs—the “Creeper Sneaker,” “Fur Slide,” and “Bow Slide”—based on Puma’s copyrights, design patents, and trade dress in the shoe designs.

10No. 2:17-cv-02523 (C.D. Cal. filed Mar. 31, 2017).

 After Puma was denied a temporary restraining order and preliminary injunction, Forever 21 brought a motion to dismiss. The district court concluded that the design patent infringement claim was adequately pleaded. However, Puma’s trade dress infringement claim was dismissed because Puma failed to plead that the trade dress (in part a thick sandal base or deep bowl for the foot) was nonfunctional. The copyright infringement claim was dismissed due to a defect in timely registration.

11At the time, the Ninth Circuit allowed for copyright infringement actions to proceed based on a pending copyright application, so long as the plaintiff had submitted the application, fee, and deposit materials with the U.S. Copyright Office prior to filing the complaint. The first amended complaint alleged that applications had been filed but lacked any allegations regarding the dates of filing or receipt by the Copyright Office of the fee and deposit materials. Since then, the U.S. Supreme Court has held that a copyright infringement action must be based on an issued registration, not merely a pending application, to provide standing under 17 U.S.C. § 411(a). Fourth Est. Pub. Benefit Corp. v. Wall-Street.com, LLC, 586 U.S. 296 (2019).

 Ultimately, the parties settled, but not without first leaving the fashion and legal community with the impression that every fur strap, raised line, and bow might be subject to challenge.

Swimsuit designs were at issue in *Triangl Group Ltd. v. Jiangmen City Xinhui District Lingzhi Garment Co., Ltd.*

12No. 16-cv-1498, 2017 WL 2829752 (S.D.N.Y. June 22, 2017).

 In that case, the court entered a default judgment granting a permanent injunction to stop the defendant from selling infringing swimwear. The court, applying *Star Athletica*, concluded that the decorative black trim and T-shape cup were works of art demonstrable and separable from the functional aspects of the “Brakini” swimwear. Notably, the plaintiff also alleged copyright infringement claims based on the defendant’s use of its photos of the goods, as well as trademark and trade dress infringement. While this case did not evolve into a full-blown trial, the fashion and legal industries took note of this early application of *Star Athletica* in favor of the copyright owner.

In *Silvertop Associates Inc. v. Kangaroo Manufacturing Inc.*, the Third Circuit affirmed a lower court’s decision to grant the plaintiff’s request for a preliminary injunction based on the defendant’s unauthorized copying of the plaintiff’s full-body banana costume.

13931 F.3d 215, 222 (3d Cir. 2019).

 The court reasoned that the costume’s artistic features (e.g., colors, lines, shape, and length) were separable from the utilitarian features (e.g., cutout holes for the wearer’s arms, legs, and face; the holes’ dimensions; or the holes’ locations on the costume) and capable of independent existence as a banana sculpture. While the district court’s preliminary injunction also rested on the plaintiff’s claim of trade dress infringement, the defendant apparently did not seek interlocutory review of that portion of the decision. Ultimately, the parties settled after remand, rather than proceeding to trial. Nonetheless, this remains one of the few precedential cases applying *Star Athletica*.

As demonstrated in these cases, overlapping IP rights can protect a single design, and various theories of infringement are often asserted in a single case with varying degrees of success. Design patents, for example, safeguard nonfunctional, ornamental, inseparable aspects of an article’s appearance *regardless of separability*. As with copyright, design patent protection for fashion designs is not a panacea. Design patent protection lasts 15 years from the grant date—longer than many fashion items stay in vogue—and litigation can outlast the term of protection.

1435 U.S.C. § 173; *see* Crocs, Inc. v. Effervescent, Inc., No. 06-cv-00605-PAB-KMT (D. Colo. filed Apr. 3, 2006) (proceedings stayed for years pending related USITC investigation, Federal Circuit appeal, USPTO reexamination, and defendant’s bankruptcy, resulting in nearly two decades of litigation over design patent infringement).

 Obtaining a design patent can be costly, time consuming, and difficult or impossible to obtain if not filed timely or if the design is surrounded by a crowded field of prior art.

15Irene Calboli & Gabrielle Armstrong, *Design Patents in the Fashion Industry: A US Perspective*, *in* The Handbook of Fashion Law, *supra* note 4, at 229.

 Moreover, to stop counterfeit imports, a design patent owner must obtain an exclusion order from the U.S. International Trade Commission (USITC), which entails costly litigation and a longer timeline compared to the process of recording registered trademarks or copyrights with U.S. Customs and Border Protection.

1619 U.S.C. § 1337; *Intellectual Property Rights (IPR)*, U.S. Customs & Border Prot. (Aug. 25, 2025), <https://www.cbp.gov/trade/priority-issues/ipr>.

## Hyperfast Fashion and Fakes

While courts were grappling with applying the 2017 *Star Athletica* decision, “hyperfast fashion” was taking off. The movement began booming in 2020, led by the Chinese fashion house Shein, which was dropping *thousands* of new styles daily.

17Louise Matsakis, Meaghan Tobin & Wency Chen, *How Shein Beat Amazon at Its Own Game—and Reinvented Fast Fashion*, Guardian (Dec. 21, 2021), <https://www.theguardian.com/fashion/2021/dec/21/how-shein-beat-amazon-at-its-own-game-and-reinvented-fast-fashion>.

 This was largely made possible by the confluence of algorithm-based trend detection, data-driven targeted advertising, the rise of influencer culture, changing online shopping habits (particularly during the COVID-19 pandemic),

18Katarzyna Bilińska-Reformat & Anna Dewalska-Opitek, *E-Commerce as the Predominant Business Model of Fast Fashion Retailers in the Era of Global COVID 19 Pandemics*, 192 Procedia Comput. Sci. 2479, 2488 (2021), <https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S1877050921017543> (explaining how pandemic-era consumer trends accelerated the growth of fast fashion because of increased consumer interest in “safe and convenient online availability”); Yukun Dai, *The Fast Fashion Industry in the Post-Pandemic*, 38 BCP Bus. & Mgmt. 598 (2023), <https://doi.org/10.54691/bcpbm.v38i.3745>.

 and an aggressive recruitment of manufacturers and suppliers.

19*What Is Fast Fashion?*, McKinsey & Co. (Jan. 23, 2025), <https://www.mckinsey.com/featured-insights/mckinsey-explainers/what-is-fast-fashion>.

Previously, luxury brands were trendsetters, and mass fashion would follow with off-the-rack designs to satisfy the demand for luxury-brand designs at more affordable prices.

20H., *How Did Luxury Fashion Become Fast Fashion?*, Pomelade (Oct. 16, 2022), <https://www.thepomelade.com/how-did-luxury-fashion-become-fast-fashion/> (explaining how the blurring lines between luxury and fast fashion due to cheap luxury imitations has diminished the exclusivity traditionally associated with luxury brands); *see, e.g.*, Bastiat USA, Inc. [Brandy Melville] v. Shein Distrib. Corp., No. 2:25-cv-5701 (C.D. Cal. filed June 23, 2025) (copyright infringement complaint); Tapestry, Inc. [Coach] v. Zoetop Bus. Co., Ltd. [Shein], No. 2:25-cv-02224-JLS-E (C.D. Cal. filed Mar. 13, 2025) (trademark infringement); AirWair Int’l Ltd. [Dr. Martens] v. Zoetop Bus. Co., Ltd. [Shein], No. 20-cv-07696 (N.D. Cal. filed Nov. 2, 2020) (settled by confidential agreement; Shein acknowledged validity of Dr. Martens trademarks, ceased sale of infringing footwear, and paid a lump sum). *From Dr. Martens to Ralph Lauren, Lawsuits Are Starting to Build for $15 Billion Ultra-Fast Fashion Brand Shein*, Fashion L. (June 15, 2021), <https://www.thefashionlaw.com/from-dr-martens-to-ralph-lauren-lawsuits-are-starting-to-build-up-against-15-billion-ultra-fast-fashion-brand-shein/>.

 As fast fashion rose, luxury designers collaborated with brands like H&M to stay relevant.

21H., *supra* note 20.

 Then, with the rise of hyperfast fashion, the trends of the masses became the dominant influence on fashion designs, leaving luxury brands to eventually incorporate popular designs into their own looks to keep up with consumer demand. Luxury brands historically included IP-infringement lawsuits as part of their business models, using brand awareness and exclusivity to support high price points.

22Global Marketing Strategies for the Promotion of Luxury Goods 224–65 (Fabrizio Mosca & Rosalia Gallo eds., 2016).

 However, fast-fashion and hyperfast-fashion brands did not follow suit (pun intended)—despite the creative flow reversal. Rather, their business models utilize tools such as continual design turnover, engineered obsolescence, and trend displacement.

23*Id.*

Now, AI presents a future where an endless torrent of designs may flood the markets and the public domain, strategically design around IP-protected features, and churn out designs that force nearly instant obsolescence.

## AI-Generated Fashion: What Can’t Be Protected

As AI-generated content becomes increasingly prevalent, legal uncertainty surrounding ownership and protection grows.

The U.S. Copyright Office has expressed its current position as follows: Only works created by human authors qualify for protection.

24Copyright Registration Guidance: Works Containing Material Generated by Artificial Intelligence, 88 Fed. Reg. 16190 (Mar. 16, 2023), <https://www.federalregister.gov/d/2023-05321>; *see also* Thaler v. Perlmutter, 687 F. Supp. 3d 140, 146 (D.D.C. 2023) (finding that human authorship is a “bedrock requirement of copyright”).

 For works that are derivative of human-made works, or that incorporate human creative choices, the human-created portions are protectable.

25*See* U.S. Copyright Off., Copyright and Artificial Intelligence, Part 2: Copyrightability 12 (2025), <https://www.copyright.gov/ai/Copyright-and-Artificial-Intelligence-Part-2-Copyrightability-Report.pdf>.

 However, the line between machine-generated and man-made may be difficult to determine and expensive to litigate. Thus, for AI-generated fashion designs, there is limited enforceability under copyright law.

26Currently, there is no global consensus on whether AI-generated outputs attract copyright. *See* Li Yunkai v. Liu Yuanchun, (2023) Jing 0491 Min Chu No. 11279 (Beijing Internet Ct. Nov. 27, 2023) (China) (copyright protection of AI-generated artwork); Shenzhen Tencent v. Shanghai Yingxun, (2019) Yue 0305 Min Chu No. 14010 (Nanshan Dist. People’s Ct. Dec. 24, 2019) (China) (granting copyright protection of AI-generated financial report); S. Š. v. Taubel Legal, Rozsudek Městského soudu v Praze ze dne 11.3.2024 [Decision of the Prague Municipal Court of Mar. 11, 2024], čj. 10 C 13/2023-16 (Czech.) (denying copyright in AI-generated image).

Fashion brands may incorporate AI-generated content in other ways—for example, to develop advertising copy and content, or to create digital models and settings to replace physical counterparts. After all, avatars do not age, demand fair pay, need rest, experience travel delays, or complain about uncomfortable poses.

27When AI is trained on thousands of images of real people, it can synthesize photo-realistic models that resemble actual humans—sometimes without consent. This raises NIL (name, image, likeness) issues. In the U.S., where there is no unified NIL law, fashion houses may be exposed to right of publicity claims. Internationally, this could also touch on personality rights, particularly in civil law countries where personal identity protections are stronger. *See, e.g.*, Kunsturhebergesetz [KUG] [Artistic Copyright Act] §§ 22–23 (Ger.) (German law requiring consent to publish someone’s likeness (photos, videos, etc.)); Denmark’s 2025 Draft Act on Protection of Individuals’ Face and Voice from AI-Generated Misuse (Den.) (pending legislation to establish explicit NIL rights). Ultimately, these issues are outside the scope of this article. However, the authors invite any interested reader to contact them for further information or discussion on this topic.

 However, if there is insufficient human creative input, it will be difficult for fashion brands to use copyright law to stop other brands from unauthorized use of the same content. Thus, if an avatar were to model a “Brakini,” the plaintiff would have limited ability to enforce any copyright in the advertisement content and would need to rely heavily on the copyright in the design of the Brakini itself, putting a lot of legal weight on the narrow copyright ledge that *Star Athletica* built.

Turning to design patents, the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) currently requires human inventorship.

28Inventorship Guidance for AI-Assisted Inventions, 89 Fed. Reg. 10043 (Feb. 13, 2024), <https://www.federalregister.gov/d/2024-02623>.

 Thus, an AI tool cannot be named as an inventor.

29Thaler v. Vidal, 43 F.4th 1207 (Fed. Cir. 2022), *cert. denied*, 143 S. Ct. 1783 (Apr. 24, 2023).

 A natural person may be a named inventor where an AI system was used if the natural person “contributed significantly” to every claim in the invention.

30This test is a series of factors, as set forth in *Pannu v. Iolab Corp.*, 155 F.3d 1344 (Fed. Cir. 1998).

 Simply recognizing a problem to be solved, or recognizing a prompt-generated output as an invention, is not enough. However, constructing a prompt with a specific problem in mind “to elicit a particular solution from the AI system” may be sufficient.

3189 Fed. Reg. at 10048.

 This seems like a very fine line between an inventor and an instrument, and one that may lead to pricey litigation and invalidation proceedings in cases where AI-generative tools are used in creating fashion designs.

In addition, to obtain design patent protection, an invention must be novel and nonobvious—meaning that the design must not have been previously invented or represent a minor variation on a previous design.

3235 U.S.C. §§ 102–103.

 However, where AI tools are trained on existing data and designs, AI-generated outputs may resemble these training materials so closely that the output design cannot clear these hurdles. Moreover, AI tools may reveal so much prior art, or pump out so many designs, that human- or human-plus-AI-made designs are preempted from patent protection.

These legal requirements present a particularly thorny issue in fashion, where AI tools can be used to generate entire collections—sketches, patterns, even simulated runway presentations. If no human hand guides the design, does the output fall into the public domain by default?

## Public Domain Explosion and Fast Fashion

The public domain has always been a resource for fashion inspiration. But with AI scraping massive swaths of the internet—including unlicensed copyrighted material—the legitimacy of those training datasets is uncertain.

33Jonathan E. Barbee, *Scratching the Surface of IP Rights: Data Scraping and Artificial Intelligence*, 96 N.Y. St. B.J., Jan./Feb. 2024, at 48 (explaining that AI systems are fundamentally built on the concept of data scraping to gather and learn from large datasets).

 If AI models are trained on proprietary fashion images, the resulting designs could be legally suspect.

Moreover, if the outputs themselves are not subject to copyright or design patent protection, this creates a strange vacuum where anyone can appropriate AI-generated designs with impunity. For hyperfast fashion houses, the “innovate or die” business model may be well suited for a deluge of public domain designs, which could be mined for creative inspiration and safely utilized without much fear of luxury brands weaponizing the IP of the inspirational source material. However, this also may turbocharge the fashion cycle, leading to even faster knockoffs being developed and brought to market. Brands may find themselves racing not just against other companies but against machines.

Given the fragility of copyright protections in fashion generally, and the added uncertainty around AI-generative authorship and inventions, fashion brands may turn to trademarks and trade dress with renewed urgency. There are no similar human authorship or inventorship requirements under trademark law, because those rights spring from use of a mark in the marketplace. For trademark and trade dress, it is the use that matters—not the muse. Strong branding—logos, color schemes, and distinctive silhouettes—can offer a bulwark against copying. However, trademark and trade dress rights are far from a sovereign remedy.

## Strategic IP Pivot: Trademarks and Trade Dress

Trademarks and trade dress protect two sides of one coin: consumer protection and brand protection. This legal regime seeks to maintain a healthy marketplace by preventing consumer confusion as to the source of goods and services. It is not concerned with rewarding originality or innovation. Its focus is to ensure that consumers are not duped into buying knockoffs—not to hand out monopolies on useful design elements that competitors need to freely use. Accordingly, trade dress protection extends to the look and feel of a product to the extent that it functions as a brand identifier, but does not protect functional aspects, whether the function is meant to have some utility (such as lower cost or increase quality, comfort, or durability) or is meant to be aesthetic (such as attracting consumers via decorative appeal).

34*See* Christian Louboutin S.A. v. Yves Saint Laurent Am. Holding, Inc., 696 F.3d 206 (2d Cir. 2012) (examining Louboutin’s assertion of trade dress rights in its iconic monochromatic red sole); Adidas-Am., Inc. v. Payless Shoesource, Inc., 546 F. Supp. 2d 1029 (D. Or. 2008) (finding that the Adidas “three-stripe mark” was strong and entitled to protection); Lois Sportswear, U.S.A., Inc., v. Levi Strauss & Co., 799 F.2d 867 (2d Cir. 1986) (holding that Levi’s trademark back pocket stitching pattern was protectable because it is instantly associated with the brand and plays a significant role in consumer purchasing decisions).

Courts have long struggled with the balance between functional design and brand identity. For example, in *Christian Louboutin, S.A. v. Yves Saint Laurent American Holding, Inc.*, shoemaker Christian Louboutin sued Yves Saint Laurent (YSL) for making and selling shoes with red soles.

35696 F.3d 206.

 Louboutin asserted trade dress rights in its “red bottom” outsole, claiming exclusive rights and seeking a preliminary injunction to stop YSL’s use of the color red on the sole of its monochromatic shoe design. YSL argued that Louboutin’s alleged trade dress was not valid because the red sole was not purely a source identifier but instead was functional—the contrast enhanced the shoe’s aesthetic function—and that allowing Louboutin to have exclusive rights would unfairly limit competition.

The district court declined to grant the preliminary injunction, and the case was appealed to the Second Circuit. On appeal, the court held that Louboutin’s red sole was entitled to trademark protection, but only in the context of a contrasting upper. YSL was permitted to continue the use of its monochromatic red shoes. The court ordered the USPTO to limit Louboutin’s registration of the trade dress accordingly. Thus, Louboutin kept its crown jewels but arguably lost the kingdom.

This case is a good example of the struggle brands and courts face when it comes to trade dress claims in the fashion industry. A brand asserting trade dress rights must show that its design feature is recognized by consumers as a source identifier and withstand arguments that the design feature is functional (either utilitarian or aesthetic). Thus, a brand may need to show that consumers recognize a design feature as a signal of the *brand’s* quality, and that the feature does not impact the cost, quality, or aesthetic appeal of the article itself;

36*Id.* at 219.

 or, that a design feature is distinctive and not diluted or made generic through use by other brands, but also that maintaining a monopoly over the design feature would not “put competitors at a significant non-reputation-related disadvantage.”

37TrafFix Devices, Inc. v. Mktg. Displays, Inc., 532 U.S. 23, 32 (2001).

These are fine hairs to split. Designers need to think strategically about which parts of their product are brand signals and which are just design flourishes. In a world where the “look” can be cloned in seconds, trademarks may be the last line of defense. But, even protectable trade dress has its limits—limits that are often determined only through costly litigation.

38It also is worth mentioning that trademark and trade dress rights are susceptible to impairment or loss if the rights are not policed adequately. When a trademark becomes a common name for the product itself, it loses protection entirely. *See, e.g.*, King-Seeley Thermos Co. v. Aladdin Indus., Inc., 321 F.2d 577, 580 (2d Cir. 1963) (finding that “thermos” had become generic). Even aggressive policing cannot stop all use, as trademark law must accommodate free expression principles such as parody. *See, e.g.*, Louis Vuitton Malletier S.A. v. Haute Diggity Dog, LLC, 507 F.3d 252, 264 (4th Cir. 2007) (holding that parody pet toys labeled “Chewy Vuiton” did not dilute or infringe Louis Vuitton’s marks because they were an obvious joke unlikely to cause confusion). This has been reigned in a bit in recent years by the Supreme Court’s ruling that parody does not automatically grant immunity from trademark infringement. *See* Jack Daniel’s Props., Inc. v. VIP Prods. LLC, 599 U.S. 140, 148 (2023) (holding that humorous dog toy resembling a Jack Daniel’s bottle was subject to traditional likelihood of confusion analysis under the Lanham Act, rejecting automatic application of heightened First Amendment protection under *Rogers*); Hermès Int’l v. Rothschild, No. 1:22-cv-00384 (S.D.N.Y. Feb. 8, 2023) (jury verdict for trademark infringement, dilution, and cybersquatting involving “MetaBirkins” non-fungible tokens (NFTs), rejecting First Amendment defense and awarding Hermès $133,000 in damages and injunctive relief; appeal pending before the Second Circuit).

## Preparing the Fashion Industry for the Future

In the U.S., the fashion industry has historically had an uneasy relationship with IP law, granting limited protection and permitting generous use of the public domain to drive the creative engine. In some ways, this makes the fashion industry well positioned to adapt to the AI revolution. In other ways, it may signal a rise in litigation, as AI-related issues will only create further uncertainty and churn up the already murky waters of fashion law.

AI hasn’t broken the fashion IP regime—it’s just revealed how fragile, antiquated, and undeveloped it already is. The coming years will force legal innovation as much as creative and technological innovation. While the public domain expands and enforcement challenges multiply, there are opportunities for smart adaptation.

Practitioners should help clients future-proof their rights by understanding the nuances of AI authorship, AI inventorship, and the shifting value of trademarks in fashion. The brands that survive this transition will be the ones that lean into change, not resist it—and the lawyers who help them will need to be equally forward-thinking, flexible, and, yes, stylish in their legal strategies.

For fashion brands, the takeaway is this: The cost of litigation—especially across borders and in ambiguous jurisdictions—could skyrocket. Stakeholders should review their legal budgets now in anticipation.

args.summary:
This article examines how AI is impacting intellectual property (IP) law in the fashion industry, published in Landslide® (December/January 2026) by Kristyn Webb and Mallory Kean.

Key points:

1. **Fashion's IP Outlier Status**: In the U.S., most clothing designs lack copyright protection unless they have artistic expression separable from functionality (the "separability doctrine" from Star Athletica v. Varsity Brands, 2017). Design patents and trade dress offer limited protection. Other jurisdictions (EU, France, Italy) offer broader protections.

2. **Hyperfast Fashion**: Shein and similar brands drop thousands of new styles daily, enabled by AI, data-driven trend detection, and influencer culture. This has disrupted the traditional luxury-to-mass fashion flow.

3. **AI-Generated Fashion Challenges**: The U.S. Copyright Office requires human authorship for copyright protection. The USPTO requires human inventorship for design patents. AI-generated outputs may fall into the public domain by default. There is no global consensus on AI-generated copyright.

4. **Public Domain Expansion**: If AI outputs are not protectable, the public domain could swell. For hyperfast fashion brands, this suits their "innovate or die" model, but may accelerate knockoffs and the fashion cycle.

5. **Strategic IP Pivot**: Trademarks and trade dress (which have no human authorship requirements) may become more important. The article discusses the Louboutin red sole case and other trade dress examples. However, these protections are limited and costly to litigate.

The article concludes that AI has revealed how fragile and antiquated fashion IP law is, and urges practitioners to help clients navigate AI authorship/inventorship issues and leverage trademarks more strategically.

###### CFDA and OpenAI Launch “Innovation Hub” to Accelerate AI Innovation Across the Fashion Industry

[![Oui Speak Fashion (OSF)®](https://ouispeakfashion.com/wp-content/uploads/2021/05/Website-Header-3.png)](https://ouispeakfashion.com/ "Oui Speak Fashion (OSF)®")

# CFDA and OpenAI Launch “Innovation Hub” to Accelerate AI Innovation Across the Fashion Industry

![CFDA/ Open AI](https://i0.wp.com/ouispeakfashion.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/CFDA.png?resize=1170%2C600&ssl=1 "CFDA and OpenAI Launch “Innovation Hub” to Accelerate AI Innovation Across the Fashion Industry 1") 

Courtesy of CFDA

Listen to this article

0:000:00

On May 13, the Council of Fashion Designers of America (CFDA) announced the launch of “Innovation Hub,” a new initiative developed in partnership with [OpenAI](https://openai.com/?utm_source=chatgpt.com) to support AI adoption across the fashion industry. The program officially kicked off in New York City with “Dev Day,” where participating designers and AI developer finalists were formally introduced.

Designed to connect fashion brands with emerging AI startups, the initiative aims to foster practical solutions for real-world industry challenges. During the event, selected developers presented live demonstrations of their technologies, showcasing applications tailored specifically to the evolving needs of fashion businesses.

## Summary

* CFDA and OpenAI have launched “Innovation Hub,” a new AI-focused initiative for the fashion industry
* Six AI developer finalists were selected: Alta, Cadenova, Curbon, O.Studio Design, OpenStudio, and Raspberry AI
* Participating brands include alice + olivia, Araks, Public School, Rebecca Minkoff, SIMKHAI, and Tory Burch
* Six designer-developer teams will collaborate over the next four months to develop practical AI-driven business solutions
* Participating teams will receive access to OpenAI tools and APIs, along with more than $300,000 in grant funding

## **Six AI Startups Selected as Finalists**

The six AI companies selected as finalists include Alta, Cadenova, Curbon, O.Studio Design, OpenStudio, and Raspberry AI. Each company presented its own AI-driven approach to addressing operational and creative challenges within the fashion industry.

Developers were asked to respond to the prompt: How does your technology solve a specific challenge within the fashion industry, and what is the impact?”

![CFDA 2](https://i0.wp.com/ouispeakfashion.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/CFDA-2.jpg?resize=1024%2C768&ssl=1 "CFDA and OpenAI Launch “Innovation Hub” to Accelerate AI Innovation Across the Fashion Industry 6")

Courtesy of CFDA

Meanwhile, participating CFDA member brands include alice + olivia, Araks, Public School, Rebecca Minkoff, SIMKHAI, and Tory Burch. Each brand will work directly with developers to explore how AI can be integrated into different areas of their businesses.

Following the presentations, designers and developers participated in curated one-on-one matchmaking sessions, ranking their preferred collaborators before final pairings are confirmed by the CFDA.

The six selected teams will now enter a four-month collaboration period supported by OpenAI mentorship and technical guidance, with the goal of developing scalable AI applications tailored to fashion businesses.

In addition, participating teams will receive a share of more than $300,000 in funding, along with access to OpenAI’s APIs and technology resources.

![Courtesy of CFDA](https://i0.wp.com/ouispeakfashion.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/CFDA4.jpg?resize=1024%2C768&ssl=1 "CFDA and OpenAI Launch “Innovation Hub” to Accelerate AI Innovation Across the Fashion Industry 8")

Courtesy of CFDA

Steven Kolb, President and CEO of the CFDA, commented on the initiative: “Fashion is a powerful driver of culture, innovation, and economic growth. The CFDA remains committed to building an American fashion industry that is forward-looking, inclusive, and positioned to inspire the next generation of global creative leadership.”

Charles Porch, Vice President of Global Creative Partnerships at OpenAI, added: “Fashion has always evolved through innovation, creativity, and self-expression, and AI has the potential to become a powerful tool for designers and creators across the industry.”

He continued: “Through this partnership, we’re excited to explore how emerging technologies can expand what’s possible beyond traditional creative constructs and inspire the next generation of fashion.”

## **AI Adoption Accelerates Across Fashion**

Interest in generative AI has rapidly expanded across the fashion sector in areas ranging from design support and product development to visual production, inventory management, and supply chain optimization. Over the past two years in particular, luxury groups and global fashion companies have significantly increased investments in AI technologies, positioning AI as a transformative infrastructure layer reshaping both business strategy and creative workflows.

[LVMH Moët Hennessy Louis Vuitton](https://ouispeakfashion.com/what-must-luxury-protect-in-the-age-of-ai-lvmhs-vision-at-nrf-2026/) has continued expanding partnerships with generative AI companies, while [Zalando](https://ouispeakfashion.com/how-brands-use-generative-ai-for-hyper-personalised-customer-experiences/) has introduced AI-generated visuals to streamline content production. H&M has strengthened AI-powered demand forecasting and supply chain optimization initiatives, and Mango has incorporated generative AI into product image creation. Across Europe and the U.S., AI implementation is accelerating at a notable pace.

At the same time, AI adoption is increasingly moving beyond operational efficiency into more creatively driven areas of fashion, including design assistance, material innovation, personalized recommendations, digital fashion, virtual try-ons, and AI styling.

Against this backdrop, “Innovation Hub” represents a broader shift taking place within the industry. By extending its involvement beyond technology access into mentorship, funding, and long-term collaboration, OpenAI is positioning itself as an active participant in shaping how AI integrates into the future of fashion. The initiative may ultimately signal a new phase in the relationship between fashion and artificial intelligence across the American industry landscape.

[News & Insights](https://cfda.com/news-and-insights/industry-insights/)

“Artificial intelligence.” Many of you have heard this term. But what does it mean? Is it akin to “artificial sweetener?” In what sense, in other words, is AI artificial? Why should you care? And does it matter whether your brand is using AI in the E.U. as opposed to say New York City?

Some studies show that as many as [60 percent or more of executives in fashion are using generative AI.](https://www.mckinsey.com/featured-insights/sustainable-inclusive-growth/charts/gen-ai-is-so-hot-right-now) The use of this technology has grown in the fashion industry, like in some others. Now AI is being used to create designs along with content in a way not seen before. But there are different rules that apply for ownership of designs when using AI as opposed to, say, a Brooklyn based human fashion designer.  
 This article will provide an overview. The subjects are AI types, varied industry uses, and AI-related legal issues. It closes with some pointers to watch out for when deciding on whether or how much to use of this powerful technology.

**1. Is AI artificial?**  
 AI has been around since the 1950s. The term was originally birthed by Professor John McCarthy of Stanford. Since then, various types of AI have proliferated. [The most common types now are generative and non-generative.](https://curve.mit.edu/exploring-shift-traditional-generative-ai#:~:text=The%20core%20distinction%20between%20traditional,new%20using%20learned%20data%20patterns.) These are important to consider for business. Non-generative or traditional AI generally involves supervised learning – where the system classifies a data point after seeing many labeled examples. Nothing new is created. This would be like a child being able to classify another sparrow after having seen many. Generative AI uses what is called unsupervised learning. This is akin to the child learning to classify a new bird even though he or she had not seen one before – after being trained on various types including sparrows, cardinals, and bluebirds. As such, new patterns can be created.

Notwithstanding the foregoing, some prominent computer scientists have critiqued AI. For instance, Professor Yoav Shoham, also of Stanford, has said, [“AI has made truly amazing strides in the past decade.”](https://news.stanford.edu/stories/2017/11/artificial-intelligence-index-tracks-emerging-field) However, “computers still can’t exhibit the common sense or the general intelligence of even a five-year-old.” Some studies from the likes of MIT have shown ChatGPT automation [can increase efficiency](https://executive.mit.edu/how-to-maximize-the-business-value-of-generative-ai-20YU100000NgubgMAB.html#:~:text=In). However, others at MIT point out the negative effects of using [these](https://nam12.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.media.mit.edu%2Farticles%2Fa-i-is-homogenizing-our-thoughts%2F&data=05%7C02%7Cf.desalu%40cfda.com%7C74a354de2f7f437cc9d108de06a3dcb4%7Ce4170ab5e2f04e11a7b7622524c4fda0%7C0%7C0%7C638955498399721141%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=4%2F1Tqqcjzwss13lZ1pksmg0LFUgIa2QpPt5TDBFxn70%3D&reserved=0) technologies on originality. This in some cases results from the similarity of data sets for training. As a result, the type of AI training that you are using is relevant for copyright infringement, as discussed below.

**2. Current uses**  
 According to some sources, the use of AI is slated to skyrocket in fashion – [to over 2 billion in 2032.](https://fashionunited.com/press/business/generative-ai-in-fashion-market-over-2-billion-usd-by-2032/2025012764147) This is relevant. The more that a fashion business likes yours leverages this powerful technology into the tech stack, the more there will be legal complexities. That’s because the technology changes very quickly. This isn’t academic. Generative AI is being used by some in the fashion industry to [“create better-selling designs, reduce marketing costs, hyperpersonalize customer communications, and speed up processes.”](https://www.mckinsey.com/industries/retail/our-insights/generative-ai-unlocking-the-future-of-fashion) The technology has also been used for trend forecasting. These uses give rise to the following legal considerations, among others.

**3. Legal issues**  
 A. Ownership  
 Ownership disputes can stem from using technologies like Chat GPT to create written content or similar technologies for designs. The E.U. and the U.S. generally follow the same line of reasoning when it comes to AI creations. In 2020, the E.U. Parliament passed a number of AI related resolutions. One goes on to clarify that “where AI is used only as a tool to assist an author in the process of creation, the current IP framework remains applicable.” See <https://www.europarl.europa.eu/doceo/document/TA-9-2020-0277_EN.pdf.> at pg. 7, ¶14 (emphasis added). Similarly, the U.S. Copyright office [“will refuse to register a claim if it determines that a human being did not create the work.”](https://cyberlaw.stanford.edu/blog/2018/05/artificial-intelligence-art-who-owns-copyright-0/#:~:text=The%20U.S.%20Copyright%20office%20%E2%80%9Cwill,or%20intervention%20from%20a%20human) (Emphasis added) The office further states that it will exclude works [“produced by machine or mere mechanical process that operates randomly or automatically without any creative input or intervention from a human author.”](https://cyberlaw.stanford.edu/blog/2018/05/artificial-intelligence-art-who-owns-copyright-0/#:~:text=The%20U.S.%20Copyright%20office%20%E2%80%9Cwill,or%20intervention%20from%20a%20human) (Emphasis added.) Consequently, AI-created designs are not likely subject to copyright registration.

B. Infringement  
 The foregoing implementations raise infringement liabilities. The first one is whether the inputs on which the model trains are being infringed. A second related one is the output: designs that are created with infringing inputs can be tainted, too.

With regard to the first, a recent case from the United States District Court for the District of Delaware is telling. The court [found that a technology like Chat GPT which trains on data can nonetheless be infringing it – as such training is not a “fair use.”](https://copyrightalliance.org/ai-training-not-fair-use/) This means that, if a designer trains on other designs from the likes of Gucci, that training by itself can be infringing – even if the eventual design doesn’t directly incorporate any of these other designs.

As for the second, your company can be liable for the technology’s infringements—regardless of what the underlying technology is trained on. A recent example of this occurred when Google was held liable for its algorithms in their ability to potentially make connections and [recommendations between users that enabled unlawful offline conduct](https://hai.stanford.edu/news/who-liable-when-generative-ai-says-something-harmful). The Gonzalez v. Google case raises the issue of the “my AI did it defense.” While the case didn’t deal with infringement, the same reasoning can be applied to AI which creates infringing offline designs. A more recent case was brought [against Singapore based Shein for using AI to scrape designs and make infringing copies](https://hai.stanford.edu/news/who-liable-when-generative-ai-says-something-harmful).

C. Contractors  
 According to some studies, approximately [97 percent of manufacturing in the U.S. is done overseas](https://apparelmagic.com/outsourcing-manufacturing-in-the-fashion-industry-pros-cons-for-small-businesses/#:~:text=As%20a%20matter%20of%20fact,its%20clothing%20to%20foreign%20countries.). Within the U.S. many fashion companies outsource their works beyond their own company doors. As can be seen above, there are potential ownership and infringement liabilities in the subcontractor’s use of AI. Relatedly, there [a slew of employment law concerns implicated,](https://fashionlawjournal.com/employment-law-and-the-rights-of-fashion-models/) too, which are beyond the scope of this article. But they can affect legalities concerning ownership.

**4. Closing**  
 The AI market is moving with lightning speed. Like molasses, the law has been slow to respond. As a result, a recommended practice is to have a clear understanding of the technology and applicable legal uncertainties via your chief technology officer and general counsel, respectively, before fully implementing.

*Ryan is the principal attorney at Long & Associates PLLC, a Malibu based boutique intellectual property (“IP”) practice. Since 2006, he has navigated pioneering brands like Apiece Apart and CFDA members through tricky IP related legal disputes —including trademark ownership and manufacturing liability. As a non-residential fellow of Stanford Law School’s Center for Internet and Society, he has written for, or has been interviewed by, the likes of the TechCrunch about AI legalities. His e-mail is: rlong@landapllc.com.*

1. **AI Types**: Differentiates between non-generative (supervised learning, classifies existing patterns) and generative AI (unsupervised learning, creates new patterns). Some experts note AI lacks common sense of a five-year-old, and MIT studies indicate AI can homogenize creativity due to similar training datasets.

2. **Industry Use**: AI in fashion is projected to reach over $2 billion by 2032. Uses include creating better-selling designs, reducing marketing costs, hyperpersonalizing communications, and trend forecasting.

# How AI, Digital Doubles, and New Laws Are Rewriting Fashion and Beauty

March 12, 2026

 ![Foley's Fashion, Apparel and Beauty attorneys](https://www.foley.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/GettyImages-94074276-1680x1116.jpg)

[Share on LinkedIn](#)

[Share on Twitter](#)

[Print](#)

[Share by Email](#)

[Share](#)

[Back to top](#page)

Artificial intelligence (AI) has gone from buzzword to backstage workhorse in the fashion, apparel, and beauty (FAB) industries. When Foley previewed this space in 2024, AI was already being used to power recommendation engines, searches, and personalization. Since then, AI now drives design tools, virtual try-on experiences, synthetic models, and even the digital “resurrection” of fashion and beauty icons — and lawmakers have noticed.

Across the industry, AI can swap outfits in lookbooks, generate virtual fabrics and prints, and build campaigns around synthetic models. Virtual try-on tools help consumers test lipstick shades, match foundation, and visualize outfits, while beauty apps offer skin diagnostics and product recommendations. Behind the scenes, these tools rely on vast training datasets: fashion photography, runway imagery, influencer content, scraped social media, and e-commerce catalogs. Increasingly, they also depend on full digital capture of models, including 3D body scans, face mapping, voice cloning, and digital replicas.

## The Business of Beauty Bots: Why Brands Should Care

For brands, the appeal is obvious. AI cuts costs, speeds creative cycles, allows assets to be generated and localized quickly, and promises highly personalized shopping experiences. Generative systems can produce new imagery in hours rather than days, while AI styling engines curate outfits and beauty routines based on individual consumers.

The catch is that these systems often rely on real people’s images, bodies, voices, and performances, or on creative works never meant to be used as training material. The same tools that let brands “do more with less” also make it easy to reuse a model’s likeness in ways they never agreed to.

## Rights on the Runway: Publicity, Digital Doubles, and Deepfakes

Because there is no comprehensive federal AI statute, FAB brands operate within a patchwork of legacy doctrines and emerging AI-specific laws. Right of publicity and name, image, and likeness (NIL) laws in states such as California, New York, Tennessee, Florida, and Arkansas have long protected commercial use of a person’s identity, often even after death. A brand that “brings back” a beloved fashion or beauty icon in an AI campaign without the estate’s permission may be inviting litigation.

New York has become the main runway for AI-and[1]model legislation. The New York Fashion Workers Act,1 effective June 19, 2025, directly addresses AI use involving fashion models. The required consent must specify scope, purpose, duration, and compensation; however, routine retouching is excluded. The New York Digital Replica Law,2 effective January 1, 2025, goes after “rights-grab” contracts. A digital replica agreement is void if it (i) allows a replica to be used instead of work the person would have done in person, (ii) fails to give a reasonably specific description of the intended use, and (iii) was negotiated when the individual did not have legal counsel or a union to consult. Brands and agencies can no longer rely on vague language to lock up a model’s digital double indefinitely.

New York’s AI Transparency in Advertising and Synthetic Performer Disclosure Law,3 effective June 9, 2026, moves to the consumer side. If a commercial ad uses an AI-generated synthetic performer, or a realistic digital person created by AI, that fact must be clearly disclosed, with civil penalties for failing to label the ad. A separate New York posthumous right of publicity law4 requires consent from heirs or executors before using a deceased person’s name, image, voice, or likeness in campaigns, which directly affects launches or collections built around “resurrected” icons.

Other states are moving in parallel. Tennessee’s ELVIS Act5 and Arkansas’s HB 10716 explicitly extend publicity rights to AI-generated likenesses and voices, banning unauthorized commercial use, and imposing civil (and in Tennessee, some criminal) penalties. At the federal level, the proposed NO FAKES Act7 would create a nationwide right against unauthorized digital replicas of a person’s likeness, voice, or performance. The Deepfake Liability Act, the Take It Down Act, and PADRA aim to make platforms and creators more accountable for harmful deepfakes and to streamline takedowns, both for influencers and models whose images are misused and for brands that distribute AI-heavy content.8

## Advertising, Privacy, and Biometrics

Traditional advertising and consumer protection rules apply even when content is created by AI. A synthetic model or AI-generated endorsement that misleads consumers can trigger the same false advertising and unfair or deceptive practices claims as any other campaign.

Privacy and biometric laws add further constraints. Statutes like Illinois’s Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA) and California’s CCPA/CPRA regulate how brands collect and use face scans for virtual try-on services, body scans for size and fit tools, and voiceprints for voice-based experiences. Failures in obtaining consent or handling this data can lead to statutory damages and class actions.

New transparency and detection proposals point to where law is heading. California’s proposed AI Transparency Act9 would require detection tools for AI-modified media. New York’s proposed synthetic content provenance bill10 would push AI systems to embed cryptographic provenance data, creating a verifiable trail of how an asset was generated. These proposed laws signal a future in which watermarking and provable origin information for AI content are expected rather than optional.

## Copyright Catwalk: Training Data and AI-Made Designs

In Thaler v. Perlmutter, 11 the D.C. Circuit confirmed that purely AI-generated works without human authorship are not copyrightable under current U.S. law. Brands using AI to generate prints, patterns, or imagery need meaningful human creative input to claim protection.

At the same time, AI training data is under increasing scrutiny. The proposed Generative AI Copyright Disclosure Act12 would require AI developers to disclose their use of copyrighted works in training data. California’s AB 412,13 which has stalled, would required AI developers to obtain permission and pay licensing fees to use copyrighted works for training.

Pennsylvania’s HR 8114 urges Congress to exclude predominantly AI-generated works from copyright protection and to clarify how copyright and fair use apply to the use of copyrighted works in AI training.

Outside the United States, the European Union’s Artificial Intelligence Act15 introduces a risk-based framework with transparency obligations for AI-generated and deepfake content. Multinational FAB brands using virtual try-on tools, recommendation engines, and synthetic models in Europe will need to align with those standards, even if U.S. law continues to evolve more slowly.

## Contract Couture

Talent and vendor contracts need to match how AI is actually being used. Agreements should spell out whether the brand will create digital replicas, scans, or 3D models; where and how those assets may be used, including specific campaign names, channels, territories, and time periods; and whether talent imagery may be used to train internal or third-party AI systems. Compensation for AI-related uses should be addressed separately from standard day rates or flat fees, rather than assuming unlimited synthetic reuse is included.

Legal drafting is only one part of the solution. FAB brands also need internal guardrails. Many are forming cross-functional AI committees that bring together legal, marketing, HR, and IT to inventory tools; map how they touch talent images, third-party content, consumer data, and creative IP; and flag higher-risk uses before launch. Vendor management is becoming more rigorous, with brands asking their business partners how tools are trained, whether they support watermarking and provenance, and demanding indemnification for claims related to use of AI. Workflows that include obtaining informed consent, especially for biometric scans, and for labeling AI[1]generated or heavily altered content where required by law or expected by consumers, are becoming standard operating procedures.

Done thoughtfully, AI can deliver meaningful efficiencies: fewer returns, better fit and shade matching, faster campaign production, smarter inventory decisions, and more relevant product recommendations. The difference between a competitive advantage and a public relations crisis often lies in how a company treats the humans behind the data, including having clear and transparent contractual provisions.

## The Rise of AI and the Expanding Risk to Talent Likeness

While brands adopt AI to streamline campaigns, reduce costs, and extend creative output, these technologies pose unique and often underappreciated risks to models and other creative talent. Chief among them is the unauthorized or overextended use of a model’s likeness beyond the scope of the original engagement.

When AI tools are used to replicate or manipulate those attributes without clear consent, models may lose control over how, where, and for how long their likeness appears.

## A Common Scenario: From Single Campaign to Synthetic Expansion

A model is hired to appear in a single campaign or to model a specific garment. The agreement contemplates traditional photography and a defined scope of use. After the campaign concludes, the brand uses AI tools to digitally replicate the model’s likeness and place it into additional outfits, campaigns, or promotional formats that were never discussed or approved.

From the brand’s perspective, this may feel like an efficient extension of licensed content. From the model’s perspective, it represents a fundamental expansion of use, one that may affect future bookings, dilute exclusivity, or associate the model with products or messaging they did not choose to endorse.

This disconnect often arises because AI-generated content blurs the line between “use of existing images” and the creation of entirely new representations. While the original photographs may have been authorized, the resulting AI-generated images may depict scenarios, garments, or branding that never existed at the time of the shoot.

## Contractual Gaps in Traditional Modeling Agreements

Currently, there’s a discrepancy between legacy modeling contracts and modern AI capabilities. Many agreements were drafted at a time when campaigns were limited to physical photographs and clearly defined deliverables. As a result, contracts frequently grant rights to use “images,” “photographs,” or “recordings,” but do not contemplate synthetic media, digital replicas, or AI-generated derivatives.

In the absence of express language addressing AI, brands may rely on broadly drafted usage clauses to justify expanded use, while models may reasonably assume that consent to appear in a single campaign does not authorize the creation of unlimited digital versions of their likeness.

This ambiguity creates legal and commercial uncertainty for both sides. For talent, it raises concerns about consent, compensation, and control.

## Potential Legal Claims Available to Talent

Depending on the jurisdiction and the specific contractual language at issue, models may have several potential legal avenues if their likeness is used beyond the agreed scope. These may include right of publicity claims, particularly where AI-generated content exploits a model’s identity for commercial gain without consent.

Models may also assert breach of contract claims where AI use exceeds the defined scope of permitted use, or where the contract implicitly limits usage to specified campaigns or formats. In certain circumstances, claims based on false endorsement or unfair competition may arise if AI-generated imagery implies an ongoing relationship or approval that does not exist.

While these claims may provide leverage, litigation is often an imperfect solution. AI-generated content can be deployed quickly and at scale, making it difficult to contain once released.

## Proactive Contractual Protections for Models and Influencers

Given these challenges, preventative strategies are increasingly critical. Models and their representatives should focus on addressing AI-related risks at the contracting stage, before any images are captured or content is created.

Key contractual protections may include explicit prohibitions on AI-generated replicas or derivatives absent separate written consent. Separate compensation structures for synthetic or extended uses can help ensure that talent is fairly compensated for the ongoing exploitation of their likeness.

Approval rights are also an important consideration. Models may seek the right to review and approve AI-generated content before it is published, particularly where such content could affect brand alignment or public perception.

## Monitoring, Enforcement, and Ongoing Oversight

Beyond initial contracting, talent should consider mechanisms for monitoring and enforcement. Audit rights, notice requirements for new uses, and contractual takedown provisions can provide meaningful leverage without immediate resort to litigation.

For higher-profile talent, additional carve-outs may be appropriate. These can include restrictions on sensitive product categories, protections against political or controversial uses, and provisions addressing moral rights or reputational harm.

## Looking Ahead: Protecting Likeness in a Synthetic Marketplace

As AI continues to reshape creative industries, the imbalance of bargaining power between brands and individual models is likely to increase. The key to navigating this evolving landscape lies in proactive contract drafting, informed negotiation, and early legal review.

By addressing AI-related risks upfront, brands and talent can better protect the integrity, value, and longevity of their likeness in an increasingly synthetic marketplace, while allowing innovation to proceed in a manner that respects consent and creative ownership.
