Discover the collection of articles in Special Feature: Law in the Age of Generative AI. [View More](https://www.pnas.org/topic/584)

One of the most pressing legal questions regarding generative AI is whether, and to what extent, the use of in-copyright works as training data for developing large-scale AI models does or does not require copyright owners’ consent or compensation. This is the subject of multiple ongoing lawsuits between copyright owners and AI developers. While a definitive ruling in the courts may be some years off, various proposals for the establishment of a collective licensing system for training data have attracted some attention. The feasibility of such a system, and its possible ramifications, should be carefully considered before proceeding.

## Background on Copyright and the Generative AI Lawsuits

Many developers of generative AI systems have trained foundation models on datasets that include massive quantities of Internet content ([1](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r1)).[*](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#fn4) While some may use their own webcrawlers to gather Internet data, AI developers often get copies of Common Crawl’s datasets of an estimated 9.5 petabytes which this nonprofit organization makes available to all comers without charge ([2](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r2)).

While some content widely available on the Internet is in the public domain (that is, free from copyright constraints), most such content is in-copyright and will be in-copyright for decades to come. This is true not only for commercially disseminated works, but also for user-generated and open source content widely available on the Internet. Copyright protection attaches to original works of authorship from the moment of their creation and generally lasts for seven decades after the deaths of their authors. While most works posted on the Internet are there with right-holders’ permission, it is well known that large quantities of Internet contents were posted without permission and infringe copyrights.

The first lawsuit to charge a generative AI developer with copyright infringement based on the developer’s use of in-copyright works as training data was brought against Stability AI in January 2023 by Sarah Andersen, on behalf of a class of visual artists whose works were used to train a model for Stability’s generative AI system Stable Diffusion ([3](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r3)). Since then, more than four dozen other lawsuits have challenged the legality of using in-copyright works as training data for generative AI models ([4](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r4)).[†](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#fn5) OpenAI, Meta, Google, and Anthropic are among the generative AI model developers who have raised fair use defenses for using in-copyright works as training data.[‡](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#fn6)

Fair uses of in-copyright works are not infringements. The U.S. copyright statute ([6](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r6)) directs consideration of four factors in assessing whether a second comer’s use of a first author’s work is fair or unfair: 1) the purpose and character of the challenged use; 2) the nature of the copyrighted work; 3) the amount and substantiality of the taking; and 4) the effect of the challenged use on the potential market for or value of the copyrighted work ([7](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r7)). Several purposes tend to favor fair use defenses: criticism, comment, news reporting, teaching, scholarship, and research. Whether the use is commercial or noncommercial is also considered in fair use cases.

Since the U.S. Supreme Court’s 1994 ruling in _Campbell v. Acuff-Rose Music, Inc._ ([8](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r8)), in which the Court considered whether a rap parody of a popular song was a fair use or infringement, it has mattered whether the putative fair user’s purpose in using the first author’s work was “transformative,” which is tested based mainly on the similarity or difference in the two works’ purposes. The more transformative (or different) the second comer’s purpose is from the first author’s purpose, the less likely it is that the second author’s use of the first author’s work will serve as a market substitute for that author’s work.

Plaintiffs in the generative AI copyright cases argue (e.g., ref. [9](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r9)) that training data uses of their works are unfair for the following reasons. First, the developers’ purposes are commercial and outputs of generative AI unfairly compete with the plaintiffs’ works. Second, the developers’ use of high quality inputs, such as the plaintiffs’ works, is the reason that the defendants’ generative AI models can produce high quality outputs. Third, the entirety of works in the dataset are copied in the training process, which disfavors fair use defenses. Fourth, the outputs of generative AI systems may have substitutive effects on markets for the plaintiffs’ works and harm the plaintiffs by depriving them of license revenues.

AI developers, by contrast, argue (e.g., ref. [10](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r10)) that their uses of works as training data is fair. First, their uses of plaintiffs’ works are for very different purposes than the authors’ original purposes in creating them, hence the defendants’ purposes are transformative. Second, training uses the works as data, not as works. That is, training does not consume the works for their expressiveness, but only processes and analyzes their parts (such as words) in relation to one another. Moreover, the public availability of works on the Internet tips in favor of fairness. Third, whole works may be copied, but this is an intermediate step in building models, which do not embody the works’ expression in any recognizable form. Fourth, developers contend that transaction costs of negotiating individual permissions for uses of the plaintiffs’ works cannot feasibly be obtained. There is consequently no cognizable harm to the plaintiffs’ markets.

Some commentators are persuaded by the generative AI developers’ fair use defenses (e.g., refs. [11](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r11) and [12](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r12)), while others think the training-data uses of works are unfair (e.g., refs. [13](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r13) and [14](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r14)). A definitive ruling on the generative AI training-data fair use defenses in the United States is likely some years off.

The next part reviews three ways that European scholars have suggested that collective licensing of in-copyright works for generative AI systems may be established. It then discusses the perceived feasibility of collective licensing of in-copyright works as training data in the United States. Finally, it discusses some considerations that courts and policymakers should bear in mind as they address generative AI copyright issues.

## European Scholars on Collective Licensing

Paying some attention to European proposals about collective licensing to address generative AI-related uses of in-copyright works is worthwhile for three reasons. First, their proponents aim to make American and other non-EU model developers pay these license fees. Second, EU policymakers aim to influence policies of other nations to follow EU AI-related initiatives. Third, the European proposals reflect a different perspective on collective licensing than U.S. proposals.

To set the stage for analyzing European scholars’ collective licensing proposals, some background about relevant EU laws is necessary. One such law is the European Directive on Copyright and Related Rights in the Digital Single Market (CDSMD) ([15](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r15)) which became effective in 2019. That directive contains two provisions requiring EU member states to adopt new exceptions in their copyright laws to authorize copying of in-copyright works for purposes of text- and data-mining (TDM), which EU officials recognize would be socially beneficial ([15](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r15), Recital 5).

Article 3(1) of the CDSMD authorizes nonprofit scientific research and cultural heritage institutions to engage in TDM on lawfully acquired copies of in-copyright works for scientific and research purposes. Article 4(1) directs member states to create a second copyright exception to authorize other entities to engage in TDM, although Article 4(3) gives copyright owners the right to opt-out of the Article 4(1) TDM privilege. In contrast, Article 7(1) of the CDSMD provides that any attempt to override the scientific and cultural heritage TDM privilege by contract will be unenforceable.

A second relevant EU law is the AI Act ([16](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r16)). While the AI Act focuses primarily on regulation of AI risks and safety, it includes important rules about copyright obligations of developers of generative AI models (which the AI Act calls “general purpose AI” or GPAI) (see e.g., ref. [17](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r17)). Article 53(1)(c) of the AI Act requires GPAI developers to adopt policies about their compliance with EU copyright laws and to articulate how they intend to enable copyright owners to opt out through state-of-the-art technologies of the TDM privilege established by Article 4(1) of the CDSDM.

Article 53(1)(d) of the AI Act further requires GPAI model developers to prepare and disclose a summary of the data on which their model was trained in accordance with a template published by the EU’s AI Office ([18](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r18)). This information may be useful when assessing whether the GPAI developer’s access to training data was lawful. It may also help copyright owners determine whether their works were used as training data which, in turn, may inform their decisions about whether to opt out of Article 4(1)’s TDM privilege.

Recital 106 of the AI Act states that any commercial GPAI provider who markets a model in the EU must have complied with EU copyright law and the CDSMD’s TDM opt-out obligation “regardless of the jurisdiction in which the copyright-relevant acts underpinning the training of those general-purpose AI models take place.” It explains that this measure is “necessary to ensure a level playing field among providers of general-purpose AI models where no provider should be able to gain a competitive advantage in the Union market by applying lower copyright standards than those provided in the Union.”

Although recitals of EU regulations do not set forth binding rules, they may inform interpretations of the AI Act. Recital 106 signals that its drafters think that GPAI developers should ensure their models’ development processes comply with EU copyright law, even if the model’s development was lawful under the national law where the models were trained. In this way, the AI Act aims to achieve a “Brussels effect,” that is, to persuade AI developers to comply with EU copyright standards and to thwart regulatory arbitrage (see ref. [19](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r19)). There is a lively debate in the United States and EU about whether the EU can achieve this kind of extraterritorial reach of its laws through a recital in the AI Act (see e.g., refs. [20](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r20) and [21](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r21)).

Neither the CDSMD nor the AI Act mentions collective licensing. This has not dissuaded European copyright scholars from endorsing the idea of a collective licensing regime under which generative AI developers would be obliged to provide right-holders with remuneration for AI-related uses of in-copyright materials ([22](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r22); see also refs. [23](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r23) and [24](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r24)). These scholars recognize the societal value of generative AI systems, but are concerned that generative AI is going to displace job opportunities for authors, artists, and other creators. These collective licensing proposals also reflect a sense of fairness to creators for the uses that generative AI model developers are making of their works. The next three sections discuss ways that a collective licensing regime might arise. A fourth section considers some pros and cons of these proposals and their feasibility in the EU and potential implications for U.S. developers.

### The Article 4(3) Opt-Out Privilege May Lead to Collective Licensing.

Even before the AI Act became effective, some AI developers were negotiating licensing deals with major European copyright industry players to use their content as training data. OpenAI, for instance, announced a deal in 2023 with Axel Springer to use this publishers’ works as training data ([25](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r25)). Other voluntary licensing agreements between AI developers and EU copyright owners have also been occurring ([26](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r26), at 95–98).

Some EU collective management organizations (CMOs), which grant licenses on behalf of their members’ copyrights in specific types of works for uses within their mandates from their member right-holders, have announced their intent to exercise opt-out rights under Article 4(3) as to all works in their repertoires for TDM uses ([27](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r27)). The opt-out rule gives CMOs heightened bargaining power with AI developers to negotiate terms that would benefit their members. Voluntary collective licensing for training-data uses can occur through direct negotiations between AI developers and CMOs.

Spain proposed an extended collective licensing (ECL) regime to enable remuneration of copyright owners for generative AI training uses of in-copyright works ([28](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r28)). CMOs are generally authorized to grant licenses only as to copyright owner members’ works. An ECL regime would empower CMOs to grant licenses for uses of works of the types they administer, including works of nonmembers, as long as CMOs treat nonmembers fairly in the allocation of revenues collected by the CMO for right-holders (see e.g., ref. [29](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r29)). Right-holders would need to opt-out of the CDSMD Article 4(1) TDM privilege to be eligible for compensation under the Spanish ECL proposal.

### Statutory Licensing as an Alternative to CDSMD’s Opt-Out Rule.

Some European commentators who favor collective licensing for generative AI-related uses of in-copyright works think that the Commission should reopen the CDSMD to repeal the opt-out rule of Article 4(3) because it will deprive developers of AI models of access to the highest quality and quantity of inputs ([30](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r30), [31](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r31)). Large numbers of right-holder opt-outs would cause AI models to be more limited in capabilities than is socially desirable. These commentators endorse a “permitted-but-paid” ([32](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r32)) model for CMOs’ grants of licenses for uses of works as generative AI training data.

The biggest disadvantage of the CDSMD opt-out approach is that it may produce a lose-lose situation. When right-holders exercise opt-out rights under Article 4(3), commentators worry that licensing may not occur as to a great many works that would be excellent training data because negotiations for licensing after opt-outs would either not happen or fail ([30](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r30), at 6; [33](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r33)). The result would be that AI developers would lose the opportunity to train on large volumes of high-quality data and copyright owners would lose the opportunity to get some compensation for the AI developers’ new uses of their works.

Professors Christophe Geiger and Vincenzo Iaia suggest that the Commission should replace Article 4(3) with a limitation-based remuneration right provision. This new provision would allow commercial developers of generative AI systems to use all manner of works as training data if they provide adequate remuneration for the licensed uses ([30](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r30), at 6).

Geiger and Iaia regard their proposal as a workable compromise: AI developers would have the right to use as much high-quality data as they need to develop high quality models. And copyright owners would benefit from compensation for the generative AI uses of their works. This proposal is in keeping with numerous other statutory license regimes adopted in the EU for socially beneficial uses of in-copyright works coupled with remuneration obligations, as well as being consistent with fundamental rights to science and culture and freedom of expression ([30](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r30), at 6–7).

Professor Giancarlo Frosio has made a similar proposal ([31](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r31)). He favors a levy regime in which “statutory remunerations could be linked to specific categories of works or right-holders, based on an empirical review of the creative markets most significantly disrupted by AI-generated creativity” ([31](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r31), at 83). This levy system should take account of generative AI’s market substitution effects on human authorship, consider the unique combinatorial nature of AI outputs, lower transaction costs compared to traditional copyright models, and support human author creativity which could then provide more data for further training of AI models. Yet, Frosio recommends that only those creators whose works are “significantly affected by AI could be entitled to these remunerations” ([31](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r31), at 83). An assessment of impacts should be revisited over time because any generative AI impacts on creative markets are likely to evolve.

### A Levy on Generative AI Commercial Products or Services.

Most European proponents of collective licensing for AI uses of in-copyright works focus on the training-data phase of generative AI development and anticipate that CMOs would provide fair remuneration to individuals for training uses of their data. Professor Martin Senftleben’s collective licensing proposal is markedly different than the training-data-oriented remuneration regimes because it would allow training to proceed without advance compensation, but would impose a levy on generative AI developers’ commercialization of their products and services ([22](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r22), [34](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r34)).

Senftleben agrees with Geiger, Iaia, and Frosio that Article 4(3)’s opt-out rule should be abandoned because of the likelihood of the lose-lose scenario ([33](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r33)). He argues that requiring remuneration at the training stage would be at odds with the societal goal of fostering the highest quality and unbiased AI systems trained on massive quantities of high quality works and promoting innovation in AI industries. Transaction costs of negotiating with copyright owners who opt-out would be very large and the opt-out rule would disadvantage small and medium-sized enterprises as well as individual authors because it would likely be only very large right-holders with whom AI developers would make deals. Senftleben also thinks a training-data-focused remuneration scheme may result in AI developers deciding against training their models on EU works, which would marginalize EU culture. He proposes instead a levy on commercialization of generative AI products and services in the EU to support human authorship ([22](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r22), at 1549).

Because human authorship is so valuable to society, as well as to AI model developers who need new quantities of creative works on which to train models, Senftleben argues that a collective licensing regime is needed to support authors and their creative work. He conceptualizes this levy on commercial developers of generative AI products and services as a delayed way to compensate creators for uses of their works as training data ([34](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r34), at 47–48).

Senftleben regards his proposal as a copyright-based solution, under which revenues generated by the levy would be administered by CMOs to support creators and their works. He characterizes CMOs as providing a “well-established infrastructure for the appropriate distribution of the monies collected,” and a more stable solution than a tax measure ([22](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r22), at 1540). He theorizes that “AI remuneration could even be set at a level that would counterbalance lower production costs and enhance human authors’ chances of competing with generative AI systems” ([22](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r22), at 1550). Senftleben expects that commercial AI model developers would pay the same lumpsum levy set by the relevant CMOs annually ([35](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r35)).

### Assessing the European Collective Licensing Proposals.

European critics of the CDSMD opt-out rule under Article 4(3) are probably right that this privilege will likely be exercised by large right-holders who can use such leverage to negotiate deals with large commercial AI model developers. Individual authors are unlikely to benefit from such deals unless the European Commission decides to impose an obligation on right-holders to share with authors some of the revenues they receive from AI model developers for training-data uses of their works. The European Copyright Society, whose members are academics from various countries in Europe, has recently urged the Commission to ensure that authors receive a fair share of revenues that large right-holders have obtained through agreements with AI model developers ([36](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r36)).

Small and medium-sized right-holders are less likely than large right-holder groups to benefit from the opt-out privilege. If small or medium-sized right-holders opt out, AI developers may not seek them out for licensing deals, and even if they do, smaller players may not have as much leverage for negotiating deals. Startups are also unlikely to be able to negotiate comparable deals with large right-holders, which means the opt-out rule will have created a significant entry barrier at least for commercial model developers.

Professor João Pedro Quintais has succinctly observed that the opt-out rule “limits data quality and availability, increases costs, reduces competition, and slows innovation and productivity in generative AI, ultimately hampering economic growth” ([20](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r20), at 13). The European scholars’ predictions that the opt-out privilege will impede access to the widest array of European works seem sound.

While a collective license solution to AI developers’ copyright problems is intuitively attractive, it would be daunting to devise a fair remuneration scheme, as Professor Frosio recognizes, given that all types of copyrighted work capable of being digitized are fodder for generative AI training ([31](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r31), at 83). His suggestion that CMOs could tailor payouts based on empirical data about which sectors of creative workers are being displaced by generative AI may be a step in the right direction, but it too would be costly to administer and adjust over time. It would likely also lead to considerable disagreements about whether this approach would be an equitable resolution to copyright owner claims.

Another complication for collective licensing in the EU is, as Professor Senftleben has pointed out, the rights clearance infrastructure in the EU is highly fragmented ([22](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r22), at 1546). One-stop-shopping for rights clearances for large volumes of EU works is virtually impossible (except for uses of musical compositions). Each of the 27 EU member states has its own national copyright law, only some parts of which are harmonized across the Union. EU-wide copyright directives have achieved only partial harmonization. Its member states sometimes enact variations even when implementing copyright rules required by directives. On many issues, the European Commission has not tried to achieve harmonization of copyright rules. The only way that generative AI developers can get EU-wide licenses is to negotiate with individual right-holders, but this must be done on a right-holder by right-holder basis.

A further complication with CMO collective licensing for training data is that CMOs are territorial to member states in which they are incorporated, and they typically represent only certain types of creators whose works are in the same sector (e.g., authors of music, literature, or photography) as to specified uses. AI model developers would have to negotiate with multiple CMOs to get blanket licenses to their repertoires. CMOs also typically grant licenses only for certain types of uses of those works. Professor Quintais has observed that it is far from clear whether CMOs currently have authorization to license TDM or AI training uses of works in their repertoires ([20](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r20), at 14). If they do not have training-data rights at present, it may be difficult and costly to acquire those rights. Although CMOs may acquire rights, they generally do not have copies of works to license to AI developers.

Quintais suggests that CMOs may “underestimate the monumental scale, complexity and cost of the right clearance endeavor” for training-data uses ([20](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r20), at 14). Each CMO’s dataset, however large, is “but a drop” in the “ocean of data” used to train models ([20](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r20), at 14). Quintais notes that while CMOs often grant blanket licenses for uses of works in their repertoires, they may not know which of their members have opted out of the Article 4 TDM privilege, given that the terms of negotiated agreements between CMO members and generative AI developers may not be publicly available. This would obviously complicate assessment of the value of their repertoires for licensing TDM or AI training uses. He adds that because “EU law contains no compulsory mechanism of collective rights management for ‘training rights,’” it may be that “only voluntary forms of collective management are possible,” although Quintais recognizes that ECL might be possible ([20](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r20), at 14).

Given these complexities, it is understandable that some European scholars propose trading the Article 4(3) opt-out right for a fair remuneration regime as a better solution to the training-data dilemma. Yet details are sparse about how they would design a fair remuneration regime, and those details matter. Would, for example, EU member state remuneration regimes cover only those in-copyright works created in their jurisdictions? Could EU works be segregated from works more broadly available on the Internet by the locations of data on European servers?

Professor Senftleben’s proposed levy on generative AI products and services has some advantages over training-data-based collective licensing options. It would support model developers’ uses of the widest range of inputs for training models, keep entry barriers lower than the opt-out regime, provide financial support for human creators and their works of authorship, and avoid expending the bulk of collected levies on CMO administration and payouts to individual creators.

Yet it too has some problematic features. Professor Quintais questions what distinct harm that Senftleben’s proposed levy would address, which “raises both conceptual problems (how to align the levy with infringement rules?) and practical ones (how to fairly calculate a levy for harm that cannot be determined?)” ([20](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r20), at 16). That proposal “challenges the central normative justification for the AI levy: if the copyright harm cannot be identified, how can we establish the substitution effect of AI outputs on human-authored works?” ([20](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r20), at 16) The levies recommended by Senftleben would be paid to CMOs, which he assumes they would use to support authors, artists, and other creators presumably through grants or other revenue-sharing arrangements ([22](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r22), at 1550–1551). But how would the CMOs identify who was worthy of being supported and what process would CMOs undertake to ensure that the revenues were properly allocated? Senftleben does not address these questions.

Expectations among European collective licensing proponents seem to be high that authors and other right-holders would be able to get substantial revenues from training-data-based or AI-product-and-service-based remuneration schemes. At present, it is impossible to assess how much value particular inputs have contributed to models on which they were trained. Because of the massive size of training datasets and the inability to pinpoint value-added by particular inputs, it seems likely that the costs of administering the licenses may be very high in relation to payouts to millions of individual right-holders ([20](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r20), at 14; [5](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r5), at 1565–1567).

The European Commission has not initiated a consultation about whether the EU should require GPAI developers to collectively license their uses of in-copyright works under Article 4 of the CDSMD. It is unclear whether it will do so, although Professor Alexander Peukert has stated that the AI Act’s “general copyright compliance obligation can function as the basis for additional duties concerning the training phase” and “is also flexible enough to cover future changes of EU copyright law, for example a codification of a mandatory AI output levy” ([17](https://www.pnas.org/doi/10.1073/pnas.2509769122#r17), at 507).

For now, the most troubling feature of the EU AI-related copyright landscape is the AI Act’s Recital 106 which aims to require GPAI developers to comply with EU copyright rules, even if their uses of works as training data are lawful in the jurisdictions where models were trained. Leading developers of generative AI systems hope that U.S. courts will rule in favor of their fair use defenses, even if those uses would not be lawful under EU law.

## U.S. Collective Licensing Proposals

Collective licensing has seldom been discussed in the United States as a solution to the AI training-data problem. The first section discusses several published statements that have endorsed collective licensing of in-copyright works as training data for AI models. The second section considers whether the class action lawsuits against generative AI developers for copyright infringement based on the unauthorized uses of works as training data may precipitate collective licensing as a solution. The third section reviews reasons to be skeptical about collective licensing as a compromise solution to the AI training-data dilemma.

args.summary:
This PNAS Perspective article by Pamela Samuelson examines the feasibility of collective licensing of in-copyright works as training data for generative AI systems. It addresses the central legal question of whether using copyrighted works as training data requires copyright owners' consent or compensation, with fair use being the main defense in ongoing U.S. lawsuits.

**Background:** Multiple lawsuits (starting with Sarah Andersen v. Stability AI in January 2023) have been filed against AI developers including OpenAI, Meta, Google, and Anthropic. AI developers argue fair use because training uses works as data (not for their expressiveness), purposes are transformative, and individual license negotiations are infeasible. Copyright owners argue uses are commercial, outputs compete with their works, and wholesale copying disfavors fair use.

**European Proposals:** Three main approaches are discussed:
1. **Article 4(3) Opt-Out Model** - The EU CDSMD allows right-holders to opt out of TDM privileges, potentially leading to collective licensing through CMOs. Spain proposed an extended collective licensing (ECL) regime.
2. **Statutory Licensing** - Scholars like Geiger, Iaia, and Frosio propose replacing the opt-out rule with a "permitted-but-paid" model with mandatory remuneration for training data uses.
3. **Levy on Commercial Products** - Senftleben proposes a levy on generative AI products/services to support human authorship, allowing training to proceed without advance compensation.

**U.S. Proposals:** Collective licensing has been less discussed in the U.S. The article notes that if fair use defenses succeed, developers can continue commercial exploitation; if copyright owners prevail, developers face billions in damages and potential destruction of models.

**Key Challenges:** The article identifies numerous feasibility problems: fragmented EU rights clearance infrastructure (27 member states with different laws), uncertainty about whether CMOs have authorization to license TDM/AI training uses, difficulty calculating fair compensation given the massive scale of training data, high administrative costs relative to potential payouts, the "lose-lose" scenario where opt-outs reduce data quality without generating compensation, and the EU AI Act's Recital 106's attempt at extraterritorial application requiring compliance with EU copyright regardless of where models were trained. The article concludes that courts and policymakers should carefully consider these complexities before implementing collective licensing regimes.

# Chapter 2: AI, the creative industries and copyright reform

12.In this chapter, we set out the existing landscape in relation to AI and copyright in the UK, before assessing the case for change.

## Copyright and the generative AI lifecycle

### The UK’s existing copyright framework

13.Generative AI refers to systems that can produce content across multiple modalities, such as text, images, audio, video and computer code, in response to user prompts.[27](#footnote-464) These systems are developed using text and data mining (TDM) techniques that involve the copying and automated analysis of vast quantities of data to identify statistical patterns and relationships.[28](#footnote-463) The resulting model can then use those patterns to generate outputs that may closely resemble human-created content.[29](#footnote-462)

14.Much of the material used in developing and operating generative AI systems consists of human-created works protected by the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 (CDPA). These include books, news articles, computer programs, photographs, musical works, films and broadcasts.[30](#footnote-461) Other material, such as raw factual data or public domain content,[31](#footnote-460) may fall outside copyright protection.

15.Copyright arises automatically in qualifying works[32](#footnote-459) and gives rightsholders exclusive control over a number of ‘restricted’ acts, including copying.[33](#footnote-458) Copyright underpins the UK’s creative economy by granting creators exclusive rights to use and distribute their works for a defined period, incentivising the creation and circulation of new works by enabling creators to control how their material is used and to seek payment for their creative effort.[34](#footnote-457) Several witnesses to our inquiry characterised the UK’s copyright framework as the international “gold standard”.[35](#footnote-456)

16.Copyright may be infringed if the whole or a substantial part of a protected work is copied without permission, unless an exception applies.[36](#footnote-455) The CDPA provides two exceptions that are worth highlighting in this context:

There is currently no broad exception that explicitly permits the use of copyrighted works for commercial TDM or the training of generative AI models, unlike in some other jurisdictions (see Table 2).[39](#footnote-452)

Article 4 permits TDM of lawfully accessible works for both commercial and non-commercial purposes, unless rightsholders have expressly reserved their rights (e.g. via machine-readable means).[41](#footnote-450) |
| Japan | Copyright Act, Article 30–4 | A broad statutory exception allowing TDM for commercial and non-commercial uses, particularly for “non-enjoyment purposes”.[42](#footnote-449) |

| United States | Copyright Act 1976, §107 (“fair use”) | No specific TDM provision. Use of copyrighted works, including for AI training, is assessed under the fair use doctrine using a four-factor test applied case by case.[44](#footnote-447) |

No specific TDM provision. Use of copyrighted works, including for AI training, is assessed under the fair use doctrine using a four-factor test applied case by case.[44](#footnote-447)

### AI model development and operation

17.Because TDM and other stages of developing and operating generative AI systems involve copying and processing protected works,[45](#footnote-446) copyright may be engaged at several points in the ‘lifecycle’[46](#footnote-445) of a model. Witnesses to our inquiry commonly distinguished between acts of copying and related processing that occur when material is collected, prepared, analysed or retrieved for use by an AI system (often referred to as ‘input’ concerns); and any later reproduction of protected expression in AI-generated outputs.[47](#footnote-444) Dr Hayleigh Bosher, Associate Professor in Intellectual Property Law at Brunel, University of London, and Dr Andres Guadamuz, Reader in Intellectual Property Law at the University of Sussex, identified four principal stages of the generative AI lifecycle at which copyright may be engaged: data collection and pre-processing; model training; inference; and output generation.[48](#footnote-443) These stages are set out in Figure 1.

## Arguments for and against copyright reform

### Use of protected works in AI training

18.Much of the current policy debate concerns how copyright applies to the use of protected works in training generative AI models, particularly at the data collection and model training stages, rather than on questions of infringement in AI-generated outputs. Originally, in its December 2024 consultation on AI and copyright, the Government characterised the present position as one of “legal uncertainty” for AI developers. It suggested that some leading developers therefore choose to train models in jurisdictions with clearer or more permissive rules, a point that was echoed in our evidence.[65](#footnote-426) The consultation sought views on whether a broad new commercial TDM exception should be introduced and initially said that an ‘opt-out’ approach was its preferred route.[66](#footnote-425) Since then, there has been a “reset” and the Government now states that it has no preferred option.[67](#footnote-424)

19.Determining whether training generative AI models on copyrighted works without a licence infringes the reproduction right is ultimately a matter for the courts. There has been no ruling in the UK on this specific question to date,[68](#footnote-423) and courts in other jurisdictions are still working through these questions under their own doctrines.[69](#footnote-422) In the absence of UK case law, the Government’s consultation suggested that it may be appropriate to consider “a more direct intervention through legislation to clarify the rules in this area”.[70](#footnote-421)

20.During our inquiry, creative industry witnesses fundamentally disagreed with the premise that the application of the current copyright framework to AI development is uncertain. They were unanimous that UK copyright law is “absolutely clear”[71](#footnote-420) on this point: in their view, copying protected works to train AI models engages the restricted act of reproduction and therefore requires rightsholders’ consent and a licence under the CDPA, unless a specific statutory exception applies.[72](#footnote-419) The Independent Society of Musicians (ISM) told us:

“In principle, UK copyright law already gives rightsholders the exclusive rights they need to control the use of their works, including reproduction, communication to the public, and adaptation. The problem is not the law’s scope, but the lack of effective enforcement in the AI context.”[73](#footnote-418)

21.Dr Bosher emphasised that the restricted act of reproduction is “a broad legal concept”, giving rightsholders the exclusive right to control “direct or indirect, temporary or permanent reproduction by any means, in any form, in whole or in part”. In her view, “it does not matter so much *how* a copy is made, it is simply enough that a protected work is used without permission”, because copyright “regulates copying, in any material form”.[74](#footnote-417) Dr Guadamuz similarly told us that “what copyright does protect, and what AI training necessarily engages, is the reproduction” of copyrighted material, since “the act of gathering, copying, and processing works to build a training dataset will, in almost every case, involve the making of a copy of a work at some point in the process”. On that basis, he concluded that “the unauthorised copying of protected works for AI training is capable of constituting infringement” under the CDPA.[75](#footnote-416)

22.Turning to whether the existing copyright exceptions permit the copying involved in AI training, the Centre for Regulation of the Creative Economy at the University of Glasgow (CREATe) commented that in its view the “narrowly conceived” non-commercial research exception makes research and development (R&D) in the UK “risky”. It proposed that section 29A of the CDPA should be reconceived to cover “all research and development before market entry, at which point transparency and licensing obligations apply”.[76](#footnote-415) On a similar note, Google and Microsoft told us that the exception is not suited to contemporary AI development practices. It is, they argued, increasingly difficult to distinguish non-commercial TDM from commercially linked activity, given that advanced AI development is frequently achieved through collaboration between universities, public sector bodies and the private sector, and where the end goal is often commercialisation.[77](#footnote-414)

23.The News Media Association (NMA) disputed strongly that the current non-commercial research exception leaves a problematic gap for AI research and development. In its view, the constraints on onward sharing of datasets are a deliberate safeguard to prevent research corpora becoming a backdoor into unlicensed commercial model training; the perceived risk to public-private partnerships is therefore a “feature, not a bug” of the law. The NMA stated that extending section 29A to all pre-market R&D would primarily benefit large commercial AI developers by allowing models to be trained on copyright works without consent “at the very stage when rightsholders’ leverage matters most”, undermining the emerging licensing market by removing incentives to seek permission up front. It also noted that relying on an undefined concept of “market entry” would make it difficult for rightsholders to monitor or enforce their rights.[78](#footnote-413)

24.Dr Bosher stated in simple terms that the current exception for TDM in section 29A “does not apply to AI models because it is only applicable for non-commercial purposes”. She also rejected reliance on the temporary copying exception in section 28A, noting that she does not consider its associated conditions to be met by large-scale generative model training. If any existing exception already authorised these uses, she argued, the Government “would not have considered implementing a new copyright exception to cover AI activity”.[79](#footnote-412)

25.Input to our inquiry from technology sector witnesses generally focused on whether using copyright-protected content for model training involves the kind of ‘copying’ that the CDPA is intended to regulate, rather than the detail of existing exceptions. Some witnesses argued that training models on publicly available content should be understood as a process analogous to ‘learning’ patterns from information, rather than copying expressive content in a way that engages the reproduction right.[80](#footnote-411) Dr Guadamuz recognised the “intuitive appeal” of the analogy: “We do not say that a novelist infringes copyright merely because they have read and been influenced by other novels. If this process of learning from existing works does not constitute infringement when performed by a human, should it when performed by a machine?”[81](#footnote-410) Matthew Sinclair, Senior Director at the Computer and Communications Industry Association (CCIA), proposed that, as such, licensing should only be considered “when copyright is used in the outputs of models” or where “distinctive datasets” are concerned.[82](#footnote-409)

26.Witnesses also drew attention to the scale and composition of training data. Google argued that “any particular work in and of itself is not necessary” to train a model; these rely instead on the “total collection of works”.[83](#footnote-408) Meta similarly characterised training as extracting “non-expressive data and grammatical patterns … from the underlying training data”,[84](#footnote-407) with no individual work having a “material influence” on the model as a whole.[85](#footnote-406) Mr Sinclair stated that as a result, the contribution of any given piece of content to a large training corpus is “in effect, zero”,[86](#footnote-405) and that material with no identifiable economic value at the level of individual works should not, in itself, be subject to a separate licensing requirement.

27.A further contention was that generative AI systems are designed to produce novel outputs, not to reproduce the works on which they were trained. Roxanne Carter, Global IP Lead for the Government Affairs and Policy team at Google, told us that since systems are intended to “produce wholly new content”, rather than to function as an “information retrieval system” or databases of underlying works, developers should be free to train on material that is freely available on the web without obtaining licences at that stage.[87](#footnote-404) However, we note that this distinction does not reflect how Google’s products operate in practice. Several of its AI tools, including Google Gemini, Google AI Overviews and Google AI Mode, integrate RAG to surface, summarise and organise information from specific sources at the point of use, and routinely direct users to those sources through hyperlinks. In these services, retrieval and generative functions are deliberately combined.[88](#footnote-403)

28.Recent official assessments and academic commentary in other jurisdictions have, however, cast doubt on the ‘non-expressive use’ and human-learning analogies advanced by some developers. The US Copyright Office, for example, has rejected the claim that generative AI training is non-expressive once datasets of protected works are used to build models capable of reproducing copyrighted expression. It concluded that the learning analogy “rests on a faulty premise”: humans retain only imperfect, filtered impressions of works, whereas generative AI training involves making perfect digital copies, analysing them almost instantaneously, and producing models that can create competing works at “superhuman speed and scale”.[89](#footnote-402)

29.Dr Guadamuz similarly emphasised “the industrial scale of the process” of AI training, which “distinguishes it from anything that occurs in human learning”. He concluded that we should analyse AI training “through the established doctrines of copyright law … rather than seeking to import a metaphor that was never designed to bear legal weight”.[90](#footnote-401) Dr Bosher characterised terms such as ‘memorisation’, ‘reading’ and ‘learning’ as “misleading metaphorical rhetoric” that is “deliberately used to influence the way in which the functioning of AI is understood”. She argued that while these “might be accepted parlance in the AI sector”, they should be “avoided in the context of policy and regulation” as they obscure the underlying technical processes and their legal and economic significance.[91](#footnote-400)

### Calls for a commercial TDM exception

30.Another common theme in evidence from technology sector representatives was that “legal uncertainty”[92](#footnote-399) arises from the UK’s current copyright framework, which then acts as a barrier to AI investment. Vinous Ali, Deputy Executive Director at the Startup Coalition, described the framework as a “ceiling to our ambition”, telling us:

“We can have the best research but that will not be enough. We can have the Government pouring £2 billion into AI and unblocking planning laws, infrastructure and energy costs, but that will not be enough if start-ups do not have access to the data they need to create.”[93](#footnote-398)

Mr Sinclair agreed that the Government’s efforts to “address issues such as energy costs and skills” could be “undermined by not having the right copyright regime.”[94](#footnote-397)

31.These stakeholders consistently identified a broad commercial TDM exception, with or without the opt-out mechanism proposed by the Government in its consultation, as the central policy lever to address these concerns.[95](#footnote-396) Google told us that without a TDM exception for commercial use, “the UK will struggle to achieve its stated ambitions in becoming an attractive place for AI investment and innovation, as training AI models in the UK will be more difficult for companies of all sizes.”[96](#footnote-395)

32.Meta cited analysis by Europe Economics and the CCIA[97](#footnote-394) which estimated that if the UK had a commercial TDM exception, it would secure $6.4 billion of AI investment overall in 2025, of which $4.3 billion would be “TDM-sensitive”. Without a TDM exception, the overall AI investment figures were estimated to be between $1.9 billion and $3.2 billion.[98](#footnote-393) As part of this analysis, a survey of developers, investors, and others in the UK AI sector was conducted. It found that if other jurisdictions implemented protections for TDM and the UK did not, 66% of respondents would undertake projects in other countries, and 25% reported that they would have to do this for “many” projects.[99](#footnote-392) However, we note that the Europe Economics analysis explicitly states that it is focused on only “one specific metric: investment in TDM-intensive activities”.[100](#footnote-391) It therefore does not address the corresponding impact that introducing a commercial TDM exception might have on the creative industries, which are already experiencing significant AI-related harms, as we explore later in this chapter.[101](#footnote-390)

33.When asked to rank the significance of copyright as a barrier, in comparison to issues such as energy prices and access to capital, Antony Walker, Deputy Chief Executive Officer of techUK, told us that it is “of pretty equal relevance”.[102](#footnote-389) In contrast, the Creative Industries Policy and Evidence Centre (Creative PEC) suggested that there is currently limited robust evidence on the precise impact of copyright legislation on AI investment decisions. In its view, there is “little evidence that copyright is the main reason” dedicated AI companies or startups choose to base key operations elsewhere.[103](#footnote-388) Ed Newton-Rex, Chief Executive Officer of Fairly Trained, noted that the trend for the largest technology companies to base themselves outside the UK predates generative AI. The reasons why, he argued, “have nothing to do with copyright law”.[104](#footnote-387)

34.In this context, we note that the Government’s *AI Opportunities Action Plan* made only limited reference to copyright.[105](#footnote-386) It set out a broader agenda for strengthening the industry, including developing a long-term plan for AI infrastructure, establishing AI Growth Zones to accelerate data-centre development, and improving access to compute.[106](#footnote-385) The Government recently reported that 38 of its 50 commitments had been met in the first year of the plan’s implementation.[107](#footnote-384) techUK said there had been “notable progress in foundational areas”, including compute planning, skills programmes and the establishment of the Sovereign AI Unit.[108](#footnote-383) The update also highlighted progress on unlocking high-value creative and research data through initiatives such as the Creative Content Exchange,[109](#footnote-382) but did not frame copyright as a material barrier to delivery.

35.In our inquiry on scaling up, access to data was raised as a factor that can limit firms’ growth. Commentary focused, however, on facilitating access to key public data assets and targeted datasets, rather than the broad range of content that a new TDM exception would cover. Challenges with accessing finance, compute and talent were viewed as more significant blockers.[110](#footnote-381) Similarly, in the Government’s Artificial Intelligence Sector Study 2024, concerns about regulatory clarity were mentioned less frequently than availability of finance and talent as barriers to firm growth. The study also highlighted the growth which has occurred in the UK AI sector with the current copyright framework and without a commercial TDM exception.[111](#footnote-380)

36.The interpretation of UK copyright law is a matter for the courts and future cases may help to set precedents in this area. However, the consistent call from technology sector stakeholders for a new, broad commercial text and data mining (TDM) exception expressly to enable more AI model training to take place in the UK suggests that they do not regard large-scale commercial training on copyright-protected works as clearly covered by the existing exceptions. If they did, a commercial TDM exception would be unnecessary.

37.On this basis, the main uncertainty for large AI developers appears to lie in the question of whether their current and proposed training practices would withstand legal challenge if tested in court. Support for a broad commercial TDM exception should therefore be understood as an attempt to lower that litigation risk by weakening the current level of copyright protection, rather than as a neutral exercise in clarifying the law. We are also not persuaded that expanding the existing non-commercial research exception to cover all “pre-market” research and development is either necessary or desirable.

38.Under existing law, copyright is engaged whenever the whole or a substantial part of a protected work is copied, including by storing it in digital form, subject only to specific statutory exceptions. We believe that the large-scale making and processing of digital copies of protected works for model training may therefore be characterised as reproduction, regardless of whether trained models retain human-readable copies or are capable of generating novel outputs. In our view, the lawfulness of using copyrighted content for AI training must be assessed under ordinary copyright principles and clearly defined exceptions. We do not accept the view that the copying and processing of protected works during training should be characterised as ‘learning’.

39.We therefore consider that the Government should rule out any reform of the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act that would remove the incentive to license copyrighted works for AI training, and should instead focus on strengthening licensing, transparency and enforcement within the existing framework.

## The impact of generative AI on the creative industries

### Harms

40.Creative industry witnesses to our inquiry argued that, at present, copyrighted works are being accessed at multiple stages of the AI lifecycle—during large-scale training of foundation models, during fine-tuning, and, in some cases, at runtime to ‘ground’ systems through RAG—without consent, transparency or payment.[112](#footnote-379) Anna Ganley, Chief Executive Officer of the Society of Authors, told us that this often involves mass scraping of music, books, images and journalism from the web, including from so-called “pirate libraries”. In her view, this amounts to “industrial-scale” copying which, in other contexts, would be licensed and remunerated.[113](#footnote-378) Isabelle Doran, Chief Executive Officer of the Association of Photographers, shared a statement from one of the organisation’s members that sets out the economic impact starkly:

“Generative AI undermines my ability to control the use of my work and therefore my IP income is reduced to 0%.”[114](#footnote-377)

41.A 2024 global study commissioned by the International Confederation of Societies of Authors and Composers predicts that generative AI will cause a €22 billion cumulative revenue loss for music and audiovisual creators by 2028 due to unlicensed content usage and market substitution. It estimated that widespread use of AI tools and surges in the AI-generated content market could put the revenues of 24% of music creators and 21% of audiovisual creators at risk.[115](#footnote-376)

42.Witnesses to our inquiry similarly stressed that unlicensed use of protected works at the input stage of AI model development feeds directly into risks at the output stage, since outputs may compete with original human-created works. Ms Doran told us that more than 58% of surveyed photographers had already lost work to generative AI.[116](#footnote-375) Among authors, 86% reported decreased earnings as a result of AI advances, with 57% saying they no longer view their work as a sustainable career.[117](#footnote-374) A recent report estimates that musicians face income cuts of 40% to 50% due to reduced commissions.[118](#footnote-373) AI systems that can generate works ‘in the style of’ identifiable creators also threaten business models that depend on the distinctiveness and controlled reuse of their work, Ms Doran explained.[119](#footnote-372)

43.Tom Kiehl, Chief Executive Officer of UK Music, drew attention to the proliferation of “inferior and low-quality” AI-generated content, or “AI slop”, on algorithmically-driven streaming services.[120](#footnote-371) Using its own AI-music detection tool, the French music streaming service Deezer revealed in September 2025 that 30,000 “fully AI-generated” tracks were being uploaded to the platform every day.[121](#footnote-370) In January 2026, Deezer said that figure had doubled to 60,000 AI tracks a day, representing 39% of total daily uploads.[122](#footnote-369) Since such content is often not clearly labelled, it can compete with music created by human artists for listener attention streams, diluting revenues for artists and rightsholders.[123](#footnote-368) A case study reported by the ISM describes how an AI-generated project cloned the vocal style of the Welsh rock band Holding Absence and accumulated millions of streams on Spotify in a matter of months, including from listeners who believed “they were hearing human artists or Holding Absence themselves”.[124](#footnote-367)

44.We also heard concerns about the use of AI to create unauthorised ‘digital replicas’,[125](#footnote-366) sometimes called ‘deepfakes’,[126](#footnote-365) and synthetic performances.[127](#footnote-364) A 2024 report by CREATe documented cases in which performers were not hired because AI systems were used instead, including voice actors being replaced in commercial work by synthetic voices. The report warned that AI-generated replicas could displace performers from large parts of the labour market, particularly lower-paid and routine roles.[128](#footnote-363) Several witnesses emphasised that this trend of AI outputs substituting for, or devaluing, human work in a range of creative labour markets is particularly concerning given that these sectors are dominated by freelance workers and small businesses.[129](#footnote-362)

45.For publishers, AI-generated summaries integrated into search results may compete by satisfying users’ information requirements without them needing to click through to the publishers’ original source material. Recent Ofcom research described a “Google Zero” effect, where “Google provides direct answers within its own ecosystem, leaving little incentive for users to visit publishers”. It linked this to reduced visibility for publisher brands and declining referral traffic, which would pose a potential threat to advertising and subscription-based revenue models even where AI summaries are accurate and attributed.[130](#footnote-361)

### Barriers to enforcement

46.The legal test for copyright infringement is whether “the whole, or a substantial part of, a copyright protected work [has] been copied without permission or the use of an exception”.[131](#footnote-360) However, rightsholders told us that even where they suspect that their work may have been used to develop an AI model, there is currently no practical way of checking whether their material was in fact ingested.[132](#footnote-359) This was primarily attributed to a lack of transparency from AI developers regarding the datasets or sources they have used for AI training.[133](#footnote-358) We discuss this further in Chapter 3.

47.Enforcement is further complicated by the international nature of AI development. We heard that most of the early stages of AI development, including large-scale data collection, processing and model training, typically occur outside the UK.[134](#footnote-357) Dr Alina Trapova, Lecturer in Intellectual Property Law at University College London, described this as an “elephant in the room”. She noted that training often occurs in jurisdictions where copyright operates differently, particularly the United States,[135](#footnote-356) and that UK courts may in some cases lack jurisdiction altogether.[136](#footnote-355)

48.In principle, it is more straightforward to establish infringement where an AI system reproduces all or a substantial part of a protected work in its outputs. Recent technical research has demonstrated that, using specialist methods, it is possible in some cases to cause models to regurgitate large amounts of in-copyright text, including near-verbatim copies of entire books.[137](#footnote-354) A recent ruling in Germany, currently under appeal, held that both such extracted outputs and the memorisation of those works encoded in a model’s weights can constitute infringing copies of in-copyright training data.[138](#footnote-353)

49.We heard that rightsholders who attempt to ‘red team’ models—probing these with targeted prompts, in this case with the aim of generating outputs that would reveal the use of copyrighted material in the model’s training[139](#footnote-352)—find “the process takes time and does not always work”.[140](#footnote-351) In addition, technology sector witnesses emphasised that newer AI systems are explicitly designed to minimise this kind of direct recitation.[141](#footnote-350)

50.A further challenge is that even where outputs clearly infringe copyright, these are difficult to detect in reality. Ms Doran cited estimates that there are now 34 million new synthetic images being created each day. She described the task of identifying a commercially significant infringement within this volume of material as “like finding a needle in a haystack”, making it unrealistic for individual creators or small rightsholders.[142](#footnote-349)

51.The perceived risks and costs of litigation act as an additional deterrent for rightsholders. The Copyright Licensing Agency (CLA) told us that enforcement in the UK is already prohibitively expensive for many creators and rightsholders, given the high cost of legal proceedings and the lack of statutory awards for damages.[143](#footnote-348) Ms Doran raised similar points. She also warned of rightsholders’ concerns that an adverse legal judgment could entrench large-scale infringements.[144](#footnote-347)

52.While acknowledging the practical barriers to enforcing their rights through the courts, witnesses underlined the importance of compensation for past, unlicensed uses of creative work for AI training. Ms Ganley told us that members of the Society of Authors “are looking for compensation for works that have already been scraped”, stressing that “compensation retrospectively is one part of it”, alongside regulation for the future.[145](#footnote-346) The Authors’ Licensing and Collecting Society reported that 92% of surveyed members wanted compensation for any historic use of their work for AI training.[146](#footnote-345) We note that the Science, Innovation and Technology Committee has described as “inevitable” both “the agreement of a financial settlement for past infringements by AI developers” and the negotiation of licensing frameworks for future uses.[147](#footnote-344) Other stakeholders have suggested “levies” on AI firms to fund cultural or public-interest schemes,[148](#footnote-343) and AI or data “dividends” that would distribute a share of AI-generated value to creators or the wider public.[149](#footnote-342)

### Potential opportunities

53.Alongside setting out the risks and barriers described above, our evidence also indicated that generative AI may offer opportunities for the creative industries.[150](#footnote-341) First and foremost, witnesses identified that licensing content for AI use could open up new revenue streams for rightsholders.[151](#footnote-340) This would, we heard, be contingent on having effective transparency arrangements and technical controls in place. We explore these areas in more detail in later chapters.

54.Others emphasised that many parts of the creative industries are already using AI and other technologies to support productivity, innovation and growth.[152](#footnote-339) The Creative Industries Policy and Evidence Centre (Creative PEC) noted that the sector has benefited from technological innovation alongside a robust copyright framework and highlighted the rise of UK ‘createch’ firms—businesses that integrate creative practice with advanced technologies—which now constitute a growing part of the creative economy.[153](#footnote-338) As detailed in our 2025 report on scaleups, these businesses have significant economic potential.[154](#footnote-337) It is promising to see that such firms have been explicitly recognised for targeted support in the Government’s *Creative Industries Sector Plan*.[155](#footnote-336)

55.The Government told us that nearly 40% of createch business had already adopted AI technologies by September 2024, and that createch businesses are expected to generate £18 billion in GVA over the next decade. It stated that “AI will therefore underpin growth and development across the creative sectors, reinforcing their role as a driver of innovation, productivity, and economic expansion.”[156](#footnote-335)

56.The UK creative industries are an economic powerhouse with huge growth potential, and a vital part of the UK’s soft power. Their success has been underpinned by what witnesses described as an internationally-respected **“**gold-standard**”** copyright framework. While generative AI may present opportunities for creative innovation and further growth where appropriate safeguards are in place, it also poses substantial material risks to the work and livelihoods of individual creators. The impact of these is already being felt.

57.We recognise that, in relation to AI-generated outputs that directly reproduce or ‘regurgitate’ protected works, existing copyright doctrines may provide a route in principle to challenge infringement. In practice, however, it is often prohibitively difficult for rightsholders to detect, evidence and enforce such claims. Despite this, the courts may be the only viable means of recovering damages for technology companies’ past use of content for training purposes.

58.AI has the potential to contribute to the UK’s future economic growth and there could be a legitimate interest in enabling more AI training to take place on UK soil. However, in 2024 the UK AI sector contributed around £12 billion to the UK economy, compared with £124 billion in gross value added from the creative industries in 2023. The evidence available to date has not convincingly demonstrated that the existing copyright framework is the primary constraint on AI investment, or that weakening it through new or broader exceptions for commercial AI training would, in itself, significantly expand the sector.

59.At the same time, the creative industries are already experiencing tangible harms from the current deployment of generative AI. Given their proven economic and cultural value, and the lack of robust evidence on the likely benefits of copyright reform to the UK AI sector, we do not consider that the case has been made for introducing new exceptions for AI training or for undertaking wider reform of UK copyright law. We welcome the Government’s forthcoming economic impact assessment as an essential basis for any future, evidence-led decisions on whether changes to copyright law are justified. It is urgent that a regime is now created to safeguard creators’ livelihoods going forward, while harnessing the potential of AI for creativity and economic growth.

## The Government’s approach and the need for clarity

60.We have previously stressed the importance of the Government swiftly reaching a definitive position on AI and copyright.[157](#footnote-334) These issues have been under consideration since the Intellectual Property Office launched a consultation on the relationship between intellectual property and AI in 2021.[158](#footnote-333) It set out its conclusions in 2022, proposing a new copyright and database right exception allowing TDM for any purpose.[159](#footnote-332) The then Government subsequently confirmed that it would not pursue a “broad copyright exception”. It committed to setting up a working group to develop a voluntary code of practice on the training of AI models using copyrighted material by summer 2023.[160](#footnote-331) However, that group was unable to reach agreement, and the planned code was not taken forward.[161](#footnote-330)

61.We are now in 2026, and a year on from the current Government’s consultation. It appears, however, that the Government is still some way from setting out a clear policy direction. Giving evidence to our inquiry, the Rt Hon Liz Kendall MP, Secretary of State for Science, Innovation and Technology, and the Rt Hon Lisa Nandy MP, Secretary of State for Culture, Media and Sport, implied that the Government would not be setting out its position in March, when updates on this area are due under the Data (Use and Access) Act.[162](#footnote-329)

62.The Secretary of State for Science, Innovation and Technology told us that this is because the Government is having a “reset moment” and “genuinely consulting to try and find a way forward”.[163](#footnote-328) The Secretary of State for Culture, Media and Sport explained:

“If we rush into this and get it wrong, we could make a mess. We are not going to rush into it; we are going to take the time to work through it with the working groups”.

She assured us, however, that “we appreciate the urgency … and want to move as quickly as possible.”[164](#footnote-327) The Secretary of State for Science, Innovation and Technology acknowledged that any eventual settlement would need to strike a balance between competing interests, but that “not everybody will get everything—that is the nature of this”.[165](#footnote-326)

63.A minority of witnesses supported the Government’s decision to proceed cautiously rather than legislate at speed. Creative PEC noted that the rapid evolution of generative AI since 2019 creates a “real risk” that moving too quickly to reform copyright law could lead to unintended and counterproductive outcomes.[166](#footnote-325) Dr Trapova likewise advocated an evidence-based approach, warning against “regulating for the sake of regulating” in a highly emotive area and urging policymakers to “slow down”.[167](#footnote-324)

64.Otherwise, there was consensus that the Government’s deliberation on this issue must be quickly brought to a close. The British Copyright Council warned that the “protracted consultation process” and continued suggestion of a possible commercial TDM exception had “generated uncertainty” that undermines the Government’s stated ambition to promote licensing.[168](#footnote-323) The Creative Rights in AI Coalition similarly argued that a “drawn-out consultation process” and “wrongly questioning the clarity provided by UK copyright law … has undoubtedly disincentivised AI developers from striking deals with UK rightsholders”.[169](#footnote-322) Mr Newton-Rex raised similar points.[170](#footnote-321)

65.Reema Selhi, Head of Policy and International at the Design and Artists Copyright Society (DACS), reported that when DACS approached image-generating AI companies about entering into copyright licences, many “basically said, ‘Well, let’s just wait and see where the Government consultation will go on copyright and AI’.”[171](#footnote-320) Mr Meredith went further, stating:

“The Government in some ways has been complicit in creating uncertainty in the market through the way it has approached its policy agenda in this area”.

This, he argued, has “allowed developer firms to exploit that uncertainty to their own benefit.”[172](#footnote-319)

## Chapter 2: AI, the Creative Industries and Copyright Reform

This chapter from a UK parliamentary report (2026) examines the relationship between AI, copyright law, and the creative industries in the UK, assessing arguments for and against reform.

### Key Findings:

**Current Legal Framework:**
- The UK's Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 (CDPA) provides only a narrow exception for text and data mining (TDM) for non-commercial research (Section 29A). There is no broad commercial TDM exception, unlike the EU (with opt-out), Japan, and Singapore (permissive regimes), or the US (fair use doctrine).
- Copyright is engaged at multiple stages of the AI lifecycle: data collection, model training, inference, and output generation.

**Arguments for Reform (from tech sector):**
- Tech companies argue legal uncertainty deters AI investment. Meta cited estimates that a commercial TDM exception could secure $6.4 billion in UK AI investment (vs. $1.9-3.2 billion without).
- Google and Microsoft argue the non-commercial research exception is ill-suited for modern AI development involving public-private partnerships.
- Some argue AI training is analogous to "learning" and should not constitute infringement.

**Arguments Against Reform (from creative industries):**
- Creative industry witnesses unanimously argue UK copyright law is "absolutely clear" — copying protected works for AI training requires a licence.
- Dr Hayleigh Bosher and Dr Andres Guadamuz reject the "learning" analogy, noting the industrial scale of AI training involves perfect digital copies at "superhuman speed and scale."
- The US Copyright Office has rejected the non-expressive use claim, stating it "rests on a faulty premise."

**Impact on Creative Industries:**
- A 2024 global study predicts €22 billion cumulative revenue loss for music and audiovisual creators by 2028 from AI.
- 86% of authors report decreased earnings from AI advances; 57% no longer view writing as a sustainable career.
- 58% of surveyed photographers have lost work to generative AI.
- Deezer reported 60,000 AI-generated tracks uploaded daily (39% of total uploads) by January 2026.

**Enforcement Barriers:**
- Rightsholders lack transparency on whether their works were used in training datasets.
- Most AI training occurs outside the UK, in jurisdictions with different copyright rules.
- Litigation costs are prohibitively expensive for individual creators.
- The UK AI sector contributed ~£12 billion to the economy in 2024, vs. £124 billion GVA from creative industries in 2023.

**Position:**
The report concludes that the case has not been made for introducing new exceptions for AI training. It recommends the Government should rule out copyright reform that would remove incentives to license works, and instead focus on strengthening licensing, transparency, and enforcement. The Government should publish a final decision within 12 months, prioritizing strong copyright protection and the long-term health of UK creative industries.

**Style Imitation Gap:**
The report identifies a gap in protection for AI-generated outputs "in the style of" an artist, as copyright protects specific expressions, not general style. This may require legislative change.
