# How AI, digital doubles and new laws are rewriting fashion and beauty

**As AI continues to reshape creative industries, Foley lawyers Laura Ganoza, Arianna Benitez Colon and Mackenna Dunna examine the key legal considerations for navigating this evolving landscape**

 [Prefer the Global Legal Post on Google](https://www.google.com/preferences/source?q=globallegalpost.com)

![Digital marekting concept](https://www-globallegalpost-static.s3.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com/images/2024SepFridownloads.jpg) 

By

[![](https://www-globallegalpost-static.s3.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com/images/2026MarTueMackenna_Dunn.jpg)](https://www.globallegalpost.com/authors/mackenna-dunn)

[Mackenna Dunn](https://www.globallegalpost.com/authors/mackenna-dunn "Mackenna Dunn")

[Foley & Lardner](https://www.globallegalpost.com/law-firms/foley-lardner-389931878 "Foley & Lardner")

[![](https://www-globallegalpost-static.s3.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com/images/2025DecWedUntitled%20design.png)](https://www.globallegalpost.com/authors/ariana-benitez-colon)

[Ariana Benitez Colon](https://www.globallegalpost.com/authors/ariana-benitez-colon "Ariana Benitez Colon")

[Foley & Lardner](https://www.globallegalpost.com/law-firms/foley-lardner-389931878 "Foley & Lardner")

[![](https://www-globallegalpost-static.s3.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com/images/2026MarTueGanoza_Laura.jpg)](https://www.globallegalpost.com/authors/laura-ganoza)

[Laura Ganoza](https://www.globallegalpost.com/authors/laura-ganoza "Laura Ganoza")

[Foley & Lardner](https://www.globallegalpost.com/law-firms/foley-lardner-389931878 "Foley & Lardner")

Artificial intelligence (AI) has gone from buzzword to backstage workhorse in the fashion, apparel and beauty (FAB) industries. When Foley previewed this space in 2024, AI was already being used to power recommendation engines, searches and personalisation. Since then, AI has driven design tools, virtual try-on experiences, synthetic models and even the digital ‘resurrection’ of fashion and beauty icons – and lawmakers have noticed.

Across the industry, AI can swap outfits in lookbooks, generate virtual fabrics and prints and build campaigns around synthetic models. Virtual try-on tools help consumers test lipstick shades, match foundation and visualise outfits, while beauty apps offer skin diagnostics and product recommendations. Behind the scenes, these tools rely on vast training datasets: fashion photography, runway imagery, influencer content, scraped social media and e-commerce catalogues. Increasingly, they also depend on full digital capture of models, including 3D body scans, face mapping, voice cloning and digital replicas.

**The business of beauty bots: why brands should care**

For brands, the appeal is obvious. AI cuts costs, speeds creative cycles, allows assets to be generated and localised quickly, and promises highly personalised shopping experiences. Generative systems can produce new imagery in hours rather than days, while AI styling engines curate outfits and beauty routines based to individual consumers.

The catch is that these systems often rely on real people’s images, bodies, voices and performances, or on creative works never meant to be used as training material. The same tools that let brands ‘do more with less’ also make it easy to reuse a model’s likeness in ways they never agreed to.

**Rights on the runway: publicity, digital doubles and deepfakes**

Because there is no comprehensive federal AI statute in the US, FAB brands operate within a patchwork of legacy doctrines and emerging AI-specific laws. Right of publicity and name, image and likeness (NIL) laws in states such as California, New York, Tennessee, Florida and Arkansas have long protected commercial use of a person’s identity, often even after death. A brand that ‘brings back’ a beloved fashion or beauty icon in an AI campaign without the estate’s permission may be inviting litigation.

New York has become the main runway for AI-and-model legislation. The New York Fashion Workers Act, effective 19 June 2025, directly addresses AI use involving fashion models. The required consent must specify scope, purpose, duration and compensation; however, routine retouching is excluded. The New York Digital Replica Law, effective 1 January 2025, goes after ‘rights-grab’ contracts. A digital replica agreement is void if it (i) allows a replica to be used instead of work the person would have done in person, (ii) fails to give a reasonably specific description of the intended use and (iii) was negotiated when the individual did not have legal counsel or a union to consult. Brands and agencies can no longer rely on vague language to lock up a model’s digital double indefinitely.

New York’s AI Transparency in Advertising and Synthetic Performer Disclosure Law, effective 9 June 2026, moves to the consumer side. If a commercial ad uses an AI-generated synthetic performer, or a realistic digital person created by AI, that fact must be clearly disclosed, with civil penalties for failing to label the ad. A separate New York posthumous right of publicity law requires consent from heirs or executors before using a deceased person’s name, image, voice or likeness in campaigns, which directly affects launches or collections built around ‘resurrected’ icons.

Other states are moving in parallel. Tennessee’s ELVIS Act and Arkansas’ HB 1071 explicitly extend publicity rights to AI-generated likenesses and voices, banning unauthorised commercial use and imposing civil (and in Tennessee, some criminal) penalties. At the federal level, the proposed NO FAKES Act would create a nationwide right against unauthorised digital replicas of a person’s likeness, voice or performance. The Deepfake Liability Act, the Take It Down Act and PADRA aim to make platforms and creators more accountable for harmful deepfakes and to streamline takedowns, both for influencers and models whose images are misused and for brands that distribute AI-heavy content.

**Advertising, privacy and biometrics**

Traditional advertising and consumer protection rules apply even when content is created by AI. A synthetic model or AI-generated endorsement that misleads consumers can trigger the same false advertising and unfair or deceptive practices claims as any other campaign.

Privacy and biometric laws add further constraints. Statutes like Illinois’ Biometric Information Privacy Act (BIPA) and California’s CCPA/CPRA regulate how brands collect and use face scans for virtual try-on services, body scans for size and fit tools and voiceprints for voice-based experiences. Failures in obtaining consent for handling this data can lead to statutory damages and class actions.

New transparency and detection proposals point to where the law is heading. California’s proposed AI Transparency Act would require detection tools for AI-modified media. New York’s proposed synthetic content provenance bill would push AI systems to embed cryptographic provenance data, creating a verifiable trail of how an asset was generated. These proposed laws signal a future in which watermarking and provable origin information for AI content are expected rather than optional.

**Copyright catwalk: training data and AI-made designs**

In *Thaler v. Perlmutter*, the District of Columbia Circuit confirmed that purely AI-generated works without human authorship are not copyrightable under current US law. Brands using AI to generate prints, patterns or imagery need meaningful human creative input to claim protection.

At the same time, AI training data is under increasing scrutiny. The proposed Generative AI Copyright Disclosure Act would require AI developers to disclose their use of copyrighted works in training data. California’s AB 412, which has stalled, would have required AI developers to obtain permission and pay licensing fees to use copyrighted works for training. Pennsylvania’s HR 81 urges Congress to exclude predominantly AI-generated works from copyright protection and to clarify how copyright and fair use apply to the use of copyrighted works in AI training.

Outside the US, the EU’s Artificial Intelligence Act introduces a risk-based framework with transparency obligations for AI-generated and deepfake content. Multinational FAB brands using virtual try-on tools, recommendation engines and synthetic models in Europe will need to align with those standards, even if US law continues to evolve more slowly.

**Contract couture**

Talent and vendor contracts need to match how AI is actually being used. Agreements should spell out whether the brand will create digital replicas, scans or 3D models; where and how those assets may be used, including specific campaign names, channels, territories and time periods; and whether talent imagery may be used to train internal or third-party AI systems. Compensation for AI-related uses should be addressed separately from standard day rates or flat fees, rather than assuming unlimited synthetic reuse is included.

Legal drafting is only one part of the solution. FAB brands also need internal guardrails. Many are forming cross-functional AI committees that bring together legal, marketing, HR and IT to inventory tools; map how they touch talent images, third-party content, consumer data and creative IP; and flag higher-risk uses before launch. Vendor management is becoming more rigorous, with brands asking their business partners how tools are trained, whether they support watermarking and provenance and demanding indemnification for claims related to the use of AI. Workflows that include obtaining informed consent, especially for biometric scans, and for labelling AI-generated or heavily altered content where required by law or expected by consumers, are becoming standard operating procedures.

Done thoughtfully, AI can still deliver meaningful efficiencies: fewer returns, better fit and shade matching, faster campaign production, smarter inventory decisions and more relevant product recommendations. The difference between a competitive advantage and a public relations crisis often lies in how a company treats the humans behind the data, including having clear and transparent contractual provisions.

**The rise of AI and the expanding risk to talent likeness**

While brands adopt AI to streamline campaigns, reduce costs and extend creative output, these technologies pose unique and often under-appreciated risks to models and other creative talent. Chief among them is the unauthorised or overextended use of a model’s likeness beyond the scope of the original engagement.

When AI tools are used to replicate or manipulate those attributes without clear consent, models may lose control over how, where and for how long their likeness appears.

*“As a content creator, I often deliver UGC [user-generated content] or campaign assets to brands, and I don’t always track how or where my content gets used afterwards. Sometimes I unexpectedly see my image on a website, in paid ads or reposted without any heads-up.” – Anya Li (@annyalii)*

**A common scenario: from single campaign to synthetic expansion**

A model is hired to appear in a single campaign or to model a specific garment. The agreement contemplates traditional photography and a defined scope of use. After the campaign concludes, the brand uses AI tools to digitally replicate the model’s likeness and place it into additional outfits, campaigns or promotional formats that were never discussed or approved.

From the brand’s perspective, this may feel like an efficient extension of licensed content. From the model’s perspective, it represents a fundamental expansion of use, one that may affect future bookings, dilute exclusivity or associate the model with products or messaging they did not choose to endorse.

This disconnect often arises because AI-generated content blurs the line between ‘use of existing images’ and the creation of entirely new representations. While the original photographs may have been authorised, the resulting AI-generated images may depict scenarios, garments or branding that never existed at the time of the shoot.

*“For creators and models, it raises questions about ownership, compensation and long-term usage. If a brand can keep using an AI version of you after a contract ends, it could affect your ability to work with other brands or control your own image.” – Anya Li (@annyalii)*

**Contractual gaps in traditional modelling agreements**

Currently, there’s a discrepancy between legacy modelling contracts and modern AI capabilities. Many agreements were drafted at a time when campaigns were limited to physical photographs and clearly defined deliverables. As a result, contracts frequently grant rights to use ‘images’, ‘photographs’ or ‘recordings’, but do not contemplate synthetic media, digital replicas or AI-generated derivatives.

In the absence of express language addressing AI, brands may rely on broadly drafted usage clauses to justify expanded use, while models may reasonably assume that consent to appear in a single campaign does not authorise the creation of unlimited digital versions of their likeness.

This ambiguity creates legal and commercial uncertainty for both sides. For talent, it raises concerns about consent, compensation and control.

**Potential legal claims available to talent**

Depending on the jurisdiction and the specific contractual language at issue, models may have several potential legal avenues if their likeness is used beyond the agreed scope. These may include right of publicity claims, particularly where AI-generated content exploits a model’s identity for commercial gain without consent.

Models may also assert breach of contract claims where AI use exceeds the defined scope of permitted use or where the contract implicitly limits usage to specified campaigns or formats. In certain circumstances, claims based on false endorsement or unfair competition may arise if AI-generated imagery implies an ongoing relationship or approval that does not exist.

While these claims may provide leverage, litigation is often an imperfect solution. AI-generated content can be deployed quickly and at scale, making it difficult to contain once released.

**Proactive contractual protections for models and influencers**

Given these challenges, preventative strategies are increasingly critical. Models and their representatives should focus on addressing AI-related risks at the contracting stage, before any images are captured or content is created. Key contractual protections may include explicit prohibitions on AI-generated replicas or derivatives absent separate written consent. Separate compensation structures for synthetic or extended uses can help ensure that talent is fairly compensated for the ongoing exploitation of their likeness.

Approval rights are also an important consideration. Models may seek the right to review and approve AI-generated content before it is published, particularly where the content could affect brand alignment or public perception.

**Monitoring, enforcement and ongoing oversight**

Beyond initial contracting, talent should consider mechanisms for monitoring and enforcement. Audit rights, notice requirements for new uses and contractual takedown provisions can provide meaningful leverage without immediate resort to litigation.

For higher-profile talent, additional carve-outs may be appropriate. These can include restrictions on sensitive product categories, protections against political or controversial uses and provisions addressing moral rights or reputational harm.

**Looking ahead: protecting likeness in a synthetic marketplace**

As AI continues to reshape creative industries, the imbalance of bargaining power between brands and individual models is likely to increase. The key to navigating this evolving landscape lies in proactive contract drafting, informed negotiation and early legal review.

By addressing AI-related risks upfront, brands and talent can better protect the integrity, value and longevity of their likeness in an increasingly synthetic marketplace, while allowing innovation to proceed in ways that respect consent and creative ownership.

This article from The Global Legal Post, authored by Foley & Lardner lawyers Laura Ganoza, Arianna Benitez Colon, and Mackenna Dunn, examines the legal implications of AI adoption in the fashion, apparel, and beauty (FAB) industries. As AI increasingly powers design tools, virtual try-ons, synthetic models, and digital "resurrections" of fashion icons, the legal landscape is rapidly evolving.

Key legal considerations include:

- **Right of Publicity & NIL Laws**: US states like California, New York, Tennessee, Florida, and Arkansas protect commercial use of a person's identity. New York's Digital Replica Law (effective Jan 1, 2025) voids contracts that allow replica use without specific descriptions and independent legal counsel. The New York Fashion Workers Act (effective June 19, 2025) requires models' consent specifying scope, purpose, duration, and compensation.
- **AI Transparency in Advertising**: New York's AI Transparency in Advertising Law (effective June 9, 2026) requires disclosure of AI-generated synthetic performers in ads, with civil penalties for non-compliance.
- **Federal Proposals**: The NO FAKES Act, Deepfake Liability Act, Take It Down Act, and PADRA aim to create nationwide protections against unauthorized digital replicas and harmful deepfakes.
- **Privacy & Biometrics**: Laws like Illinois' BIPA and California's CCPA/CPRA regulate collection of face scans, body scans, and voiceprints for virtual try-on tools.
- **Copyright**: Per *Thaler v. Perlmutter*, purely AI-generated works without human authorship are not copyrightable. The proposed Generative AI Copyright Disclosure Act would require AI developers to disclose copyrighted works used in training data.
- **EU AI Act**: Introduces a risk-based framework with transparency obligations for AI-generated content affecting multinational FAB brands.

The article emphasizes that traditional modeling contracts often lack AI-specific language, creating ambiguity over usage of digital replicas. It recommends proactive contractual protections including explicit prohibitions on AI-generated replicas without separate consent, separate compensation structures for synthetic uses, and approval rights for AI-generated content. Brands are advised to form cross-functional AI committees, implement rigorous vendor management, and establish informed consent workflows for biometric data.

# AI & Copyright Case Tracker

This is Taylor Wessing's AI & Copyright Case Tracker, providing an up-to-date overview of ongoing lawsuits at the intersection of AI and copyright law across Europe. It covers cases involving copyright and related rights, focusing on European jurisdictions (excluding US cases). The tracker includes decisions and pending cases from Denmark, Germany, Italy, the UK, Hungary, France, the Netherlands, and the Czech Republic.

## Key Cases (as of August 2026):

**Recent Decisions:**
- **BoligPortal v. ReData (Denmark, May 2026)** – Appeal overturned earlier ruling; court held that a TDM opt-out in human-readable HTML format did not meet machine-readable requirements.
- **Photographer v. Editor (Germany, April 2026)** – Düsseldorf Higher Regional Court dismissed claim, finding AI-generated image did not reproduce protected creative elements.
- **Graphic designer v. Logo user (Germany, Feb 2026)** – Munich court ruled AI-generated works may enjoy copyright protection depending on human creative influence, but logos in question did not meet threshold.
- **Getty Images v. Stability AI (UK, Nov 2025)** – High Court found trademark infringement only for earlier Stable Diffusion versions; primary copyright infringement claims were dropped. Under appeal.
- **GEMA v. OpenAI (Germany, Nov 2025)** – Munich Regional Court ruled ChatGPT stores reproductions of song lyrics, constituting "reproduction" even if intermediate steps required.
- **Robert Kneschke v. LAION (Germany, Dec 2025)** – Appeal court rejected plaintiff's claim; LAION could rely on TDM exceptions. Further appeal pending to Federal Supreme Court.

**Key Issues Emerging:**
- Whether TDM opt-outs must be machine-readable vs. natural language
- Whether AI-generated outputs can infringe copyright
- Whether AI training on copyrighted works constitutes reproduction
- Copyrightability of AI-generated works vs. human authorship requirements
- Validity of contractual clauses requiring journalists to grant AI training rights

**Pending Cases:**
- Penguin Random House v. OpenAI (Germany, filed March 2026)
- GEMA v. Suno Inc. (Germany, oral hearing March 2026, decision expected July 2026)
- Perplexity AI (Italy, filed December 2025)
- KODA v. Suno AI (Denmark, filed November 2025)
- DJV v. Süddeutsche Zeitung (Germany, filed April 2025)
- Like Company v. Google Ireland (CJEU, preliminary ruling requested, Advocate General opinion expected September 2026)
- French publishers v. Meta (France, filed March 2025)
</summary>

URL: https://copyrightalliance.org/ai-copyright-lawsuit-developments-2025

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article from the Copyright Alliance, authored by Kevin Madigan, reviews major developments in AI copyright lawsuits throughout 2025. The key events include:

**Major Decisions & Settlements:**
- The $1.5 billion settlement in *Bartz v. Anthropic*, where Anthropic paid approximately $3,000 per book for 482,460 books downloaded from pirate libraries (Library Genesis, Pirate Library Mirror). This followed a June 2025 summary judgment order finding Anthropic's LLM training "exceedingly" transformative for fair use purposes, but the company still faced massive statutory damages.
- In *Kadrey v. Meta* (June 2025), a separate court found Meta's use of books for LLM training "highly transformative" and fair use, though the decision was narrow due to limited evidence. The case continues on claims related to Meta's use of BitTorrent (seeding) for distributing copyrighted works.

**Other Settlements:**
- UMG settled with Udio (October 2025), including licensing agreements for a new subscription service launching in 2026 with artist opt-in control.
- WMG settled with both Udio (November 2025) and Suno (November 2025), with Suno launching new licensed models in 2026. Artists retain control over use of their names, images, and works.
- Confidential settlements in *Vacker v. ElevenLabs* and *Planner 5D v. Facebook*.

**New Cases Filed (2025 saw cases grow from ~30 to over 70):**
- Film studios (Disney, Universal, Warner Bros.) sued Midjourney in June and September 2025 over AI image generation infringing characters from Marvel, Star Wars, and other franchises.
- The first AI copyright lawsuit against a foreign company (China-based Minimax) was filed by Disney, Universal, and Warner Bros.
- RAG-focused cases: Perplexity was sued by Encyclopedia Britannica, Merriam-Webster, Chicago Tribune, and New York Times. Cohere was sued by Advance.
- New defendants: Apple was sued for using books to train OpenELM (via Books3/RedPajama datasets containing pirated books). Salesforce was sued for using books to train CodeGen and XGen LLMs. Adobe was sued for using SlimPajama dataset. ByteDance was sued by Ted Entertainment under DMCA anticircumvention provisions for scraping YouTube videos.
- Independent musicians filed class actions against Suno, Udio, and Kunlun Tech, including DMCA stream-ripping claims.

**Looking Ahead to 2026:**
- Next fair use decisions expected in *In re Google Generative AI*, *UMG v. Suno*, *Concord v. Anthropic*, and *In re Mosaic LLM Litigation* — not before summer 2026.
- *Thomson Reuters v. Ross Intelligence* is on appeal at the Third Circuit on copyrightability and fair use issues, with oral arguments pending.
- Settlement negotiations ongoing in *In re OpenAI* multidistrict litigation (over a dozen cases centralized in SDNY, including *New York Times v. OpenAI* and *Authors Guild v. OpenAI*).

The article concludes that settlements of 2025 demonstrate AI companies can afford to compensate copyright owners, and litigation is increasingly leading to collaborative licensing arrangements rather than purely monetary judgments.
</summary>

The article discusses legal challenges, referencing the Getty Images (US) v. Stability AI case where Getty asserts trademark claims over AI-generated outputs containing modified versions of Getty watermarks.

Key legal questions include whether generative AI output constitutes "commercial use" and whether it creates consumer confusion as to source. Under current law, a fashion designer using AI to commercialize infringing products could face direct infringement liability. However, AI companies themselves may evade direct infringement liability because they don't "use" the infringing mark in commerce. They could face indirect (contributory) infringement liability, but plaintiffs may struggle to prove the AI company had the requisite knowledge that its tool was being used to infringe trademarks.

The article notes that many AI companies have implemented safeguards—for example, ChatGPT refused a prompt to create a trademark similar to Nike's Swoosh logo. The authors conclude that courts and lawmakers will need to adapt existing legal frameworks to address the unique challenges AI technology poses.

The U.S. Copyright Office released Part Three of its Copyright and Artificial Intelligence Report in May 2025, addressing the critical question of whether generative AI developers need permission or compensation to use third-party copyrighted works for training, or if such use qualifies as fair use. The Report concludes that training GenAI models using copyrighted material involves multiple acts that could establish prima facie infringement, including reproduction rights during dataset creation, training, and when model weights demonstrate "memorization" of protected expression. On fair use, the Office emphasizes a case-by-case analysis with the purpose-and-character and market-effect factors carrying the most weight. Rather than recommending new legislation, the Office encourages voluntary licensing solutions and market-driven approaches, noting stakeholders prefer "opt-in" licensing models. The Office found little support for compulsory licensing schemes at this time. The Report acknowledges its analysis is limited to current circumstances and commits to monitoring developments, with Part 4 (addressing infringement liability and transparency) forthcoming. --- SOURCE 8: Using CC-Licensed Works for AI Training - Creative Commons ---
URL: https://creativecommons.org/using-cc-licensed-works-for-ai-training-2

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This Creative Commons webpage provides a primer on using CC-licensed works for AI training. It acknowledges that the application of copyright law to AI training is complex, and that CC licenses are copyright licenses, adding to that complexity. The page offers guidance from two angles:

**How to Follow CC Licenses for Training Data (Conservative Approach):**
- **Attribution (BY):** All CC licenses require attribution. For AI training, a simple link to the dataset source may suffice. For RAG methods, attribution tied to specific outputs is ideal.
- **ShareAlike (SA):** CC BY-SA and CC BY-NC-SA require adaptations to be shared under the same license. If AI models or outputs based on SA content are shared publicly, developers would need to use the same CC license.
- **NonCommercial (NC):** CC BY-NC and CC BY-NC-SA permit non-commercial use only. Following NC means all stages—from copying data to sharing the model—must not be for commercial gain.
- **NoDerivatives (ND):** CC BY-ND and CC BY-NC-ND prohibit derivative works. Following ND means ND-licensed content should not be used as training data.

**When Compliance is Legally Required:**
CC licenses apply only when copyright permission is required. The analysis involves two steps: (1) Does copyright apply? — AI training typically involves copying works, and memorization of copyrightable expressions can have implications; and (2) When do CC license conditions apply? — If exceptions or limitations to copyright apply, then CC license terms don't apply. The page directs readers to a detailed legal analysis PDF and a flow chart for deeper exploration.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 9: Collective Licensing for Gen AI Training: Feasible or Flawed? – Part 1 | Kluwer Copyright Blog ---
URL: https://legalblogs.wolterskluwer.com/copyright-blog/collective-licensing-for-gen-ai-training-feasible-or-flawed-part-1

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This blog post (Part 1 of a series) from Wolters Kluwer's Copyright Blog examines the feasibility of collective licensing models for generative AI (GenAI) training data, following the European Parliament's March 10, 2026 resolution urging the EU Commission to clarify the copyright framework for GenAI. The post analyzes three approaches:

**Why the TDM Framework Falls Short:** The CDSM Directive's Article 4 permits commercial text and data mining (TDM) subject to a rightsholder opt-out, but this mechanism is widely considered inadequate. There is no standardized format for machine-readable opt-outs, technical measures like robots.txt are often ignored by crawlers, and national courts in Germany, the Netherlands, and Hungary have reached divergent conclusions on what constitutes a valid opt-out. The opt-out model offers only a binary choice: exclusion or uncompensated use. Additionally, the TDM exception does not address post-training issues like model "memorization" and "regurgitation" of training data, which the Munich Court found could constitute copyright infringement in GEMA v. OpenAI.

**Voluntary Collective Licensing:** While requiring no legislative reform, voluntary licensing through CMOs (Collective Management Organizations) can only cover rightsholders who choose to participate, leaving smaller creators at risk. CMOs also lack sufficient bargaining power against major AI companies. The EU Parliament's resolution called for sector-based collective licensing agreements with EUIPO support.

**Statutory Licensing and Mandatory Collective Management:** These face significant legal headwinds under the Berne three-step test. A statutory license broad enough to offer AI developers legal certainty would struggle to meet the test's conditions, while one narrow enough to pass would be too restrictive. Such regimes risk reducing authors' rights to mere remuneration claims and stripping them of the ability to refuse objectionable uses. Upfront remuneration also imposes costs at the wrong stage of the value chain.

The post notes that between March 2023 and February 2025, over 79 individual licensing agreements between AI developers and content owners were signed globally, but this creates a two-tier market favoring well-capitalized players.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Article 4 of the CDSM Directive permits commercial text and data mining subject to a rightsholder opt-out. In practice, the opt-out mechanism is widely considered to fall short.", "The opt-out model offers only a binary choice: exclusion or uncompensated use.", "Empirical studies show that GenAI models can 'memorise' and 'regurgitate' verbatim snippets of training data - a risk the Munich Court found capable of constituting copyright infringement in its GEMA v. OpenAI ruling.", "The 2025 EU Council questionnaire reveals that 'licensing of protected works by CMOs for the purpose of AI-training remains rare in the EU.'", "A statutory licensing regime which would be narrow enough to satisfy the three-step test would likely be too restrictive to offer AI developers meaningful legal certainty, while one broad enough to serve that purpose would struggle to meet the test's cumulative conditions."

URL: https://mitsloan.mit.edu/ideas-made-to-matter/how-learnrights-would-compensate-creators-ai-model-training

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This MIT Sloan article explores 'learnright' laws proposed by Professor Thomas Malone and co-authors Frank Pasquale and Andrew Ting to address the unresolved legal question of whether using copyrighted content to train AI models constitutes fair use or infringement. The U.S. Copyright Office has not made a binding determination, and no generative AI cases have reached the Supreme Court. Learnright would give copyright holders the exclusive right to license their content to AI companies for model training, rather than expanding fair use to include AI learning. The authors outline an opt-in program where creators register copyrighted content and AI companies negotiate compensation either directly or through literary/artistic agents, arguing this would create a robust licensing market. They contend that without such laws, incentives for human content creation will be greatly reduced, and that learnright benefits both creators and AI providers in a flourishing information marketplace.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"Copyright law wasn't designed for a world with generative AI, and without something like learnright laws, the incentives for people to create new content are likely to be greatly reduced," said Malone. "In short, learnright law is a promising way for both content creators and AI providers to benefit in a flourishing information marketplace," Malone said. "there are substantial grounds for predicting that a robust market for learnrights, with reasonable and fair licensing fees, would emerge," write Malone and co-authors.

A Baker Botts "Our Take" blog post by Associate Jasmine Boyer reports on the Getty v. Stability AI trademark ruling. In August 2025, Getty Images sued Stability AI in the Northern District of California, alleging unlawful copying of millions of Getty images and metadata to train AI models, bringing copyright claims and Lanham Act claims (trademark infringement, false designation of origin, and dilution) over AI outputs bearing distorted Getty watermarks. On April 23, 2026, the court denied Stability AI's motion to dismiss all Lanham Act claims. The court found Getty's allegations of direct competition and user reports of distorted watermarks sufficient to infer likely consumer confusion. It ruled that AI-generated images commercially distributed by Stability AI constitute "goods" under the Lanham Act, and that distorted watermarks could mislead consumers as to source or affiliation. The dilution claims were also allowed to proceed, as Getty sufficiently alleged its marks are "famous" based on decades of nationwide use, extensive advertising, and a large global customer base. </summary>

**2. Fashion Design Creation Pre- and Post-AI:**
- Pre-AI: The fashion industry normalizes some degree of "copying" as "inspiration" or "flocking" to trends. Differentiation is a desirable feature alongside participation in trends.
- Post-AI: Gen-AI enhances design workflows by processing vast data, generating trend-led designs, and offering endless combinations of design elements. Models are typically "pruned" or "fine-tuned" versions of pre-trained models.

**3. Copyright Originality:**
- Under EU law (Cofemel, Infopaq), works must be the "author's own intellectual creation" (AOIC), reflecting free and creative choices and the author's personality.
- UK law operates on a closed-list system (CDPA 1988), but fashion designs can qualify as "artistic works" or "works of artistic craftsmanship."
- Technical functionality cannot solely dictate the design; creative freedom must remain.
- The Ganni Buckle Ballerina case (Danish courts) affirmed that designs inspired by prior works can still meet originality if they reflect the designer's personal interpretation.

- AI-assisted designs can potentially be original if designers exercise free and creative choices in prompts, modifications, and finalization.

**4. Infringement Analysis:**
- Gen-AI models with high generalization performance are less likely to produce infringing outputs.
- Poor generalization, overfitting, or fine-tuning on limited datasets increases the likelihood of outputs that closely mimic training data.
- Under EU InfoSoc Directive 2001/29/EC and UK CDPA 1988, the right of reproduction is central.
- The article argues that infringement cannot be simply attributed to AI tools due to technical underpinnings; even if infringing derivative outputs emerge, subsequent modification by a designer can "transform" them into new, non-infringing expressions.

--- SOURCE 11: Blockchain Provenance for Digital Content Authenticity | InCyan ---
URL: https://www.incyan.com/resources/blockchain-provenance

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This white paper by InCyan, authored by Nikhil John, explains how blockchain-anchored attestations and invisible watermarking work together to protect digital media at scale. It addresses the "provenance problem"—the challenge of proving where content came from, who can use it, and whether it has been altered.

**Key Concepts:**

- **The Content Authenticity Crisis:** Synthetic media (AI-generated imagery, voice cloning, deepfakes) is now cheap and easy to create, making it difficult to verify whether content is genuine, who owns it, or how it can be used. Traditional metadata and visible watermarks are easily stripped or forged.

- **Blockchain as a Provenance Layer:** Blockchain provides an immutable, cryptographically linked ledger for recording content fingerprints (hashes). It offers tamper-resistant timestamping and global ordering of claims, allowing anyone to verify when an assertion was made and who signed it—without needing to trust a single operator.

- **Hash-to-Chain Model:** Content is reduced to a cryptographic hash (a fixed-length fingerprint that is collision-resistant and sensitive to changes). Rather than storing files on-chain, only the hash is stored, preserving privacy. Merkle trees enable batching many hashes into a single root hash for cost efficiency, with built-in proof mechanisms for verification.

- **Combined Watermarking + Blockchain:** Invisible watermarks embed durable identifiers within media that survive compression and cropping. Blockchain records anchor those identifiers with timestamped, signed assertions about ownership and licensing. Together, they create a chain of custody—from detection of a watermark in the wild, to resolution of the identifier against an immutable blockchain record, to retrieval of licensing terms.

- **Integration Patterns:** The paper outlines enterprise and platform workflows—registration at creation/publication, verification APIs, dispute resolution with evidentiary packages, and interoperability with standards like C2PA (Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity) and IPTC metadata.

- **Strategic Outlook:** Regulatory trends (e.g., EU AI Act), industry standards, and the convergence of adaptive watermarking, AI-assisted detection, and blockchain records point toward a future where content authenticity is demonstrable rather than assumed. The paper advises executives to evaluate solutions based on scale, long-term durability, privacy/confidentiality, and integration with existing workflows.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This PNAS Perspective article by Pamela Samuelson examines the feasibility of collective licensing of in-copyright works as training data for generative AI systems. It addresses the central legal question of whether using copyrighted works as training data requires copyright owners' consent or compensation, with fair use being the main defense in ongoing U.S. lawsuits.

**Background:** Multiple lawsuits (starting with Sarah Andersen v. Stability AI in January 2023) have been filed against AI developers including OpenAI, Meta, Google, and Anthropic. AI developers argue fair use because training uses works as data (not for their expressiveness), purposes are transformative, and individual license negotiations are infeasible. Copyright owners argue uses are commercial, outputs compete with their works, and wholesale copying disfavors fair use.

**European Proposals:** Three main approaches are discussed:
1. **Article 4(3) Opt-Out Model** - The EU CDSMD allows right-holders to opt out of TDM privileges, potentially leading to collective licensing through CMOs. Spain proposed an extended collective licensing (ECL) regime.
2. **Statutory Licensing** - Scholars like Geiger, Iaia, and Frosio propose replacing the opt-out rule with a "permitted-but-paid" model with mandatory remuneration for training data uses.
3. **Levy on Commercial Products** - Senftleben proposes a levy on generative AI products/services to support human authorship, allowing training to proceed without advance compensation.

**U.S. Proposals:** Collective licensing has been less discussed in the U.S. The article notes that if fair use defenses succeed, developers can continue commercial exploitation; if copyright owners prevail, developers face billions in damages and potential destruction of models.

**Key Challenges:** The article identifies numerous feasibility problems: fragmented EU rights clearance infrastructure (27 member states with different laws), uncertainty about whether CMOs have authorization to license TDM/AI training uses, difficulty calculating fair compensation given the massive scale of training data, high administrative costs relative to potential payouts, the "lose-lose" scenario where opt-outs reduce data quality without generating compensation, and the EU AI Act's Recital 106's attempt at extraterritorial application requiring compliance with EU copyright regardless of where models were trained. The article concludes that courts and policymakers should carefully consider these complexities before implementing collective licensing regimes.
</summary>

## Chapter 2: AI, the Creative Industries and Copyright Reform

This chapter from a UK parliamentary report (2026) examines the relationship between AI, copyright law, and the creative industries in the UK, assessing arguments for and against reform.

### Key Findings:

**Current Legal Framework:**
- The UK's Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 (CDPA) provides only a narrow exception for text and data mining (TDM) for non-commercial research (Section 29A). There is no broad commercial TDM exception, unlike the EU (with opt-out), Japan, and Singapore (permissive regimes), or the US (fair use doctrine).
- Copyright is engaged at multiple stages of the AI lifecycle: data collection, model training, inference, and output generation.

**Arguments for Reform (from tech sector):**
- Tech companies argue legal uncertainty deters AI investment. Meta cited estimates that a commercial TDM exception could secure $6.4 billion in UK AI investment (vs. $1.9-3.2 billion without).
- Google and Microsoft argue the non-commercial research exception is ill-suited for modern AI development involving public-private partnerships.
- Some argue AI training is analogous to "learning" and should not constitute infringement.

**Arguments Against Reform (from creative industries):**
- Creative industry witnesses unanimously argue UK copyright law is "absolutely clear" — copying protected works for AI training requires a licence.
- Dr Hayleigh Bosher and Dr Andres Guadamuz reject the "learning" analogy, noting the industrial scale of AI training involves perfect digital copies at "superhuman speed and scale."
- The US Copyright Office has rejected the non-expressive use claim, stating it "rests on a faulty premise."

**Impact on Creative Industries:**
- A 2024 global study predicts €22 billion cumulative revenue loss for music and audiovisual creators by 2028 from AI.
- 86% of authors report decreased earnings from AI advances; 57% no longer view writing as a sustainable career.
- 58% of surveyed photographers have lost work to generative AI.
- Deezer reported 60,000 AI-generated tracks uploaded daily (39% of total uploads) by January 2026.

**Enforcement Barriers:**
- Rightsholders lack transparency on whether their works were used in training datasets.
- Most AI training occurs outside the UK, in jurisdictions with different copyright rules.
- Litigation costs are prohibitively expensive for individual creators.
- The UK AI sector contributed ~£12 billion to the economy in 2024, vs. £124 billion GVA from creative industries in 2023.

**Position:**
The report concludes that the case has not been made for introducing new exceptions for AI training. It recommends the Government should rule out copyright reform that would remove incentives to license works, and instead focus on strengthening licensing, transparency, and enforcement. The Government should publish a final decision within 12 months, prioritizing strong copyright protection and the long-term health of UK creative industries.

**Style Imitation Gap:**
The report identifies a gap in protection for AI-generated outputs "in the style of" an artist, as copyright protects specific expressions, not general style. This may require legislative change.
</summary>

Title: EU AI Act’s Opt-Out Trend May Limit Data Use for Training AI Models | Greenberg Traurig LLP
# EU AI Act’s Opt-Out Trend May Limit Data Use for Training AI Models. *With the introduction of the EU AI Act, companies that train AI models should be vigilant of which datasets they use. Certain copyright-protected works may no longer be available for use in training AI models.*. On the input side, a main concern is whether publicly available, copyright-protected works may be used to train AI models used by commercial companies. Compared to the organic way that humans gain knowledge, those who train AI models have more control over how and whether AI learns from data fed to it. ## Machine Learning under the EU AI Act. The EU AI Act, approved by the EU Council 21 May 2024, takes a first stab at answering this question. The EU AI Act contains a provision that equates AI/machine learning with “text-and-datamining” (TDM) under the EU Text and Data Mining Directive. Therefore, the TDM exception for machine learning can already be enforced in anticipation of the EU AI Act’s interpretation. While it is not yet clear how a legally valid opt-out request would be made, various organizations, such as the Dutch collecting society Pictoright (pictures) and the French collecting society Sacem (music), have drafted general reservation of rights statements, allowing creators to opt out of their data being used to train AI models. While no case law or other authoritative document exists to determine the sufficiency of such statements to trigger the opt-out criteria, the trend may intensify now that the EU AI Act has been adopted. Although the EU AI Act and its TDM exception have yet to become formally applicable, AI system providers and developers should consider implementing measures and configurations to avoid infringement claims by rightsholders. For copyright-protected content that may be used for TDM purposes, consider implementing technical and organizational limitations on the use of the content to ensure it is only used for training the AI model. **2. Fashion Design Creation Pre- and Post-AI:**
- Pre-AI: The fashion industry normalizes some degree of "copying" as "inspiration" or "flocking" to trends. Differentiation is a desirable feature alongside participation in trends.

**3. Copyright Originality:**
- Under EU law (Cofemel, Infopaq), works must be the "author's own intellectual creation" (AOIC), reflecting free and creative choices and the author's personality.
- UK law operates on a closed-list system (CDPA 1988), but fashion designs can qualify as "artistic works" or "works of artistic craftsmanship."
- Technical functionality cannot solely dictate the design; creative freedom must remain.
- The Ganni Buckle Ballerina case (Danish courts) affirmed that designs inspired by prior works can still meet originality if they reflect the designer's personal interpretation.
- AG Szpunar's Opinion in Mio/konektra (pending) confirms that the focus should be on expressive elements visible in the design, not merely the author's intentions or creative process.
- AI-assisted designs can potentially be original if designers exercise free and creative choices in prompts, modifications, and finalization.

**4. Infringement Analysis:**
- Gen-AI models with high generalization performance are less likely to produce infringing outputs.
- Poor generalization, overfitting, or fine-tuning on limited datasets increases the likelihood of outputs that closely mimic training data.
- Under EU InfoSoc Directive 2001/29/EC and UK CDPA 1988, the right of reproduction is central.
- The article argues that infringement cannot be simply attributed to AI tools due to technical underpinnings; even if infringing derivative outputs emerge, subsequent modification by a designer can "transform" them into new, non-infringing expressions.

# Summary: UK Government Consultation on Copyright and Artificial Intelligence

This is a UK Government consultation (December 2024) presented to Parliament by the Secretary of State for Science, Innovation and Technology, exploring reform of the copyright framework as it applies to AI training. The consultation ran from 17 December 2024 to 25 February 2025.

## Key Context

The UK government recognizes that the current copyright framework does not meet the needs of either the creative industries (worth £124.8 billion GVA annually) or the AI sector. The legal uncertainty means leading AI developers do not train models in the UK, harming both sectors.

## Three Core Objectives

1. **Control** – Right holders should control and be remunerated for use of their content by AI models
2. **Access** – AI developers should be able to lawfully access large volumes of content for training
3. **Transparency** – Greater transparency about works used to train AI models and their outputs

## Proposed Approach (Option 3 - Preferred)

The government is consulting on introducing a **text and data mining exception** that allows AI developers to train on copyright works where right holders have **not reserved their rights**, underpinned by transparency measures. This is similar to the EU's Article 4 approach under the Digital Single Market Copyright Directive.

Key features:
- Applies to data mining for any purpose, including commercial
- Only applies where the user has **lawful access** to works
- Right holders can **reserve rights** using machine-readable formats
- Would be underpinned by **transparency requirements** on AI developers
- Would come into operation when effective technical solutions are in place

## Other Options Considered

- **Option 0**: Do nothing – maintaining current legal uncertainty
- **Option 1**: Strengthen copyright requiring licensing in all cases – risk of making UK uncompetitive
- **Option 2**: Broad data mining exception without rights reservation – would not meet right holders' needs

## Additional Issues Covered

- **Technical standards** – Need for standardisation of rights reservation protocols (e.g., robots.txt, metadata)
- **Contracts and licensing** – Including collective licensing and concerns about creators' control
- **Labelling** – Clear labelling of AI outputs
- **Computer-generated works** – Potential reform of protections for purely AI-generated works
- **Digital Replicas (deepfakes)** – Evidence gathering on challenges posed by AI-generated replicas of voice, image, or likeness
- **Emerging issues** – Including synthetic data and AI systems generating content at inference

## Ministerial Position

The government states it "cannot allow" the current situation to continue, warning it "risks limiting investment, innovation, and growth in the AI sector, and in the wider economy" while "effectively preventing creative industries from exercising their rights."

URL: https://www.clearyiptechinsights.com/2023/04/us-copyright-office-guidance-on-ai-generated-works

SUMMARY:
<summary>
On March 16, 2023, the US Copyright Office (USCO) published guidance on the registration of works containing AI-generated content. The guidance reaffirms that copyright law requires "human authorship" and rejects extending copyright to works generated with AI beyond the user's control. The USCO's policy followed the case of *Zarya of the Dawn*, a graphic novel using Midjourney AI, where the original copyright was cancelled because AI-generated images were "not the product of human authorship."

Key principles from the guidance include:
- **Human authorship requirement**: An "author" must be human; mere influence over AI input/output is insufficient for copyright protection.
- **Manipulation of output**: Significant human editing of AI content may qualify for copyright, but only for the human-added elements, not the underlying AI-generated material.
- **Copyrightability of input**: Creative prompts may be copyrightable, but the material generated from such prompts is not automatically copyrightable.
- **Registration requirements**: Applicants must disclose AI-generated content, identify human authors, and disclaim non-de minimis AI-generated content. AI tools cannot be listed as authors.
- **Future guidance**: The USCO launched an agency-wide initiative and plans to seek public input on additional legal and policy topics, including use of copyrighted works in AI training.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
The United States Copyright Office (USCO) released its second report on AI and copyright on January 29, 2025, addressing the copyrightability of AI-generated materials. This is part of a three-report series, with the first report (July 2024) covering digital replicas and a third report expected later in 2025 on training AI models on copyrighted works, licensing, and liability.

**Key Positions Reiterated in the Report:**
- Human authorship is a bedrock requirement; works entirely generated by AI are not copyrightable.
- Mere prompt selection, even with detailed prompts, does not yield a copyrightable work (though this could change as technology evolves).
- Where works combine human and AI content, only human contributions are potentially copyrightable.
- Using AI as a tool to enhance human creativity (e.g., ideation, editing) does not render the entire work uncopyrightable.

**Four Categories of Human Contributions Analyzed:**
1. **AI to facilitate creative process** – Using AI for enhancement (e.g., scrubbing images) does not limit copyright protection.
2. **Use of prompts** – Prompts alone, even with multiple refinements, do not provide sufficient human control over expression. The Report analogizes this to someone describing a commissioned work to an author—they are not a joint author. The "sweat of the brow" argument is rejected.
3. **Expressive inputs** – If a human-generated work (e.g., a hand-drawn image) is perceptible in the AI output, the human can claim copyright in the perceptible portion, similar to derivative works. The Report distinguishes this from mere prompts.
4. **Modifying or arranging AI content** – Humans can select, arrange, or modify AI-generated material in sufficiently creative ways to warrant protection, subject to case-by-case determination.

**Additional Findings:**
- The USCO concluded no new *sui generis* law is needed; existing laws are adequate, and additional protection could undermine human creativity.
- Internationally, countries that have addressed the issue agree that copyright requires human authorship.
- The Report does not modify existing USCO positions. Creators using prompts alone should expect outputs to be uncopyrightable; only human-authored elements in mixed works may be protectable.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article by Addison Hichman compares how the U.S. and EU address copyright authorship for AI-generated works, focusing on recent developments through 2025.

**U.S. Approach:**
- The D.C. Court of Appeals in *Thaler v. Perlmutter* (March 18, 2025) reaffirmed that copyright requires human authorship, denying registration for Dr. Stephen Thaler's AI system's work (*A Recent Entrance to Paradise*). The court declined to address hybrid human-AI works.

It clarified that human modification/arrangement may qualify as authorship, and that generic prompts alone are insufficient. The USCO concluded existing law is flexible enough and no new legislation is needed.
- Protection extends only to human-authored portions in mixed works.

**EU Approach:**
- The EU requires works to reflect the "author's own intellectual creation" per CJEU jurisprudence (e.g., *Infopaq*, *Painer*), which cannot be satisfied without human input.
- The EU Artificial Intelligence Act (June 2024) classifies AI by risk and requires transparency about training data and copyright compliance for general-purpose AI models.
- The European Commission's *General-Purpose AI Code of Practice* (July 2025) supplements the AI Act with disclosure requirements.
- Directive 2019/790/EU does not define AI authorship, but AI-assisted works may qualify if a human maintains creative control. Fully autonomous AI outputs are excluded.

**Comparison:**
Both jurisdictions require human authorship. The U.S. takes a judicial/administrative approach focused on copyrightability under existing law, while the EU integrates copyright into a broader regulatory framework. Both recognize potential protection for AI-assisted works where humans exercise meaningful creative control, but the precise threshold of human input remains unsettled.
</summary>

--- SOURCE 1: Algorithmic Creativity: How Should the UK Copyright Regime Accommodate Autonomous AI-generated Works? – LSE Law Review Blog ---
URL: https://blog.lselawreview.com/2023/03/24/algorithmic-creativity-how-should-the-uk-copyright-regime-accommodate-autonomous-ai-generated-works

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This article by Emma Chew, published on the LSE Law Review Blog (24th March 2023), examines how UK copyright law should treat works generated by autonomous AI systems. It argues that AI-generated works fail the traditional human authorship requirement for originality under UK law, and that Section 9(3) of the Copyright, Designs and Patents Act (CDPA) 1988—which provides a legal fiction of authorship for computer-generated works—is ill-equipped to handle modern generative AI due to its vague language and outdated drafting. The article analyzes the case of Nova Productions v Mazooma Games, which identified the programmer as the author, but notes that with autonomous AI, multiple stakeholders (programmers, companies, data providers, users) are involved, creating ambiguity over who made the "necessary arrangements." From a policy perspective, the article argues that granting copyright to AI-generated works would over-reward developers (who already have sufficient incentives through software copyright, licensing, database rights, and trade secrets), stifle human creativity, and promote monopolistic practices. The article proposes that AI-generated works should immediately enter the public domain, which would eliminate legal uncertainties, foster innovation, ensure fair access, and protect the value of human creativity, all without significant loss of incentive to AI developers.
</summary>

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This blog post from Authors Alliance (authored by student intern Syn Ong) examines Section 9(3) of the UK's Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 (CDPA), which provides copyright protection for computer-generated works (CGWs) without a human author. The provision states that "the author shall be taken to be the person by whom the arrangements necessary for the creation of the work are undertaken." It was enacted in 1988 following lobbying from the software industry to protect investment in computer-generated outputs.

Key points:
- CGWs receive 50 years of copyright protection, and imputed "authors" receive no moral rights.
- Judicial interpretation has been remarkably sparse—only two notable cases. In *Nova Productions v Mazooma Games*, the court held a programmer was the author under Section 9(3). In *THJ Systems v Sheridan*, the Court of Appeal bypassed Section 9(3) entirely, finding traditional human authorship instead.
- Courts show a tendency to locate human authorship wherever possible, treating Section 9(3) as a fallback provision.
- The UK government and UKIPO have begun reassessing the provision, with a 2024 statement suggesting it might be repealed unless a strong case for retention is made.
- Contrast with the US: the US maintains a firm human authorship requirement (e.g., *Thaler v. Perlmutter*, *Zarya of the Dawn*).
- The author argues Section 9(3) is neither a legislative relic nor a ready-made solution, but an invitation to rethink authorship, originality, and protection as human and machine creativity become increasingly intertwined.

--- SOURCE 3: Ownership of AI-generated content in the UK ---
URL: https://www.aoshearman.com/en/insights/ownership-of-ai-generated-content-in-the-uk

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This webpage from A&O Shearman is a detailed legal article titled "Ownership of AI-generated content in the UK," published on August 20, 2024, authored by Neville Cordell and Beverley Potts. The article examines UK copyright protection for computer-generated works under s.9(3) of the UK Copyright, Designs and Patents Act 1988 (CDPA).

**Key points:**

- The UK is one of the few countries with a specific legal framework for copyright in computer-generated works. S.9(3) states that for LDMA (literary, dramatic, musical, artistic) works generated by computer with no human author, the author is deemed to be "the person by whom the arrangements necessary for the creation of the work are undertaken."

- There is an inherent inconsistency: LDMA works require originality (human intellectual creation), but s.9(3) applies to works with no human author. The article suggests a presumption that protection is granted to computer-generated works that would be original had they been created by a human.

- Three categories of potential authors are analyzed: (1) AI developers/programmers, who may have contributed through hyperparameters, training data selection, and fine-tuning but have less control over outputs in modern AI systems; (2) users, who provide prompts but may only contribute ideas rather than expression—the article compares UK, US, Chinese, and Czech approaches; and (3) joint authorship (unlikely in most AI contexts).

- The article contrasts UK positions with the US Copyright Office (which refused protection for Midjourney images, finding no human authorship), the Beijing Internet Court (which found copyright could exist if user prompts were sufficiently detailed and specific), and the Municipal Court in Prague (which denied protection for a simple DALL-E prompt).

- Under s.9(3), copyright lasts 50 years from creation (vs. 70 years post-mortem for human-authored works), and no moral rights arise. The only case expressly applying s.9(3) is Nova v Mazooma Games, where the programmer was deemed the author.

- The article concludes that the UK legislation would benefit from further clarity on the originality threshold for computer-generated works and who qualifies as the person making the "necessary arrangements."
</summary>

--- SOURCE 5: Copyright and Artificial Intelligence ---
URL: https://www.gov.uk/government/consultations/copyright-and-artificial-intelligence/copyright-and-artificial-intelligence

SUMMARY:
<summary>
# Summary: UK Government Consultation on Copyright and Artificial Intelligence

This is a UK Government consultation (December 2024) presented to Parliament by the Secretary of State for Science, Innovation and Technology, exploring reform of the copyright framework as it applies to AI training. The consultation ran from 17 December 2024 to 25 February 2025.

## Key Context

The UK government recognizes that the current copyright framework does not meet the needs of either the creative industries (worth £124.8 billion GVA annually) or the AI sector. The legal uncertainty means leading AI developers do not train models in the UK, harming both sectors.

## Three Core Objectives

1. **Control** – Right holders should control and be remunerated for use of their content by AI models
2. **Access** – AI developers should be able to lawfully access large volumes of content for training
3. **Transparency** – Greater transparency about works used to train AI models and their outputs

## Proposed Approach (Option 3 - Preferred)

The government is consulting on introducing a **text and data mining exception** that allows AI developers to train on copyright works where right holders have **not reserved their rights**, underpinned by transparency measures. This is similar to the EU's Article 4 approach under the Digital Single Market Copyright Directive.

Key features:
- Applies to data mining for any purpose, including commercial
- Only applies where the user has **lawful access** to works
- Right holders can **reserve rights** using machine-readable formats
- Would be underpinned by **transparency requirements** on AI developers
- Would come into operation when effective technical solutions are in place

## Other Options Considered

- **Option 0**: Do nothing – maintaining current legal uncertainty
- **Option 1**: Strengthen copyright requiring licensing in all cases – risk of making UK uncompetitive
- **Option 2**: Broad data mining exception without rights reservation – would not meet right holders' needs

## Additional Issues Covered

- **Technical standards** – Need for standardisation of rights reservation protocols (e.g., robots.txt, metadata)
- **Contracts and licensing** – Including collective licensing and concerns about creators' control
- **Labelling** – Clear labelling of AI outputs
- **Computer-generated works** – Potential reform of protections for purely AI-generated works
- **Digital Replicas (deepfakes)** – Evidence gathering on challenges posed by AI-generated replicas of voice, image, or likeness
- **Emerging issues** – Including synthetic data and AI systems generating content at inference

## Ministerial Position

The government states it "cannot allow" the current situation to continue, warning it "risks limiting investment, innovation, and growth in the AI sector, and in the wider economy" while "effectively preventing creative industries from exercising their rights."

**Copyright & IP Rights:** Japan applies existing legislation (Copyright Act) to generative AI. Under Article 30-4, using copyrighted works for AI training ("information analysis") is generally allowed unless it unreasonably prejudices the copyright owner's interests. At the output stage, copyright infringement requires both "reliance" on a pre-existing work and "similarity" of expression. AI-generated works may be copyrightable if a human user has creative intention and makes a creative contribution, using AI as a "tool." Works generated solely by AI are not copyrightable.

**Data Privacy:** The Act on the Protection of Personal Information (APPI) governs data privacy. Collection and use of personal data requires notification of purpose; consent is not generally needed if the purpose is announced. Inputting personal data into third-party generative AI systems risks violating APPI if the third party uses data for broader purposes. Provision of personal data to third parties generally requires consent, with an outsourcing exemption available. Cross-border transfers require consent unless the jurisdiction has adequate protections. The PPC (Personal Data Protection Commission) issued guidance in June 2023 with specific recommendations for OpenAI regarding sensitive personal data, but did not impose a blanket prohibition on generative AI use.

**Liability & Accountability:** Under the Civil Code, liability requires wilful misconduct or negligence. Japanese courts are unlikely to award large damages and do not award punitive damages. Service providers can mitigate risks through preventive measures (regular program reviews, showing information sources) and well-drafted terms of service with limitation of liability clauses (though gross negligence cannot be excluded, especially for consumers under the Consumer Protection Act).

**Regulatory Landscape:** Japan has not enacted specific AI legislation, preferring soft law approaches, similar to Singapore and the UK. The G7 Hiroshima AI Process (May 2023) is developing guiding principles for AI, with final principles expected by end of 2023. The regulatory landscape may evolve, and organizations are encouraged to monitor developments.

--- SOURCE 23: [PDF] COPYRIGHT PROTECTION OF FASHION DESIGNS CUSTOMIZED ... ---
URL: https://www.etd.ceu.edu/2021/mrsa_lana.pdf

SUMMARY:
<summary>
This LL.M. Capstone Thesis by Lana Mrša (Central European University, May 2021) examines copyright protection of fashion designs customized via apps in the EU and the US. The thesis is structured into three main chapters: (1) copyright protection of fashion designs generally; (2) copyright protection of app-customized fashion designs; and (3) protection by other IP rights (industrial designs/design patents and trademarks).

**Key Findings:**

**EU Copyright Protection:** Following the CJEU's Cofemel decision (2019), fashion designs are eligible for copyright protection if they meet two requirements: (1) originality (reflecting the author's own intellectual creation, i.e., freedom of choice and personality), and (2) expression in a precise and objective manner. National requirements of "artistic value" are contrary to EU law. The EU offers more expansive protection than the US.

**US Copyright Protection:** Fashion designs as useful articles are generally not copyrightable. Only design features (fabric designs, patterns, embellishments, etc.) may qualify if they pass the "separability test" established in Star Athletica v. Varsity Brands (2017): features must (1) be perceivable as a work of art separate from the useful article, and (2) qualify as protectable pictorial, graphic, or sculptural work on their own merits. The originality threshold is very low (minimal creative spark per Feist). Several legislative attempts (DPPA 2007, Innovative Design Protection Act 2012) failed to expand protection.

**Authorship of App-Customized Designs:** The designer and app-user are not joint authors. The designer is entitled to copyright over design features programmed into the app. The app-user enjoys copyright over the arrangement of those features. The programmer (executor) cannot be considered the author. In the EU, both could potentially meet the originality threshold. In the US, app-user protection is limited to original arrangements that result in new design features, not the garment in its entirety.

**Other IP Rights:** EU unregistered industrial design protection offers an adequate alternative due to optional registrability and short-term protection that balances innovation incentives. US design patents are less suitable due to challenging registration requirements. Trademark protection is only viable for highly distinctive designs.

**Policy Analysis:** The thesis argues that more extensive EU-type protection does not hinder innovation but incentivizes it, particularly for small and unestablished designers vulnerable to misappropriation by larger fashion houses. The "piracy paradox" theory (Raustiala & Sprigman) is criticized for not addressing technology-facilitated rapid copying and its disproportionate harm to smaller designers.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"The CJEU decided that products of utilitarian and aesthetic purpose such as fashion designs were eligible for copyright protection if fulfilling the requirements set by Infopaq and Levola Hengelo. Consequently, the only requirements for fashion designs to enjoy copyright protection in accordance with EU law were the originality requirement and an expression in a precise and objective manner.", "The US Supreme Court confirmed that copyright protection could not extend to the 'shape, cut, and physical dimensions' of the fashion item, but features thereof were copyrightable upon fulfillment of two requirements: the features (1) can be perceived as a two- or three-dimensional work of art separate from the useful article, and (2) would qualify as a protectable pictorial, graphic, or sculptural work—either on its own or fixed in some other tangible medium of expression—if it were imagined separately from the useful article into which it is incorporated.", "I would argue that both designers and app-users could be considered as authors entitled to copyright protection; however, the objects thereof would not be the same. While the designers are entitled to copyright over the design features, the app-users enjoy copyright protection of the arrangement of design features, provided that the design features and their arrangement fulfilled other copyrightability criteria.", "I will argue that the comparison of the broader European protection and narrower US protection and the reactions of designers and scholars thereto show that an extensive protection does not hinder innovation, but in fact serves as an incentive to create, particularly in the case of small fashion houses and unestablished designers, which represent a significant driving force for innovation, but lack the financial means, motivation or the manpower to endure frequent design misappropriations.", "I would argue that EU industrial design protection could be considered as an adequate alternative thereto, particularly due to its optional registrability and the lack of necessity to prove the validity of the industrial designs in litigation, with the short-term protection of unregistered industrial design rights striking the best balance between providing protection and incentivizing innovation in the most common case of seasonal and trend-dependent fashion designs."

URL: https://www.quinnemanuel.com/the-firm/publications/noted-with-interest-copyrightability-of-ai-generated-content-in-china-and-the-us

SUMMARY:
<summary>
# Summary: Copyrightability of AI-Generated Content in China and the US

This article compares the evolving legal treatment of AI-generated content copyright in China and the United States, highlighting a convergence in principles despite persistent differences in application.

## Key Developments in China

- **Beijing Internet Court (Nov 27, 2023)**: Recognized copyright in AI-generated images created with Stable Diffusion. The court found that the plaintiff's selection of 150+ prompts, arrangement of their order, and adjustment of parameters constituted sufficient "intellectual investment" reflecting "personalized expression," not merely "mechanical intellectual achievements."

- **Zhangjiagang People's Court (March 19, 2025)**: Dismissed a copyright suit against defendants who used Midjourney to recreate designs based on publicly shared prompts. The court distinguished between content produced with "original human intellectual" input (potentially protectable) and content "mainly autogenerated by AI with minimal human contribution" (not protectable).

## Key Developments in the United States

**2023 USCO Guidance**: Held that "authorship" requires "human authorship" and that AI-generated material must be disclosed if more than de minimis.

**Notable USCO decisions**:
- *Thaler v. Perlmutter* (Feb/Aug 2023): Rejected copyright for AI-autonomously generated work lacking "traditional human authorship."
- *Zarya of the Dawn* (Feb 2023): Rejected Midjourney images due to "significant distance" between user input and output.
- *Rose Enigma* (Mar 2023): Granted partial protection for hand-created elements only.
- **A Single Piece of American Cheese (Jan 30, 2025)**: First-time USCO grant of copyright protection to an AI image, using "inpainting" technique where the artist manually selected and substantially modified parts of the work.

**2025 USCO Report (Jan 29, 2025)**—Key findings:
- **Assistive uses**: AI as a tool enhancing human expression does not limit copyright protection.
- **Prompts alone**: "Do not provide sufficient human control to make users of an AI system the authors of the output" — even with highly detailed or repeatedly revised prompts.
- **Expressive inputs**: If a human's original creative work remains perceptible in the AI output, the human can claim copyright in that perceptible portion.
- **Modifying/Arranging**: Human authorship may be added when AI is used as an intermediate step and the human "select[s] or arrange[s] AI-generated material in a sufficiently creative way."

## Comparison

The 2025 USCO Report brings US law closer to the Chinese approach, recognizing that AI can be a tool for human creativity. However, a key divergence remains: Chinese courts (e.g., the 2023 BIC case) have found that repeatedly adjusting prompts and parameters can lead to copyright, whereas the USCO still concludes that "prompts alone do not provide sufficient human control" for authorship.
</summary>

<key_excerpts>
"creativity is expressed through the use of AI systems, it continues to enjoy protection" — USCO, January 2025 Report, "prompts alone do not provide sufficient human control to make users of an AI system the authors of the output" — 2025 USCO Report at 18, "The BIC found that the resultant images were thus not just 'mechanical intellectual achievements' but rather were independently completed by the author and reflected the author's personalized expression", "The court differentiated content produced by a user exercising their 'original human intellectual' input in the creation process with the assistance of AI as a tool with content mainly autogenerated by AI with minimal human contribution", "Even as courts and agencies on both sides of the Pacific begin to align on the basic concept that some AI-generated content qualifies for copyright protection, questions remain as to how much input is required"
